additional_notes: Used for exact percentages (“cem por cento” is also common in speech) and, very often, to show strong agreement or certainty (“I’m totally with you”). In Brazilian Portuguese you may also see “100%” or the informal variant “cem por cento”.
target_language_example: Eu concordo 100 por cento com você.
native_language_example: I agree with you 100 percent.

additional_notes: Used mainly in grammar contexts. It’s an abbreviation of "primeira pessoa" and refers to verb forms and pronouns that talk from the speaker’s point of view (e.g., "eu" = I, "nós" = we). You’ll often see it in explanations like "verbo na 1ª pessoa do singular" (I-form) or "na 1ª pessoa do plural" (we-form).
target_language_example: Conjuga o verbo na 1ª pessoa do singular: eu falo.
native_language_example: Conjugate the verb in the first person singular: I speak.

additional_notes: A geographic region/continent name. Usually capitalized in Portuguese. Often used after the preposition "na" (em + a) to mean "in South America": "na América do Sul".
target_language_example: Eu moro na América do Sul.
native_language_example: I live in South America.

additional_notes: A proper noun used for the beverage/brand. In Portugal and Brazil you’ll also hear the informal short form “coca”. Often used with “uma” when ordering ("uma Coca-Cola, por favor").
target_language_example: Queria uma Coca-Cola, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a Coca-Cola, please.

meaning: World Cup (usually the FIFA soccer World Cup).
additional_notes: A fixed phrase meaning “World Cup.” In Portuguese it most often refers to the FIFA Men’s World Cup, but it can also refer to other World Cups depending on context (e.g., “Copa do Mundo de Rugby”). Often used with the verb “assistir” (to watch) or “torcer” (to root for).
target_language_example: Você vai assistir à Copa do Mundo este ano?
native_language_example: Are you going to watch the World Cup this year?

additional_notes: Used to express regret, guilt, or that you feel you might be doing/saying something wrong (often before/after a critical, rude, or tempting comment). It can be serious (moral/religious sense) or used more lightly for emphasis. Literally: “God” + “forgive me” (subjunctive: perdoe).
target_language_example: Deus me perdoe, mas eu não aguento mais essa conversa.
native_language_example: God forgive me, but I can’t stand this conversation anymore.

meaning: “God knows” (meaning: I don’t know / nobody knows / it’s uncertain).
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or that the answer is unknown: “Deus sabe quando/como/onde...” It can also emphasize that only God knows the real truth (“Só Deus sabe”). It’s common in everyday speech; the tone depends on context and can be neutral, resigned, or dramatic.
target_language_example: Deus sabe quando ele vai voltar.
native_language_example: God knows when he’ll come back.

additional_notes: Common well-wish said after someone sneezes, or to express kindness, gratitude, or good wishes. Literally “God” + “you” + “bless” (subjunctive). You may also hear “Deus lhe abençoe” (more formal) or “Deus te abençoe!” with emphasis.
target_language_example: —Obrigado por me ajudar. —Deus te abençoe.
native_language_example: —Thanks for helping me. —God bless you.

additional_notes: Proper name for the country; commonly shortened to "os EUA" (plural) in writing and speech. Often used with plural agreement because it refers to "states" (e.g., "Os Estados Unidos são..." / "nos Estados Unidos").
target_language_example: Eu moro nos Estados Unidos.
native_language_example: I live in the United States.

meaning: Great Britain (the island containing England, Scotland, and Wales).
additional_notes: A geographic term, not the same as the United Kingdom (Reino Unido), which also includes Northern Ireland. Often appears in formal contexts (news, history, geography) and in the phrase “Grã-Bretanha e Irlanda do Norte” (as part of the full name of the UK).
target_language_example: A Grã-Bretanha é uma ilha que inclui a Inglaterra, a Escócia e o País de Gales.
native_language_example: Great Britain is an island that includes England, Scotland, and Wales.

additional_notes: Proper place name used the same in Portuguese. Commonly used with the preposition “em” (in/at): “em Hong Kong”. It’s typically written without an article (not *o/a* Hong Kong).
target_language_example: Eu moro em Hong Kong há dois anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in Hong Kong for two years.

additional_notes: Used as a religious proper name (in Christianity). It can also be used as an exclamation to show shock, frustration, or emphasis; that use can be considered impolite/offensive in some contexts, especially around religious people, so be cautious.
target_language_example: Jesus Cristo, eu esqueci a carteira em casa!
native_language_example: Jesus Christ, I forgot my wallet at home!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the international sports event held every four years (summer and winter editions). Often appears with the definite article: "os Jogos Olímpicos". You may also see "Olimpíadas" in Brazil (common in everyday speech), but "Jogos Olímpicos" is the official name.
target_language_example: Você vai assistir aos Jogos Olímpicos este ano?
native_language_example: Are you going to watch the Olympic Games this year?

meaning: Las Vegas (a city in Nevada, USA).
additional_notes: Used as a proper noun (place name). In Portuguese you generally keep the English name and pronunciation, and you don’t use an article (you say "em Las Vegas", not *"na Las Vegas"*). Common in travel contexts.
target_language_example: Vamos passar o fim de semana em Las Vegas.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend the weekend in Las Vegas.

meaning: Los Angeles (a city in California, USA).
additional_notes: A proper noun (place name). In Portuguese it’s usually kept as “Los Angeles,” though you may also see “Los Angeles, na Califórnia” (“Los Angeles, in California”). Used with the preposition “em” (“in”): “em Los Angeles.”
target_language_example: Moro em Los Angeles há dois anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in Los Angeles for two years.

meaning: “Our Lady” (the Virgin Mary); also an exclamation like “Oh my God!”
additional_notes: Literally means “Our Lady” and is used as a respectful Catholic title for the Virgin Mary (often in names of churches, festivals, or prayers). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese it’s also a common exclamation of surprise, shock, or frustration, similar to “Oh my God!”; it may be shortened to “Nossa!” or “Nossa senhora!” (less formal, but not a swear).
target_language_example: Nossa Senhora! Eu esqueci minha carteira em casa.
native_language_example: Oh my God! I forgot my wallet at home.

meaning: New York (the U.S. state or the city).
additional_notes: Used for both the city (New York City) and the state of New York; context usually makes it clear. In Portuguese, place names are often preceded by a preposition/article (e.g., "em Nova Iorque" = "in New York").
target_language_example: Moro em Nova Iorque há dois anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in New York for two years.

meaning: New York (the U.S. state or New York City, depending on context).
additional_notes: A proper name used for both the state and the city; if you mean the city specifically, you can also say "a cidade de Nova York" or "Nova York (NYC)". Often used with "em" (in/to): "em Nova York".
target_language_example: Vou viajar para Nova York na próxima semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel to New York next week.

additional_notes: The Brazilian Portuguese name for Santa Claus, used especially around Christmas. Often written with capital letters. In Portugal, you may also hear "Pai Natal."
target_language_example: As crianças escreveram uma carta para o Papai Noel.
native_language_example: The children wrote a letter to Santa Claus.

additional_notes: Proper noun used for the country: the UK (United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland). It’s typically used with the definite article: "o Reino Unido". In Portuguese, "Grã-Bretanha" refers to the island (Great Britain), which is not exactly the same as "Reino Unido".
target_language_example: Eu moro no Reino Unido, mas viajo muito para a Europa.
native_language_example: I live in the United Kingdom, but I travel a lot to Europe.

meaning: Rio de Janeiro (a city and state in Brazil).
additional_notes: Proper name. In everyday use, "Rio" often refers to the city. "O Rio de Janeiro" can refer to the state, while "a cidade do Rio de Janeiro" specifies the city. Often shortened in writing as "RJ" (especially for the state).
target_language_example: Eu moro no Rio de Janeiro, mas trabalho em Niterói.
native_language_example: I live in Rio de Janeiro, but I work in Niterói.

meaning: Abbreviation for “São Paulo” (the city or the state).
additional_notes: Common in addresses, headlines, signs, and official writing where abbreviations are used. It can refer to the city of São Paulo or the state of São Paulo, depending on context. In English, it’s usually kept as “São Paulo” (not translated as “St. Paul”).
target_language_example: Moro em S. Paulo.
native_language_example: I live in São Paulo.

meaning: Saint Francis; also the city of San Francisco.
additional_notes: Often refers to Saint Francis of Assisi in religious contexts ("São Francisco de Assis"). In everyday conversation, "São Francisco" can also mean the U.S. city San Francisco, especially when talking about travel, work, or geography; people may also just say "San Francisco" when referring to the city. Capitalization is fixed because it’s a proper name.
target_language_example: Eu morei em São Francisco por dois anos.
native_language_example: I lived in San Francisco for two years.

additional_notes: A proper name used for both a Brazilian state and its capital city (the largest city in Brazil). In speech and writing, context usually makes it clear which one is meant; you can specify "a cidade de São Paulo" (the city) or "o estado de São Paulo" (the state). Often abbreviated as "SP" in addresses and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Eu moro em São Paulo, mas trabalho em Campinas.
native_language_example: I live in São Paulo, but I work in Campinas.

additional_notes: Used as a proper name for our galaxy. In Portuguese it’s normally written with capitals: “a Via Láctea.” You’ll often see it in astronomy contexts, or when talking about the night sky.
target_language_example: Numa noite sem nuvens, dá para ver a Via Láctea a olho nu.
native_language_example: On a cloudless night, you can see the Milky Way with the naked eye.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is on a means of transport (bus, train, plane, ship) or has boarded it. Common in travel announcements and instructions. Can also be used more figuratively in Portuguese, but beginners will mostly see it in the literal travel sense.
target_language_example: Todos a bordo, por favor — o trem vai partir.
native_language_example: Everyone on board, please — the train is about to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is traveling toward a place or that something is in progress toward completion. Often followed by a destination with "para" (e.g., "a caminho para o trabalho") or used on its own ("Estou a caminho"). Also common in the expression "a caminho de" + place ("a caminho de casa").
target_language_example: Estou a caminho de casa.
native_language_example: I'm on my way home.

meaning: on the way to; heading to.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is traveling toward a destination. Often followed by a place, event, or person (e.g., a caminho de casa / do trabalho / do aeroporto). You can also use it more generally to mean “on the path to” a goal or state (e.g., a caminho da recuperação = on the road to recovery).
target_language_example: Estou a caminho do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m on my way to work.

additional_notes: Used in restaurants or cafés to ask for the bill. In Brazil, you can also say “a conta, por gentileza.” In Portugal, it’s also common to say “a conta, se faz favor.”
target_language_example: Garçom, a conta, por favor.
native_language_example: Waiter, the check, please.

additional_notes: Common in expressions like “à distância” (meaning “from afar / remotely”). Often used with learning/work/communication: “trabalho/estudo/curso/aulas à distância” = remote work/study/online course/classes. Also used to describe physical separation: “ver de longe / observar à distância” (to watch from a distance). In Brazil you may also see “EAD” (Educação a Distância) for distance learning.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho à distância e falo com a equipe por videochamada.
native_language_example: I work remotely and talk to the team by video call.

additional_notes: Used to express support or agreement, often with "de" + a noun/idea: "a favor de" (in favor of). Common in voting/discussion contexts: "Sou a favor" (I’m in favor) and "votar a favor" (to vote in favor). Contrast with "contra" (against).
target_language_example: Sou a favor de reduzir o barulho à noite.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of reducing noise at night.

additional_notes: Used to express support/opinion in favor of something, often in debates or votes: “sou a favor de…” (I’m in favor of…). You can also use it to mean “for someone” in the sense of “to benefit/advantage”: “Isso é a favor de você” (That’s in your favor). Often contrasted with “contra” (against).
target_language_example: Eu sou a favor de mais parques na cidade.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of more parks in the city.

meaning: “in order (to)” (usually in **a fim de**); also “keen/eager; feel like” (in **estar a fim de**).
additional_notes: Most common as **a fim de + infinitive** = “in order to”: *a fim de aprender* (“in order to learn”). It can also appear with **estar/ficar a fim de** (especially in Brazil) meaning “to feel like / be up for / be interested in,” which is more informal: *Estou a fim de sair* (“I feel like going out”).
target_language_example: Eu estou a fim de sair hoje.
native_language_example: I feel like going out today.

meaning: in order to; so as to.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose/goal, usually followed by an infinitive: “a fim de + infinitive” (e.g., “a fim de estudar”). It’s fairly formal and common in writing; in everyday speech, people often use “para” instead. Not to be confused with “a fim” meaning “into (someone)”/interested (informal), which is a different expression.
target_language_example: Cheguei cedo a fim de terminar o trabalho antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I arrived early in order to finish the work before the meeting.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazil as an informal alternative to “nós” (“we”). Although it refers to “we,” it usually takes 3rd-person singular verb forms: “a gente vai” (not “vamos”). It can also mean “people” in general depending on context.
target_language_example: A gente vai ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: We’re going to the movies today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that prevents something from happening. It’s followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese (present or imperfect), e.g., "a menos que eu tenha" / "a menos que eu tivesse".
target_language_example: Vou amanhã, a menos que chova.
native_language_example: I’ll go tomorrow, unless it rains.

additional_notes: Very common connector. Often used as **a não ser que** + subjunctive to mean “unless” introducing an exception/condition: *A não ser que chova...* (“Unless it rains...” ). Can also mean “except for” before a noun/pronoun: *Não conheço ninguém, a não ser a Ana.* (“I don’t know anyone except Ana.”).
target_language_example: A não ser que você esteja doente, venha amanhã.
native_language_example: Unless you are sick, come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used before a clause in the subjunctive to express an exception: something will happen except if another thing happens. Common with future plans and conditions. Often interchangeable with “a menos que” (“unless”), and typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “seja”, “tenha”, “possa”).
target_language_example: Vou amanhã, a não ser que chova.
native_language_example: I’ll go tomorrow, unless it rains.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "estar/ficar" and frequently with "de": "estar/ficar a par de (algo)" = to be/stay informed about something. Common in more formal or written Portuguese. Don’t confuse "a par" with English "apart".
target_language_example: Quero ficar a par das novidades.
native_language_example: I want to stay up to date with the news.

meaning: “from” (starting at/in; beginning from a point in time, place, number, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a starting point in time (from Monday on), place (from Lisbon), or quantity/price (starting at $10). Very common in signs and schedules. Often followed by an article or a specific reference: “a partir de hoje” (from today), “a partir das 9h” (from 9 a.m.), “a partir do centro” (from the center).
target_language_example: A partir de amanhã, a loja abre às 9h.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, the store opens at 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very close to happening, often with an infinitive verb: "a ponto de + infinitivo". It can describe an action that almost happens (sometimes but not always with a negative outcome). Similar to "prestes a". Example patterns: "Estou a ponto de sair" (I’m about to leave), "Ele estava a ponto de chorar" (He was about to cry).
target_language_example: Eu estava a ponto de sair quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

additional_notes: Common in descriptions or instructions (e.g., keep/leave the door shut). With verbs you’ll often see: “com a porta fechada” (with the door closed) or “deixe/mantenha a porta fechada” (leave/keep the door closed). “Fechada” agrees with the feminine noun “porta”.
target_language_example: Por favor, deixe a porta fechada.
native_language_example: Please leave the door closed.

meaning: ready; on standby; at one’s post.
additional_notes: Often used to say someone is ready to start or is standing by (especially in work, service, or emergency contexts). Common with verbs like “estar/ficar”: “Estou a postos” = “I’m ready/standing by.” It can also imply being in position or on duty.
target_language_example: Se precisar de ajuda, estou a postos.
native_language_example: If you need help, I’m ready / I’m standing by.

additional_notes: Commonly used to describe an initial situation or first impression that may change later (similar to “at first”). It can also mean “in principle” (based on the theory/rules), especially in more formal contexts. Often contrasted with later information: “A princípio..., mas depois...”.
target_language_example: A princípio eu não queria ir, mas depois mudei de ideia.
native_language_example: At first I didn’t want to go, but then I changed my mind.

meaning: by the way; on purpose (depending on context).
additional_notes: Has two common meanings. (1) As a discourse marker, it means “by the way” to introduce a new topic or add a side comment: “A propósito, …”. (2) It can mean “on purpose / intentionally,” often with verbs like “fazer” (to do) or “de propósito” as a stronger variant. Context and placement in the sentence usually make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: A propósito, você já pagou a conta?
native_language_example: By the way, have you already paid the bill?

additional_notes: Used to say you go somewhere by walking, or that something is within walking distance. Common after verbs like “ir”/“chegar” (Ir a pé, Chegar a pé) and in phrases like “estar a pé” (to be without a vehicle/stranded without transportation).
target_language_example: Vou a pé porque é perto.
native_language_example: I’m going on foot because it’s close.

additional_notes: A common formal/neutral prepositional phrase used to introduce the topic of a message, question, email, etc. Often interchangeable with "sobre" or "acerca de" ("a respeito de" can sound a bit more formal). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., "a respeito disso").
target_language_example: Tenho uma pergunta a respeito do seu pedido.
native_language_example: I have a question regarding your order.

meaning: namely; that is to say; as follows.
additional_notes: Used in formal or written Portuguese to introduce an explanation or a list of items that clarify what was just mentioned. Common after a colon or comma (often like “namely” in English). Not used much in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Precisamos de três documentos, a saber: o passaporte, o comprovante de residência e uma foto.
native_language_example: We need three documents, namely: the passport, proof of address, and a photo.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like estar/ficar/pôr (estar a salvo = to be safe; ficar a salvo = to become safe; pôr a salvo = to put someone/something in a safe place). Common in news and emergencies. Often used with em: estar a salvo em casa (safe at home).
target_language_example: Depois do incêndio, todos estão a salvo.
native_language_example: After the fire, everyone is safe.

additional_notes: Common in instructions and announcements meaning “next” or “coming up” (e.g., on a schedule, in a list). It can also mean “right after/then” in time: “A seguir, vamos…” = “Next/then, we’re going to…”. In “seguir a alguém/alguma coisa,” seguir means “to follow,” so “a seguir” can imply “to follow (right after).”
target_language_example: A seguir, vamos falar sobre o tempo.
native_language_example: Next, we’re going to talk about the weather.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true or meant genuinely (not as a joke). It can describe how someone is doing something ("falar a sério" = to speak seriously) or be used on its own as a reaction ("A sério?" = Really?). Often contrasts with "a brincar" (joking).
target_language_example: A sério? Eu pensei que era a brincar.
native_language_example: Really? I thought you were joking.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is determined to do something even if it requires sacrifice, effort, or negative consequences. Common with verbs like "evitar" (avoid), "conseguir" (achieve), "manter" (keep), and "impedir" (prevent).
target_language_example: Ele quer vencer a todo custo.
native_language_example: He wants to win at all costs.

meaning: 'let's see' / 'we'll see' (used to think, check, or wait for a result).
additional_notes: Very common in conversation. Used when you’re about to check something or consider an option ("A ver..." = "Let me see..."). Also used to express uncertainty about the future ("Vamos a ver" = "We’ll see"). In European Portuguese it’s often pronounced like "avér" in fast speech. Not the same as "haver" (to exist/there to be).
target_language_example: A ver... onde é que pus as chaves?
native_language_example: Let me see... where did I put the keys?

additional_notes: A preposition used for physical position (something is under/below something else) and for quantities/limits (less than a number). Often used with measurements, prices, temperatures, age limits, and floors in a building. Common contrasts: "acima de" (above/more than), "embaixo de" (under, more physical/colloquial), and "inferior a" (more formal for comparisons).
target_language_example: A temperatura ficou abaixo de 0°C e o preço está abaixo de 20 euros.
native_language_example: The temperature stayed below 0°C and the price is under 20 euros.

additional_notes: Used in medical and formal contexts to refer to the natural loss of a pregnancy (not an induced abortion). You may also hear the more common everyday term "perda gestacional" (pregnancy loss) in sensitive conversations.
target_language_example: Ela teve um aborto espontâneo no primeiro trimestre.
native_language_example: She had a miscarriage in the first trimester.

meaning: to make way; to clear a path; (figurative) to pave the way.
additional_notes: Used literally for physically creating space or a passage (people moving aside, clearing obstacles), and figuratively for creating opportunities or enabling progress. Common in requests/commands like “Abra caminho!” (Make way!).
target_language_example: A polícia abriu caminho para a ambulância passar.
native_language_example: The police made way for the ambulance to pass.

additional_notes: Used when you renounce something (a right, an advantage, time, money, a plan) often to achieve something else or to help someone. Very common pattern: "abrir mão de" + noun/infinitive (e.g., "abrir mão de um direito", "abrir mão de sair cedo"). Not usually the physical meaning of "open a hand".
target_language_example: Eu não vou abrir mão das minhas férias este ano.
native_language_example: I’m not going to give up my vacation this year.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something happened very recently: "acabar de" + infinitive. Conjugate only "acabar" (e.g., "acabo de", "acabou de", "acabámos/acabamos de"). In the negative, it means "to not have ... yet" (e.g., "Ainda não acabei de comer" = "I haven’t finished eating yet"). In Brazil, the recent-past meaning is very common; in Portugal it’s also used, alongside "ter acabado de".
target_language_example: Acabei de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: Used to agree, but with some uncertainty. Literally “I think that yes” (acho = “I think”, que = “that”, sim = “yes”). Common in casual conversation; you can also soften it further with “acho que sim, mas…” (“I think so, but…”).
target_language_example: —Você vem amanhã? —Acho que sim.
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —I think so.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position (physically higher than) and also quantities/limits (greater than). Common in measurements and comparisons: "acima de 18 anos" (over 18), "acima de 30°C" (above 30°C). Often contrasts with "abaixo de" (below/under).
target_language_example: O preço ficou acima de 100 euros.
native_language_example: The price ended up over 100 euros.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has the highest priority or is the most important consideration. Common in speech and writing, often followed by a value or principle (e.g., "acima de tudo, respeito"). It can also introduce what matters most after listing other things.
target_language_example: Quero que você seja feliz, acima de tudo.
native_language_example: I want you to be happy, above all.

meaning: after all; in the end; when you think about it.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a final conclusion, correction, or reason—often after reconsidering something. Common in speech and writing. It can sound like “anyway/ultimately,” or “after all (considering everything).”
target_language_example: Eu não vou sair hoje; afinal de contas, estou muito cansado.
native_language_example: I’m not going out today; after all, I’m very tired.

meaning: just now; a short time ago.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened very recently (minutes ago). It’s stronger/more immediate than "há pouco" on its own and close in meaning to "há um instante". Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu falei com ela agora há pouco.
native_language_example: I spoke with her just now.

meaning: “Now it’s done / it’s over now” (often: “too late now”).
additional_notes: Used when something can’t be changed anymore and you’re accepting the situation (resigned or matter-of-fact). Common in Brazilian Portuguese in everyday speech. It can refer to a mistake, a missed chance, or something that has already happened and can’t be undone.
target_language_example: Eu esqueci de enviar o e-mail, mas agora já foi — vou mandar amanhã cedo.
native_language_example: I forgot to send the email, but it’s too late now — I’ll send it early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize immediacy. With the present tense it often means “right now” (Eu preciso falar com você agora mesmo. = I need to talk to you right now). Depending on context it can also mean “just now / a moment ago” (Ele saiu agora mesmo. = He left just now).
target_language_example: Estou ocupado agora mesmo, mas posso falar daqui a pouco.
native_language_example: I’m busy right now, but I can talk in a little while.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a consequence or next step after a change or new information. Often followed by a verb (usually in the present or past) and can start a sentence or come after a pause.
target_language_example: Agora que você chegou, podemos começar.
native_language_example: Now that you’ve arrived, we can start.

additional_notes: Used for a business that plans and sells trips (flights, hotels, packages, tours). You’ll often hear it in phrases like “ir a uma agência de viagens” (go to a travel agency) or “trabalhar numa agência de viagens” (work at a travel agency).
target_language_example: Vou à agência de viagens para comprar as passagens e reservar o hotel.
native_language_example: I’m going to the travel agency to buy the tickets and book the hotel.

additional_notes: Used when you realize, remember, or acknowledge something someone just said. It can sound a bit like “I see” or “right” in English. Intonation matters: it can be neutral/agreeing, or lightly sarcastic depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ah, sim, agora entendi o que você quis dizer.
native_language_example: Oh, yes—now I understand what you meant.

meaning: “Oh, OK / alright.” (showing you understand or accept what was said)
additional_notes: Very common in casual Brazilian Portuguese. Used as a quick acknowledgment after someone explains something (“I see,” “got it,” “right”). Intonation matters: it can sound neutral/agreeing, mildly surprised, or even a bit skeptical/annoyed depending on tone and context. Often written with a comma and sometimes with emphasis: “Ah, tá.” / “Ah tá.”
target_language_example:
—O ônibus vai atrasar uns 20 minutos.
—Ah, tá.
native_language_example:
—The bus is going to be about 20 minutes late.
—Oh, OK.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to show disbelief, skepticism, or mild annoyance at what someone just said. Tone depends on context and intonation; it can sound teasing or rude. Common in Brazilian Portuguese. Not usually a literal “go.”
target_language_example: —Eu ganhei na loteria. —Ah, vá!
native_language_example: “I won the lottery.” “Yeah, right!”

meaning: “Oh, really?” / “Oh, is that so?” (showing realization or mild surprise).
additional_notes: Common conversational reaction to new information. Intonation matters: said neutrally, it can simply mean “I see / got it”; said with a skeptical tone, it can imply doubt (“Oh, yeah?”). Often written with a comma and sometimes repeated for emphasis (e.g., “Ah, é?”).
target_language_example: —Eu vou me mudar amanhã. —Ah, é? Não sabia.
native_language_example: —I’m moving tomorrow. —Oh, really? I didn’t know.

additional_notes: Used to show contrast: something is true or happens despite what was just said. Often comes at the start of a sentence ("Ainda assim, ..."), but can also appear mid-sentence. Close in meaning to "mesmo assim" and "ainda assim" is slightly more formal.
target_language_example: Estava cansado, mas ainda assim foi trabalhar.
native_language_example: He was tired, but even so he went to work.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or that something turned out well. Commonly followed by “que” + a clause: “Ainda bem que…” (“Good thing that…”). It can also stand alone as a reaction: “—Perdi o ônibus.” “—Ainda bem!” (“—I missed the bus.” “—Good!” / “Thank goodness!”), but context determines whether it sounds like relief or simply “good!”.
target_language_example: Ainda bem que você chegou a tempo.
native_language_example: Thank goodness you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison or statement, often after something already mentioned: “more than that / to an even greater degree.” Common patterns: (1) With comparisons: “ainda mais + adjective/adverb” (e.g., ainda mais caro = even more expensive). (2) To strengthen a point: “Ainda mais que…” / “Ainda mais quando…” (“All the more since/when…”). Can also be used as a short add-on meaning “even more so.”
target_language_example: Depois do aumento, a conta ficou ainda mais cara.
native_language_example: After the increase, the bill got even more expensive.

meaning: “on top of that,” “to make matters worse,” or “besides that.”
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point, often emphasizing that the situation is even worse or more annoying than before (similar to “and what’s more…”). It can also be neutral, meaning “besides/plus.” Common in everyday speech; usually followed by another clause.
target_language_example: Perdi o autocarro e, ainda por cima, começou a chover.
native_language_example: I missed the bus and, on top of that, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants or needs an additional item or service, especially in shops, restaurants, or at the end of a request. It can also mean an extra/additional thing in general. In questions, it’s often said as “Mais alguma coisa?” or “Algo mais?”
target_language_example: Quer algo mais?
native_language_example: Would you like anything else?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you hope, plan, or expect will happen in the future, but without saying when exactly. Often appears with the future tense (vou/iremos…) or expressions of desire (quero/esperto…). It can also mean “one day” in a more vague sense, but it usually points to the future rather than the past.
target_language_example: Algum dia eu vou visitar Portugal.
native_language_example: Someday I’m going to visit Portugal.

additional_notes: An indefinite expression used when you don’t specify what it is. In statements it usually means “something” (Quero alguma coisa para beber. = I want something to drink). In questions and with negatives it often corresponds to “anything” (Você quer alguma coisa? = Do you want anything? / Não vi alguma coisa. = I didn’t see anything).
target_language_example: Você quer alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Do you want anything?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the person you feel you were “meant” to be with. You’ll also see it without the accent in Brazil (“alma gemea”) in informal writing, but the standard spelling is “alma gêmea”. Often used with “minha”/“sua”: “minha alma gêmea” = “my soulmate”.
target_language_example: Eu acho que ela é a minha alma gêmea.
native_language_example: I think she is my soulmate.

additional_notes: A noun for an audio output device. Common in electronics and events (e.g., a phone’s speaker, a PA system). Plural: alto-falantes. Often used with "o/um" (masculine): "o alto-falante".
target_language_example: O alto-falante do meu celular não está funcionando.
native_language_example: My phone’s speaker isn’t working.

meaning: ups and downs; highs and lows.
additional_notes: Used to talk about good and bad moments in life, a relationship, a job, or a situation. Very common in expressions like "ter altos e baixos" (to have ups and downs).
target_language_example: Todo relacionamento tem seus altos e baixos.
native_language_example: Every relationship has its ups and downs.

meaning: besides; in addition to; as well as.
additional_notes: Used to add extra information or an extra item. It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive verb: “além de dinheiro” (besides money), “além disso” (besides that), “além de estudar” (besides studying). Often introduces an additional point, sometimes with emphasis like “on top of that.”
target_language_example: Além de trabalhar, eu estudo à noite.
native_language_example: Besides working, I study at night.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information or another point, often at the start of a sentence or after a pause. Common in both speaking and writing; slightly more formal than "também" in many contexts. It can refer back to what was just said: "X. Além disso, Y."
target_language_example: Está chovendo e, além disso, está muito frio.
native_language_example: It’s raining and, besides that, it’s very cold.

additional_notes: Used to add an extra point or argument, often in a slightly formal tone. Common in writing and speech. Similar to "além disso" and "além de tudo". Often followed by a comma: "Além do mais, ...".
target_language_example: Além do mais, não tenho tempo para isso hoje.
native_language_example: Besides, I don’t have time for that today.

additional_notes: European Portuguese spelling with a hyphen: verb + object pronoun (amo + te). In Brazilian Portuguese, people usually say "eu te amo" (or "te amo") instead. Used mainly for romantic love (partners); for family/friends, "gosto muito de ti/você" is often more common depending on the relationship and region.
target_language_example: Amo-te muito.
native_language_example: I love you very much.

additional_notes: A fixed expression used to say you fell in love immediately when you first saw or met someone (or sometimes something, like a place). In Portuguese, it often appears with the verb "ser" ("Foi amor à primeira vista") or "acontecer" ("Aconteceu amor à primeira vista").
target_language_example: Foi amor à primeira vista quando eu a vi.
native_language_example: It was love at first sight when I saw her.

additional_notes: Commonly used as a spoken prompt, usually in the imperative: “Anda logo!” It can sound impatient or teasing depending on tone and context. Uses: telling someone to move faster, to leave, or to start doing something right away.
target_language_example: Anda logo, a gente vai se atrasar!
native_language_example: Hurry up, we’re going to be late!

meaning: pet (a domesticated animal you keep at home).
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a pet. Often used with the verb "ter" (to have): "Tenho um animal de estimação." In everyday speech, people also say "pet" or use specific animals ("cão/cachorro", "gato"). Plural: "animais de estimação".
target_language_example: Você tem algum animal de estimação?
native_language_example: Do you have any pets?

meaning: guardian angel; someone who protects you.
additional_notes: Often used literally in religious contexts (a protective angel assigned to a person) and figuratively to mean a protector or benefactor who helps you in a difficult moment. You can call a person your “anjo da guarda” to thank them for looking out for you. Plural: “anjos da guarda.”
target_language_example: Obrigado por me ajudar ontem — você foi meu anjo da guarda.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me yesterday — you were my guardian angel.

meaning: New Year (the new calendar year; also New Year’s holiday/period).
additional_notes: Used for the calendar year that begins on January 1 and for New Year’s celebrations (especially around Dec 31/Jan 1). Common in greetings like "Feliz Ano Novo!" (Happy New Year!). Often appears with the definite article: "o Ano Novo" (New Year / New Year’s Day).
target_language_example: Feliz Ano Novo! Que este ano traga muita saúde e alegria.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! May this year bring lots of health and joy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the year after the current one. Often appears with plans, predictions, or future arrangements. You can also say “no ano que vem” (“next year”) when it’s the time frame of an action. Closely related to “mês que vem” (next month) and “semana que vem” (next week).
target_language_example: Vou viajar para Portugal no ano que vem.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel to Portugal next year.

additional_notes: Used mainly in science/astronomy and sometimes figuratively to mean “very far” or “a long way ahead/behind” (e.g., in progress or technology). It’s a masculine noun: um ano-luz / dois anos-luz. Hyphenated in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Essa estrela fica a cerca de 10 anos-luz da Terra.
native_language_example: That star is about 10 light-years from Earth.

additional_notes: Hyphenated form commonly used when referring specifically to the New Year holiday/celebrations (like New Year’s Eve/Day). Often appears in greetings like “Feliz Ano-Novo!” or “Bom Ano-Novo!”. Without the hyphen (“ano novo”), it more literally means “a new year” in a general sense.
target_language_example: Feliz Ano-Novo!
native_language_example: Happy New Year!

meaning: first of all; before anything else.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in an explanation, or to emphasize what should come first (a priority). Often followed by a comma. Similar to "antes de mais" and "primeiro".
target_language_example: Antes de tudo, precisamos confirmar a data da reunião.
native_language_example: First of all, we need to confirm the date of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is NOT true, often as a correction or ironic response. It’s an ellipsis of "Antes fosse (verdade)" or "Antes fosse assim" and is followed by the real situation (often with "mas..."). Common in European and Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: — Então está tudo resolvido? — Antes fosse! Ainda falta muito.
native_language_example: — So is everything solved? — If only! There’s still a lot left.

additional_notes: Used to say something was not planned or chosen carefully. Common with verbs like escolher (to choose), pegar (to pick up), encontrar (to find), and andar (to wander): escolher ao acaso = choose randomly; encontrar ao acaso = meet by chance.
target_language_example: Escolhi um livro ao acaso e comecei a ler.
native_language_example: I picked a book at random and started reading.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like estar/ficar/entrar/sair: estar no/ao ar = to be broadcasting (on TV/radio/online). Also used for things that are “up/available” online (e.g., site, episode). Common collocation: (estar) ao vivo e a cores. Note: you’ll often hear both “no ar” and “ao ar” with very similar meaning.
target_language_example: O programa vai estar ao ar às oito.
native_language_example: The show will be on the air at eight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about activities, events, or places that are outside (not indoors). Common with verbs like "fazer" (to do) and nouns like "atividades" (activities): "fazer exercício ao ar livre". Also appears as an adjective phrase after a noun: "um concerto ao ar livre" (an outdoor concert).
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar ao ar livre hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s have lunch outdoors today.

additional_notes: Used to express the opposite of what was said or expected. Often appears as “pelo contrário” (“on the contrary”) or in contrasts like “Ao contrário de X, Y...” (“Unlike X, Y...”).
target_language_example: Eu não acho difícil; ao contrário, acho bem fácil.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s difficult; on the contrary, I think it’s pretty easy.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a contrast or substitution (choosing one option rather than another). Commonly followed by an infinitive verb or a noun phrase: "ao invés de + infinitive" (Ao invés de sair, fiquei em casa.) or "ao invés de + noun" (ao invés de café). Often written/said as "em vez de" with the same meaning in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ao invés de pegar o ônibus, fui a pé.
native_language_example: Instead of taking the bus, I went on foot.

additional_notes: Often used to indicate physical location (or metaphorically, support/being on someone's side). Common patterns: "ao lado de" + noun/pronoun (next to), and "do meu/teu/seu lado" (by my/your/his/her side).
target_language_example: O banco fica ao lado da farmácia.
native_language_example: The bank is next to the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum amount/degree or to soften a request/statement (similar to “at least” or “at least, anyway”). Often interchangeable with “pelo menos” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ao menos me avisa se você se atrasar.
native_language_example: At least let me know if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to say two things happen together, or to contrast two ideas in the sense of “and yet” / “while also.” Common in both spoken and written Portuguese. Often appears after a comma when introducing a contrast: “..., ao mesmo tempo, ...”.
target_language_example: Ele está cansado e, ao mesmo tempo, animado para a viagem.
native_language_example: He is tired and, at the same time, excited for the trip.

meaning: at the foot of; next to (usually in “ao pé de …”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with “de” to locate something: “ao pé de” = “at the foot of / right next to / beside.” It can refer to a physical base (a mountain, stairs) or simply being very close to something or someone.
target_language_example: O hotel fica ao pé da praia.
native_language_example: The hotel is right next to the beach.

meaning: next to; at the foot/base of (a place or object).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is very close to something else (physical proximity). Literally refers to being at the “foot” of something (e.g., a mountain, building, bed), and it can also be used in directions to mean “right by/near.” Common with verbs like ficar/estar (to be) and morar (to live).
target_language_example: O banco fica ao pé do supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is next to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Means “around” in the sense of “in the area surrounding something” or “all around.” Often used as **ao redor de** (“around” / “around the …”). It can refer to physical space (people, buildings) or a general area nearby. In Brazil you also commonly hear **em volta (de)** with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Há muitas lojas ao redor da praça.
native_language_example: There are many shops around the square.

additional_notes: Used to give the final total number/amount after adding everything up. Very common with numbers, often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., “Ao todo, …” / “…, ao todo”).
target_language_example: Ao todo, somos dez pessoas.
native_language_example: In total, there are ten of us.

meaning: live (not recorded); in person/in real time.
additional_notes: Used for broadcasts, performances, or events happening right now (TV, radio, livestreams): “transmissão ao vivo”, “show ao vivo”. It can also mean “in person” (as opposed to online or by phone): “aula ao vivo”.
target_language_example: O jogo vai passar ao vivo na TV hoje à noite.
native_language_example: The game will be broadcast live on TV tonight.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to mean “to any place/wherever (someone/something goes).” It’s similar to **onde quer que** (“wherever”), but **aonde** emphasizes destination/direction (going to a place). Often followed by the subjunctive in more formal phrasing: **aonde quer que você vá** (“wherever you go”).
target_language_example: Eu vou com você aonde quer que você vá.
native_language_example: I’ll go with you wherever you go.

additional_notes: Common question used to ask someone’s destination. In everyday speech, many people also say “onde você vai?”; “aonde” is often used when the idea is movement (going to a place). You can make it more polite by adding “para onde” (“Para onde você vai?”) or “Aonde o senhor/a senhora vai?”
target_language_example: Aonde você vai agora?
native_language_example: Where are you going now?

additional_notes: Used to describe something happening slowly over time, step by step. Often translates as “gradually” in English, and can be used with many verbs (e.g., aprender, melhorar, entender, acostumar-se).
target_language_example: Aos poucos, eu estou aprendendo português.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to greet someone, introduce yourself, or seal an agreement. It’s a common, polite expression. You’ll also hear the singular form "apertar a mão" (to shake someone’s hand).
target_language_example: Prazer em conhecê-lo — vamos apertar as mãos.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you — let’s shake hands.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: something happens even though there is an obstacle or opposing fact. It is followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive: "apesar da chuva" (despite the rain), "apesar disso" (despite that), "apesar de ser tarde" (despite it being late). With a full clause, Portuguese often uses "apesar de que" or "apesar que" + subjunctive in many varieties (e.g., "apesar de que esteja chovendo").
target_language_example: Apesar de estar cansado, vou sair hoje.
native_language_example: Despite being tired, I’m going out today.

additional_notes: A common term in environmental and climate discussions. Often used with verbs like "causar" (to cause), "combater" (to fight), and "reduzir" (to reduce): "combater o aquecimento global". It’s usually understood as the long-term rise in Earth’s average temperature due to greenhouse gases.
target_language_example: Precisamos reduzir as emissões para combater o aquecimento global.
native_language_example: We need to reduce emissions to fight global warming.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative “aquele” to point to something distant from both the speaker and the listener (often far away, or a place neither of you is currently in). For a closer place, you’ll usually hear “este lugar” (this place) or “esse lugar” (that place near you / previously mentioned).
target_language_example: Vamos para aquele lugar depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s go to that place after lunch.

meaning: "here and now"; immediately, in the present moment.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize urgency or focus on the present, often meaning you should deal with something right away (not later). It can also be used in a more philosophical sense about living in the present. Common in spoken Portuguese: "Preciso disso aqui e agora".
target_language_example: Eu preciso da resposta aqui e agora.
native_language_example: I need the answer here and now.

meaning: here and there; in scattered places.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or exists in a few different places, not everywhere. Can also mean “now and then” in a casual way, depending on context.
target_language_example: Há alguns problemas aqui e ali, mas no geral está tudo bem.
native_language_example: There are a few problems here and there, but overall everything is fine.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a building or car’s cooling system. Often used with the verb "ligar" (turn on) or "desligar" (turn off): "ligar o ar condicionado" / "desligar o ar condicionado". In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s frequently shortened to "ar" when the context is clear (e.g., "Liga o ar").
target_language_example: Está muito quente aqui. Pode ligar o ar condicionado?
native_language_example: It’s very hot in here. Can you turn on the air conditioning?

additional_notes: Used when talking about going outside or opening windows to breathe cleaner/cooler air. Common with verbs like "tomar" or "apanhar" (to get) and "precisar de" (to need): "tomar ar fresco", "preciso de ar fresco".
target_language_example: Vamos lá fora tomar um pouco de ar fresco.
native_language_example: Let’s go outside to get some fresh air.

additional_notes: Usually used with the preposition in the fixed phrase “ao ar livre” (“outdoors / in the open air”). Common in contexts like “atividades ao ar livre” (outdoor activities), “evento ao ar livre” (open-air event), and “fazer exercício ao ar livre” (to work out outdoors).
target_language_example: No verão, gostamos de fazer piqueniques ao ar livre.
native_language_example: In the summer, we like to have picnics outdoors.

additional_notes: Used both for the system in a place (“tem ar-condicionado”) and for the device itself (“o ar-condicionado”). Very common in weather/comfort and travel contexts (hotels, buses, cars). Often shortened in speech to “ar”.
target_language_example: O quarto tem ar-condicionado?
native_language_example: Does the room have air conditioning?

additional_notes: A masculine noun: "o arco-íris" (plural: "os arco-íris"). Often used with the verb "ver" (to see) or with "depois da chuva" (after the rain). Can also refer to "cores do arco-íris" (rainbow colors).
target_language_example: Depois da chuva, vimos um arco-íris no céu.
native_language_example: After the rain, we saw a rainbow in the sky.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: "o arco-íris" (plural: "os arco-íris"). Often used with "há/tem" (there is/are): "Há um arco-íris no céu". You can also say "as cores do arco-íris" (the colors of the rainbow).
target_language_example: Depois da chuva, apareceu um arco-íris no céu.
native_language_example: After the rain, a rainbow appeared in the sky.

additional_notes: A formal/neutral term used in news, politics, and military contexts. Plural: "armas nucleares". Related: "energia nuclear" (nuclear energy) is different from "arma nuclear".
target_language_example: O país disse que não vai usar arma nuclear.
native_language_example: The country said it will not use a nuclear weapon.

meaning: to make a scene; to cause a big fuss.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used when someone starts an argument or creates public drama/commotion (often by complaining loudly). Literally it’s “to set up the tent,” but the real meaning is about causing trouble or a scene, not camping.
target_language_example: Quando disseram que não havia mais ingressos, ela armou a barraca na bilheteria.
native_language_example: When they said there were no more tickets, she made a big scene at the ticket office.

additional_notes: A noun. Plural: arranha-céus. Often used when talking about city skylines and modern downtown areas. Hyphenated in standard spelling.
target_language_example: São Paulo tem muitos arranha-céus no centro.
native_language_example: São Paulo has many skyscrapers downtown/in the city center.

meaning: to roll up your sleeves; to get ready to work (often hard).
additional_notes: Literally means “to roll up the sleeves.” Used both in a physical sense (rolling up sleeves before doing something messy or manual) and figuratively to mean getting down to work, taking action, or tackling a task seriously. Common in everyday speech and work contexts.
target_language_example: Vamos arregaçar as mangas e terminar esse projeto hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s roll up our sleeves and finish this project today.

additional_notes: Used for disciplines like karate, judo, taekwondo, etc. Often appears in the plural as "artes marciais" (martial arts). You can talk about practicing with "praticar" or doing training with "treinar".
target_language_example: Eu pratico uma arte marcial duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I practice a martial art twice a week.

additional_notes: Feminine plural of “a senhora” (“ma’am,” “Mrs.,” or “lady”). Used as a respectful way to refer to adult women, especially in formal contexts (e.g., in customer service). It can also be used when addressing a group directly: “As senhoras querem...?”
target_language_example: As senhoras podem esperar aqui, por favor.
native_language_example: The ladies can wait here, please.

additional_notes: Used for the household appliance that cleans floors by sucking up dust. In Brazil, people also commonly say "aspirador" when the context is clear. Plural: "aspiradores de pó".
target_language_example: Vou passar o aspirador de pó na sala hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to vacuum the living room today.

additional_notes: Used to compare or add items. Common patterns: (1) linking two nouns/ideas: “A assim como B” = “A as well as B”; (2) making a comparison: “assim como X, Y” = “just like X, Y”; (3) paired with “tão” for equality: “tão … assim como …” = “as … as …”.
target_language_example: Ele fala inglês assim como espanhol.
native_language_example: He speaks English as well as Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action that happens immediately after another one. It’s often followed by the present subjunctive when talking about a future event (e.g., “Assim que eu chegar...” = “As soon as I arrive...”). It can also be used with past tenses for past events (“Assim que chegou, ligou.”).
target_language_example: Assim que eu chegar em casa, eu te ligo.
native_language_example: As soon as I get home, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement or acceptance of something (“so be it”), or as a solemn closing in prayers/speeches, similar to “amen.” It’s somewhat formal/solemn in tone.
target_language_example: Que tudo corra bem — assim seja.
native_language_example: May everything go well — amen / so be it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion based on what was just said. Common in writing and formal speech; in casual conversation you’ll also hear "então" or "por isso".
target_language_example: Não há mais vagas; assim sendo, teremos que esperar.
native_language_example: There are no more openings; therefore, we’ll have to wait.

additional_notes: A trained professional who helps individuals and families access social services (benefits, housing support, child protection, healthcare resources, etc.). Often used in hospitals, schools, city halls, and social-service agencies. Feminine/masculine form is the same: "o assistente social" / "a assistente social".
target_language_example: A assistente social me ajudou a pedir apoio para moradia.
native_language_example: The social worker helped me apply for housing support.

additional_notes: Medical/emergency term for a heart attack. In everyday speech, people also say "infarto" (short for "infarto do miocárdio"). In an emergency you might hear: "Ele/ela está tendo um ataque cardíaco" (He/she is having a heart attack) or "Chame uma ambulância!" (Call an ambulance!).
target_language_example: Acho que ele está tendo um ataque cardíaco — chame uma ambulância!
native_language_example: I think he’s having a heart attack—call an ambulance!

additional_notes: Used to indicate the means/method used to do something, or the channel something happens through (e.g., via email, through an app). It can also mean physical movement from one side to the other (through/across). In more formal writing, it’s common; in everyday speech, people may also use "por" or "via" depending on the context.
target_language_example: Enviei o documento através de e-mail.
native_language_example: I sent the document by email.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned or incarcerated. Literally means “behind the bars/grates,” and it’s common in news and everyday speech (more idiomatic than just describing a physical location). Often appears with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/to end up).
target_language_example: Depois do julgamento, ele ficou atrás das grades por cinco anos.
native_language_example: After the trial, he was behind bars for five years.

additional_notes: Used mainly with two meanings: (1) physical position: "behind" (often interchangeable with "por trás de" in many contexts); (2) pursuit/search: "after" or "looking for" someone/something (e.g., "estar atrás de" = to be after/trying to get). It’s also common in time expressions like "dias atrás" (days ago), but that use doesn’t require "de."
target_language_example: Estou atrás de um emprego novo.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a new job.

meaning: See you soon. / See you later.
additional_notes: A common, friendly way to say goodbye when you expect to see the person again relatively soon (later today or in the near future). More casual than "até breve" (see you soon) and often interchangeable with "até mais" (see you later). Literally "until soon."
target_language_example: Estou com pressa — até logo!
native_language_example: I’m in a hurry—see you soon!

additional_notes: A common, friendly goodbye used when you expect to see the person again (not necessarily soon). Often shortened to "até". More informal than "adeus" and similar in tone to "tchau".
target_language_example: Estou indo embora — até mais!
native_language_example: I’m leaving — see you later!

additional_notes: Used to react to something you think is unlikely, exaggerated, or untrue. Tone is often sarcastic and can sound dismissive. Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech; in more formal contexts you might say “acho difícil” (I doubt it) or “não acredito”.
target_language_example: Você vai me devolver o dinheiro hoje? Até parece!
native_language_example: You’re going to pay me back today? Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Used to express doubt, disbelief, or irony about what someone said or what might happen. Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. You can also hear the shorter form “Até parece!” (“Yeah right!”).
target_language_example: Até parece que ele vai chegar no horário!
native_language_example: As if he’s going to arrive on time!

additional_notes: Used to mark an endpoint in time or the moment when something finally happens. Often followed by the subjunctive when referring to a future/uncertain event (e.g., "até que ele chegue" = "until he arrives"), and by the indicative for past facts (e.g., "até que ele chegou" = "until he arrived"). It can also mean "so much so that" in some contexts, but the most common beginner meaning is "until".
target_language_example: Espere aqui até que eu volte.
native_language_example: Wait here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to express relief, impatience, or satisfaction that something happened after a long wait or delay. Often said as an exclamation ("Até que enfim!") and can sound mildly complaining depending on tone.
target_language_example: Até que enfim você chegou!
native_language_example: Finally you arrived!

additional_notes: Used to describe birds that hunt other animals or feed on carrion, such as eagles (águias), hawks (falcões/gaviões), and owls (corujas). In Brazilian Portuguese, it can also be used figuratively for a predatory or exploitative person (like “a vulture”).
target_language_example: A águia é uma ave de rapina.
native_language_example: The eagle is a bird of prey.

additional_notes: Used to point something out, present something, or confirm that something is now available or correct. Often said when handing someone an item (like “here you go”), or when you find/notice something (“there it is”). The pronoun “aí” refers to “there/at your place/where you are,” so it can also feel like “there you are/there it is” rather than “here.”
target_language_example: Você estava procurando as chaves? Aí está!
native_language_example: Were you looking for the keys? There they are!

meaning: “there you have it / there it is” (used to point something out or conclude an explanation).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech. Often used after giving information or an explanation, meaning something like “see?” / “that’s why” / “there you go.” It can also literally mean “there is/has” when talking about what a place has (e.g., a store, an app, a city), but in everyday conversation it frequently works as a discourse marker to wrap up a point.
target_language_example: Você pega o ônibus na esquina e desce no centro — aí tem a estação.
native_language_example: You take the bus on the corner and get off downtown — then there’s the station.

additional_notes: Used for a collection of information stored and organized (usually on a computer). Common in tech/business contexts. Plural: "bancos de dados".
target_language_example: Precisamos atualizar o banco de dados dos clientes.
native_language_example: We need to update the customer database.

additional_notes: Literally “bath of sun,” it refers to spending time in the sun (often to tan or enjoy warmth). Common with verbs like “tomar” or “fazer”: “tomar/fazer um banho de sol.”
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou tomar um banho de sol na varanda.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to sunbathe on the balcony.

meaning: a gay bar (a bar popular with LGBTQ+ people).
additional_notes: Common way to refer to a bar aimed at or popular with gay/LGBTQ+ customers. In Portuguese, adjectives often come after the noun, so you’ll also hear it like this (borrowed from English): “bar gay”. You may also see “bar LGBT” or “bar LGBTQIA+”.
target_language_example: Vamos a um bar gay hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we go to a gay bar tonight?

additional_notes: In Brazil, batata frita usually refers to French fries (often served as a side dish). In Portugal, batatas fritas can also mean potato chips/crisps depending on context, so you may need to clarify (e.g., batatas fritas de pacote = chips in a bag). Often used in the plural: batatas fritas.
target_language_example: Eu vou pedir um hambúrguer com batata frita.
native_language_example: I’m going to order a hamburger with fries.

additional_notes: Idiom meaning to pull back/leave a situation, especially when things are going badly or there’s danger. Common in news, formal speech, and storytelling; in everyday conversation you can also say “recuar” or “ir embora”. Often used with “é melhor…” or in the past: “bateu em retirada”.
target_language_example: Quando viram a polícia chegar, eles bateram em retirada.
native_language_example: When they saw the police arrive, they retreated.

additional_notes: Common way to describe knocking (usually with your hand) on a door to get someone’s attention. You can also hear it used more generally as “to knock” (e.g., bater na janela = knock on the window). In everyday speech, people may shorten it to “bater à porta” as well.
target_language_example: Antes de entrar, você pode bater na porta?
native_language_example: Before coming in, can you knock on the door?

additional_notes: Used for clapping to show approval or appreciation (e.g., after a performance). In Portuguese you’ll often see it in the plural: “bater palmas”. You can also use it with “para” to say what you’re applauding: “bater palmas para alguém/para uma banda”.
target_language_example: Todo mundo começou a bater palmas no final do show.
native_language_example: Everyone started clapping at the end of the show.

meaning: to masturbate (slang; often said about men).
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese slang. Usually means “to masturbate,” often implying male masturbation, and is used mostly in casual conversation. It can sound crude, so avoid in formal settings. The verb may appear as: “bater uma” / “bater uma punheta.”
target_language_example: Ele confessou que foi pro banheiro bater uma.
native_language_example: He admitted he went to the bathroom to masturbate.

additional_notes: Used when someone knocks to get the attention of the people inside. You can conjugate it as needed (e.g., "bati", "está batendo"). Also common: "bater na porta" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Alguém está batendo à porta.
native_language_example: Someone is knocking on the door.

meaning: to have a drink (usually a beer).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech. Literally “to drink one,” but it’s used more generally as “to grab a drink,” often implying alcohol (especially beer). You can specify: “beber uma cerveja” (have a beer).
target_language_example: Vamos beber uma depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Shall we have a drink after work?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the strip of land next to the sea (beachfront/seafront), often in the sense of a coastal area or promenade. Common in place names and descriptions (e.g., avenida beira-mar). The plural is "beiras-mar". Related: "à beira-mar" = "by the sea".
target_language_example: Vamos passear na avenida beira-mar ao pôr do sol.
native_language_example: Let’s take a walk along the seafront at sunset.

additional_notes: Used to add an extra person/thing/action to a list, often in more formal writing and speech. It links similar items (nouns, phrases, or clauses): X, bem como Y. In everyday conversation, people often use "e também" instead. It’s not the same as "ou" (or).
target_language_example: A empresa oferece treinamento, bem como suporte técnico aos clientes.
native_language_example: The company provides training, as well as technical support to customers.

additional_notes: Commonly used in two main ways: (1) as praise or congratulations (“good job”), and (2) as a reaction when someone gets a deserved negative consequence (“that’s what you get”), often with a teasing or scolding tone. The exact meaning depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Você quebrou as regras e foi punido? Bem feito!
native_language_example: You broke the rules and got punished? Serves you right!

meaning: the greater good; a higher/common good.
additional_notes: Often used in expressions like “pelo bem maior” (“for the greater good”), meaning doing something for a broader benefit (society, a group, the long term), even if it involves a personal sacrifice. In everyday Portuguese, you’ll more often see it with an article or preposition: “o bem maior”, “um bem maior”, “para/pelo bem maior”.
target_language_example: Ele aceitou a mudança pelo bem maior da equipe.
native_language_example: He accepted the change for the greater good of the team.

meaning: (1) “I really did …” (emphasis); (2) “you could/should at least …” (mild reproach/suggestion).
additional_notes:
Common in Brazilian Portuguese to add emphasis or a sense of regret. 
• Emphasis: “Bem que eu avisei.” = “I really did warn you / I told you so.” 
• Mild reproach/suggestion (often with podia/poderia/devia): “Bem que você podia me ajudar.” = “You could at least help me.” 
It doesn’t translate word-for-word from bem (“well”) + que (“that”).
target_language_example: Bem que você podia me avisar antes.
native_language_example: You could at least let me know beforehand.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning a good physical, mental, or social state. Often used in contexts like health, quality of life, and work/life balance (e.g., "bem-estar físico/mental", "bem-estar no trabalho"). Can also refer to general welfare in a group or society ("o bem-estar da população").
target_language_example: O exercício faz bem para o meu bem-estar.
native_language_example: Exercise is good for my well-being.

additional_notes: An adjective meaning “successful,” often used to describe a person, career, plan, project, or business. It agrees in gender and number: bem-sucedido (m. sg.), bem-sucedida (f. sg.), bem-sucedidos (m. pl.), bem-sucedidas (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ela é uma empreendedora bem-sucedida.
native_language_example: She is a successful entrepreneur.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "bem-vindo". Used to welcome a female person; you can say it by itself or in phrases like "Seja bem-vinda" (more formal) or "Bem-vinda a(o)...". Use "bem-vindo" for a man and "bem-vindos/bem-vindas" for groups (mixed groups usually take masculine plural).
target_language_example: Bem-vinda ao Brasil!
native_language_example: Welcome to Brazil!

additional_notes: Used to welcome two or more women, or a mixed group where the people being welcomed are referred to with a feminine word (e.g., "pessoas", "visitas"). It’s the plural of "bem-vinda". In Portuguese, "bem-vindo/bem-vinda" changes to match gender and number: bem-vindo (m. sing.), bem-vinda (f. sing.), bem-vindos (m. pl. or mixed group), bem-vindas (f. pl.). Often appears in greetings like "Sejam bem-vindas!" or "Boas-vindas!".
target_language_example: Sejam bem-vindas à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone in a place, event, or situation. It agrees with the person: bem-vindo (male), bem-vinda (female), bem-vindos/bem-vindas (plural). Commonly used in the phrase “Seja bem-vindo(a)” (“Welcome”).
target_language_example: Seja bem-vinda à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

additional_notes: Plural form of "bem-vindo". Used to welcome a group (or mixed-gender group). For only women, use "bem-vindas". For one person: "bem-vindo" (man) / "bem-vinda" (woman). Often used in greetings like "Sejam bem-vindos" (“You are welcome”/“Welcome”) or on signs and announcements.
target_language_example: Sejam bem-vindos à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

meaning: a good person; good people (nice, decent).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone as kind and trustworthy: “Ele é boa gente.” It can also refer to a group (“Eles são boa gente”). Often used in informal everyday speech, but not slang. As a compliment, it’s closer to “nice person” than “good-looking.”
target_language_example: Pode confiar nele — ele é boa gente.
native_language_example: You can trust him—he’s a good guy.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening and also as a farewell meaning “good night” (e.g., when leaving at night or going to sleep). It’s polite and standard (not slang).
target_language_example: Boa noite! Tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good evening! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck, often before an exam, job interview, trip, or any difficult task. It can be said on its own or followed by "com" + noun (e.g., "Boa sorte com a prova" = "Good luck with the test"). Also common: "Boa sorte!" as a friendly send-off.
target_language_example: Boa sorte na entrevista amanhã!
native_language_example: Good luck in the interview tomorrow!

additional_notes: A standard, polite greeting used from around lunchtime until early evening (before “boa noite”). Often used when arriving, entering a shop, or starting a conversation. In very informal situations people may shorten it to “tarde”.
target_language_example: Boa tarde, tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to wish someone a good journey when they’re about to leave (or sometimes right after they leave). Often said with verbs like “Desejo-lhe/Desejo-te uma boa viagem” (I wish you a good trip) or simply on its own. Similar to “boa sorte” (good luck), but specifically for travel. In Brazil and Portugal it’s common and polite.
target_language_example: Boa viagem! Manda notícias quando chegar.
native_language_example: Have a good trip! Let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used for a friendly, cooperative attitude ("goodwill") or readiness to do something ("willingness"). Often appears in phrases like "com boa vontade" (willingly / in good faith) or "ter boa vontade" (to be willing / to show goodwill). Depending on context it can also imply acting with good intentions.
target_language_example: Ele resolveu o problema com boa vontade e paciência.
native_language_example: He solved the problem with goodwill and patience.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening/night and also as a farewell when someone is going to sleep or leaving at night. Very common and polite. You’ll also hear the singular form "boa noite"; both are widely used, with "boa noite" often treated as the standard.
target_language_example: Boas noites! Tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good evening! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to greet someone in the afternoon and early evening. Common in Portugal; in Brazil, people more often say "boa tarde" (singular), but "boas tardes" may still be understood. Often used when arriving somewhere, starting a conversation, or addressing a group politely.
target_language_example: Boas tardes, pode ajudar-me, por favor?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Used to express or offer a welcome, often in the fixed phrase “dar as boas-vindas (a alguém)” = “to welcome (someone)”. Can also appear in plural as a noun meaning “a welcome” (e.g., a welcome message/party).
target_language_example: Queremos dar-lhe as boas-vindas à nossa casa.
native_language_example: We want to welcome you to our home.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "bola" (ball) + "de" (of/for) + "golfe" (golf). Used in everyday contexts (sports, shopping, describing size: "do tamanho de uma bola de golfe" = "the size of a golf ball").
target_language_example: Eu perdi a minha bola de golfe no mato.
native_language_example: I lost my golf ball in the bushes.

additional_notes: Used for money (full or partial) that helps pay for studying, often awarded by a school, government, or organization. Common with verbs like ganhar/receber (to get), pedir/candidatar-se a (to apply for), and oferecer (to offer).
target_language_example: Ela ganhou uma bolsa de estudos para estudar na universidade.
native_language_example: She got a scholarship to study at the university.

additional_notes: A common polite phrase said before someone starts eating. You can say it to one person or a group. Often used on its own (just “Bom apetite!”), or with “Tenha/tenham” (“Tenha um bom apetite!” / “Tenham um bom apetite!”).
target_language_example: O jantar está servido — bom apetite!
native_language_example: Dinner is served—enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting, especially in the morning and early afternoon. In Portugal it’s mainly for the morning (later people often say "boa tarde"). Can be used when arriving or starting a conversation (in person, on the phone, in emails). Often followed by "tudo bem?" (how are you?).
target_language_example: Bom dia! Tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good morning! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking and sensible behavior. Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have), "usar" (to use), and "faltar" (to lack): "Tenha bom senso" (Use common sense), "Falta bom senso" (There’s a lack of common sense).
target_language_example: Por favor, tenha bom senso e não estacione aqui.
native_language_example: Please use common sense and don’t park here.

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for the weapon, especially in historical, political, or news contexts. In everyday conversation it’s uncommon unless discussing history (e.g., World War II) or nuclear weapons. Plural: "bombas atômicas".
target_language_example: O filme fala sobre o impacto da bomba atômica no fim da guerra.
native_language_example: The movie talks about the impact of the atomic bomb at the end of the war.

additional_notes: A common winter/Christmas expression. Literally “snow doll/figure,” meaning a figure made of snow. Plural: "bonecos de neve."
target_language_example: As crianças fizeram um boneco de neve no jardim.
native_language_example: The children made a snowman in the garden.

additional_notes: Literally the plural of "bom dia" (good morning/good day). As a greeting, standard Portuguese uses the singular: "Bom dia". "Bons dias" is usually not used as a normal greeting; it may sound unusual or playful and is more likely to appear in sentences wishing someone well (e.g., hoping they have good days ahead).
target_language_example: Desejo-lhe bons dias pela frente.
native_language_example: I wish you good days ahead.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone pleasant dreams, usually when saying goodnight. Common with "Boa noite" (Good night): "Boa noite, bons sonhos." You can also say it alone as a friendly bedtime wish.
target_language_example: Boa noite! Bons sonhos.
native_language_example: Good night! Sweet dreams.

meaning: a trusted right-hand person; main assistant.
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean someone’s most trusted helper or second-in-command (at work, in politics, etc.). Literally it means “right arm,” but in everyday speech it commonly refers to a person rather than a body part. You can also say “ser o braço direito de alguém” (“to be someone’s right-hand person”).
target_language_example: A Ana é o braço direito do diretor.
native_language_example: Ana is the director’s right-hand person.
