meaning: to play with fire (to take a dangerous risk).
additional_notes: Usually used figuratively to warn that someone is doing something risky or reckless and may face bad consequences. It can also be literal (actually playing with fire), but most often it means “you’re asking for trouble.” Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: brincar (eu brinco, você brinca, ele/ela brinca…).
target_language_example: Se você continuar mentindo, vai acabar brincando com fogo.
native_language_example: If you keep lying, you’ll end up playing with fire.

additional_notes: Used for the astronomy concept (a region in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape). In everyday speech it can also be used metaphorically for something that “swallows” money, time, information, etc. Plural: buracos negros.
target_language_example: Os cientistas descobriram um buraco negro enorme no centro da galáxia.
native_language_example: Scientists discovered a huge black hole at the center of the galaxy.

additional_notes: Very common name in Brazil for a hot dog. Often appears on menus and snack stands (lanchonetes). Despite the literal words (“hot dog”), it refers to the sandwich, not an animal. You may also see the spelling without a hyphen: “cachorro quente.”
target_language_example: Eu vou pedir um cachorro-quente, por favor.
native_language_example: I’m going to order a hot dog, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to individuals in a group one by one. Often appears in expressions like “cada um por si” (every person for themselves) and can be followed by “de” + noun: “cada um de nós” (each of us). For feminine reference, you may see “cada uma” (each one, feminine).
target_language_example: Cada um paga a sua parte.
native_language_example: Each person pays their share.

additional_notes: Used to refer to each individual item/person in a group when the noun is feminine or implied to be feminine (e.g., “cada uma das pessoas”). For masculine, use “cada um.” Often followed by “de” + plural (“cada uma das…” = “each of the…”).
target_language_example: Cada uma das crianças ganhou um presente.
native_language_example: Each of the children got a present.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens on every occasion (“cada vez que…” = “every time that…”). It can also be used in comparisons like “cada vez mais/menos” (“more and more/less and less”), meaning something is changing progressively.
target_language_example: Cada vez que eu venho aqui, está mais cheio.
native_language_example: Every time I come here, it’s more crowded.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that keeps growing or happening with greater intensity/frequency over time. Often placed before adjectives or adverbs (e.g., cada vez mais difícil = more and more difficult), or with verbs to show an increasing trend (e.g., estou cada vez mais cansado = I’m getting more and more tired).
target_language_example: As cidades estão cada vez mais caras.
native_language_example: Cities are getting more and more expensive.

additional_notes: Used for a chair with wheels for someone who has difficulty walking. Often appears with articles and verbs like usar (to use) or precisar de (to need): "uma cadeira de rodas", "na cadeira de rodas", "Ele usa cadeira de rodas". Also common in accessibility contexts: "acesso para cadeira de rodas" (wheelchair access).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma cadeira de rodas para entrar no hospital.
native_language_example: I need a wheelchair to enter the hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the colloquial word "cadê" (common in Brazil) to ask where someone/something is, often with an impatient or concerned tone. It’s informal and can sound a bit demanding depending on context. More neutral alternatives: "Onde você está?" or "Onde é que você está?".
target_language_example: Cadê você? Estou te esperando na entrada.
native_language_example: Where are you? I’m waiting for you at the entrance.

additional_notes: A common way to order a milky coffee. In Brazil it often means brewed coffee mixed with milk (usually a large amount of milk). In Portugal you may also hear similar drinks called "galão" (more milk) or "meia de leite" (half milk), but "café com leite" is widely understood.
target_language_example: Para mim, um café com leite, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: Standard, everyday term for the morning meal in Brazil. Literally “coffee of the morning,” but it refers to breakfast in general (not just coffee). In Portugal, “breakfast” is more commonly called “pequeno-almoço.”
target_language_example: Eu tomo café da manhã às sete.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at seven.

meaning: “Get out of here!” / “Leave!” (also: “Get out of my way!”).
additional_notes: Informal command, often said angrily or urgently. Used to tell someone to leave a place or to stop bothering you. You can also hear it as advice: “Cai fora daqui!” = “Get out of here!” / “Let’s get out of here.”
target_language_example: Cai fora daqui agora!
native_language_example: Get out of here right now!

meaning: to leave; to get out of here (often suddenly).
additional_notes: Very common in informal spoken Portuguese. Often used as an imperative: "Cai fora!" = "Get out!" / "Leave!". Can also mean leaving a place or ending an interaction: "Vou cair fora" = "I’m going to head out." Not usually used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Já está tarde, vou cair fora.
native_language_example: It’s already late, I’m going to head out.

additional_notes: Common, neutral expression meaning to begin sleeping (often unintentionally or because you’re very tired). Used with conjugated forms of "cair": "caí no sono" (I fell asleep), "caiu no sono" (he/she fell asleep), "vou cair no sono" (I’m going to fall asleep).
target_language_example: Eu estava tão cansado que caí no sono no sofá.
native_language_example: I was so tired that I fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical mailbox/letterbox where mail is delivered or posted. In tech contexts, it can also mean an email inbox ("caixa de correio eletrónico" in European Portuguese; "caixa de entrada" is very common for "inbox"). Plural: "caixas de correio".
target_language_example: Pode colocar a carta na caixa de correio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put the letter in the mailbox, please?

additional_notes: Common in Brazil. You can also say "ATM" in conversation, but "caixa eletrônico" is the standard Portuguese term. Used when you need to withdraw cash ("sacar"), check your balance, or use banking services. The plural is "caixas eletrônicos".
target_language_example: Tem um caixa eletrônico perto daqui?
native_language_example: Is there an ATM near here?

additional_notes: A very direct command telling someone to stop talking. Often sounds rude or aggressive, especially with "cala a boca!" You can soften it with alternatives like "fica quieto/quieta" (be quiet) or "por favor" (please), but it can still feel harsh. In Portugal you may also hear "cala-te"; in Brazil "cala a boca" is common.
target_language_example: Cala a boca e presta atenção!
native_language_example: Shut up and pay attention!

meaning: to shut up; to be quiet (often as an order).
additional_notes: A strong, often rude way to tell someone to stop talking. Literally "to silence the mouth." You’ll also hear it as an imperative: "Cala a boca!" (very harsh). In polite situations, prefer "Fique/Fica quieto(a)" or "Pode fazer silêncio?"
target_language_example: Cala a boca e presta atenção.
native_language_example: Shut up and pay attention.

additional_notes: A very strong, rude command telling someone to stop talking. Often used in arguments and can sound aggressive. In polite situations, use softer alternatives like "fique quieto(a)" (be quiet), "silêncio" (quiet), or "por favor, pare de falar" (please stop talking).
target_language_example: Cale a boca e me deixe explicar!
native_language_example: Shut up and let me explain!

additional_notes: Common, informal way to ask someone to pause, slow down, or stop for a moment. Used in conversation to interrupt gently, buy time, or react to something surprising (similar to “whoa, wait”). Often said as "Calma aí!" and can be followed by what you want to clarify or do next.
target_language_example: Calma aí, deixa eu entender: você quer ir agora?
native_language_example: Hold on, let me understand: you want to go now?

additional_notes: Used in science/engineering contexts to talk about the area around a magnet or electric current where magnetic forces act. Often appears with verbs like "gerar" (to generate), "medir" (to measure), and "afetar" (to affect), and with adjectives like "forte" (strong) or "fraco" (weak).
target_language_example: O ímã cria um campo magnético ao seu redor.
native_language_example: The magnet creates a magnetic field around it.

additional_notes: Used for an outer garment you wear over your clothes to keep dry in the rain. In Brazil, it can also refer to a simple plastic poncho (common in emergencies). Often used with the verb "levar" (to bring) or "vestir" (to put on/wear).
target_language_example: Leva uma capa de chuva porque vai chover mais tarde.
native_language_example: Bring a raincoat because it’s going to rain later.

additional_notes: Used to say people are meeting or talking directly (not by phone, text, or online). Common with verbs like "conversar/falar" (to talk) and "encontrar-se" (to meet). It can also describe a confrontation or direct discussion.
target_language_example: Prefiro conversar cara a cara para esclarecer tudo.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk face to face to clear everything up.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning a fast, sporty-looking car. It’s typically used with an article (um/uma, o/a) and can be modified with adjectives (e.g., carro esportivo vermelho). In Brazil you’ll often also hear "carro esporte" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Ele comprou um carro esportivo vermelho.
native_language_example: He bought a red sports car.

additional_notes: Used for a romantic letter (traditionally on paper, but it can also be used for a written romantic message). The plural is “cartas de amor”.
target_language_example: Ele escreveu uma carta de amor para ela.
native_language_example: He wrote her a love letter.

additional_notes: Common in Brazil for an official identity document (often called "RG"). Used when asked for identification (e.g., by police, at banks, or to enter buildings). In Portugal, you may also see "cartão de cidadão" for the main national ID.
target_language_example: Preciso da sua carteira de identidade para fazer o cadastro.
native_language_example: I need your ID card to register you.

additional_notes: Used for paying in shops or online. You’ll often hear/see it in questions like “Aceita cartão de crédito?” (Do you take credit cards?) or “Posso pagar no cartão de crédito?” (Can I pay by credit card?). In Portuguese, the related phrase “cartão de débito” means “debit card.”
target_language_example: Posso pagar com cartão de crédito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: Used for a postcard you send through the mail, often with a short message and a photo/illustration (common on trips). Also used in expressions like “mandar/enviar um cartão postal” (to send a postcard) and “comprar um cartão postal” (to buy a postcard).
target_language_example: Comprei um cartão postal e vou mandar para a minha família.
native_language_example: I bought a postcard and I’m going to send it to my family.

additional_notes: A noun for a postcard you send while traveling, usually with a short message and a stamp. Plural: cartões-postais. You can say "mandar/enviar um cartão-postal" (to send a postcard) or "escrever um cartão-postal" (to write a postcard).
target_language_example: Vou mandar um cartão-postal para você de Lisboa.
native_language_example: I’m going to send you a postcard from Lisbon.

additional_notes: Very common in Portugal (European Portuguese). In Brazil, people more often say "banheiro". Literally means "bath house," but it’s used for any bathroom/toilet in a home, restaurant, etc. You can also say "a casa de banho" (the bathroom) and ask "Onde é a casa de banho?" (Where is the bathroom?).
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde é a casa de banho?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

meaning: country house; cottage (a house in the countryside).
additional_notes: Used for a house outside the city, often for weekends, vacations, or as a second home. Commonly refers to a rural/quiet setting (the countryside), not necessarily a farm. Also appears as “casa no campo” with the same general meaning.
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos para a casa de campo dos meus avós.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we’re going to my grandparents’ country house.

additional_notes: Used to give a consequence or alternative if the previous condition is not met. Common in instructions and warnings. Often followed by a comma: "..., caso contrário, ...".
target_language_example: Paga hoje; caso contrário, vais pagar uma multa.
native_language_example: Pay today; otherwise, you’ll pay a fine.

additional_notes: Used literally for a castle made of sand (usually at the beach). It can also be used figuratively to mean something fragile or based on unrealistic plans (like “a castle in the air”). Plural: “castelos de areia”.
target_language_example: As crianças fizeram um castelo de areia na praia.
native_language_example: The children made a sandcastle at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a very large (often approximate) quantity, typically with countable nouns: “centenas de milhares de + noun” (e.g., “centenas de milhares de pessoas”).
target_language_example: Havia centenas de milhares de pessoas na rua.
native_language_example: There were hundreds of thousands of people in the street.

additional_notes: Used before numbers to give an estimate (time, quantity, distance, price, etc.). It often translates as “about/around” in English; in time expressions you can also say “por volta de”. Not the same as “perto de” (“near”).
target_language_example: Chego aí cerca de meia hora.
native_language_example: I’ll get there in about half an hour.

meaning: to draw attention; to get someone’s attention; to call someone out (warn/reprimand).
additional_notes: Common with "para" + noun/verb: "chamar a atenção para um problema" (draw attention to a problem). With "de" + person: "chamar a atenção de alguém" often means to scold/reprimand someone or point out they did something wrong. Also used literally to mean something is eye-catching: "A vitrine chamou a atenção."
target_language_example: O professor chamou a atenção do aluno por falar durante a aula.
native_language_example: The teacher scolded the student for talking during class.

meaning: to attract attention; to call attention (to something).
additional_notes: Used when something/someone draws notice or when you want to point something out. Often appears as “chamar a atenção” (to attract attention) or “chamar a atenção para + [thing]” (to draw attention to). It can also mean to scold/reprimand someone (“chamar a atenção de alguém”).
target_language_example: Esse cartaz chama a atenção, mas o professor chamou a atenção do aluno por falar alto.
native_language_example: That poster attracts attention, but the teacher reprimanded the student for speaking loudly.

meaning: to call (someone) names; to insult verbally.
additional_notes: Used when someone uses rude or offensive words to insult another person (often in arguments, bullying, or teasing). You can add the person with "a" (e.g., "chamar nomes a alguém"). Commonly used with "não" to tell someone not to insult others.
target_language_example: Não chames nomes ao teu irmão!
native_language_example: Don’t call your brother names!

additional_notes: From the verb "chamar-se" (to be called). Used with your name: "Chamo-me Ana." In Brazil, it’s common to drop the hyphen in writing and speech: "Me chamo Ana" or simply "Eu sou Ana".
target_language_example: Olá, chamo-me David. Prazer em conhecê-lo.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is David. Nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Common tool term. Literally “slot key,” referring to the slotted (flat) screw head (“parafuso de fenda”). In Brazil you’ll also hear “chave de fenda” contrasted with “chave Phillips” (Phillips screwdriver).
target_language_example: Você tem uma chave de fenda para apertar esse parafuso?
native_language_example: Do you have a flathead screwdriver to tighten this screw?

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often hear "chave de fenda" (singular). Used for screws with a single straight slot (not Phillips/"cruz").
target_language_example: Preciso de uma chave de fendas para apertar este parafuso.
native_language_example: I need a flathead screwdriver to tighten this screw.

additional_notes: A common tool name. Despite the literal meaning “English key,” it refers to an adjustable wrench used to tighten/loosen nuts and bolts. Often used with verbs like "apertar" (tighten) and "afrouxar" (loosen).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma chave inglesa para apertar esse parafuso.
native_language_example: I need an adjustable wrench to tighten that screw.

additional_notes: A common drink. Used like English “green tea” in cafés, restaurants, and supermarkets. You may also see it with an article: “um chá verde” (a green tea) or “o chá verde” (the green tea).
target_language_example: Eu queria um chá verde, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a green tea, please.

additional_notes: Used for the belt that keeps you restrained in a car (and sometimes in other vehicles). Common in safety instructions and reminders: “Coloque/Ponha o cinto de segurança” (Put on your seat belt) and “Aperte o cinto de segurança” (Fasten your seat belt).
target_language_example: Por favor, aperte o cinto de segurança.
native_language_example: Please fasten your seat belt.

additional_notes: A common sociological/economic term for people/households with an intermediate income level (neither poor nor rich). Often used when talking about society, living standards, buying power, and politics. You can say "a classe média" (the middle class) or "da classe média" (from the middle class).
target_language_example: Ela vem de uma família de classe média.
native_language_example: She comes from a middle-class family.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone who studies in the same class as you (at school, university, or a course). It’s neutral and common; you can also hear "colega da turma" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: A Ana é minha colega de classe na universidade.
native_language_example: Ana is my classmate at the university.

meaning: roommate (someone you share a room with).
additional_notes: Used for someone who shares the same bedroom/dorm room with you (more specific than “colega de casa”, which is a housemate). You can also say “companheiro(a) de quarto”, especially in student housing. In Portuguese, “colega” is fairly neutral (not necessarily a close friend).
target_language_example: No intercâmbio, eu tinha um colega de quarto espanhol.
native_language_example: On the exchange program, I had a Spanish roommate.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something. Common as a short reply meaning “definitely / of course.” Also works inside a sentence to emphasize certainty.
target_language_example: —Você vem amanhã? —Com certeza!
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —For sure!

additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention, interrupt, pass by, or ask permission to enter/leave. Very common in everyday situations (shops, elevators, meetings). Can also be used alone as a polite way to move through a crowd (“Com licença!”).
target_language_example: Com licença, você pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me?

meaning: over time; as time goes by.
additional_notes: Used to talk about change that happens gradually. Often implies that something will become easier/better/different in the future ("you’ll get used to it"). Can also mean "with time" in a more general sense.
target_language_example: Com o tempo, você vai se acostumar com a cidade.
native_language_example: Over time, you’ll get used to the city.

additional_notes: Used as a polite, friendly way to accept a request or offer help. It can also be used after someone thanks you, similar to 'my pleasure' or 'glad to help.'
target_language_example: —Você pode me ajudar? —Com prazer!
native_language_example: —Can you help me? —With pleasure!

additional_notes: Used to ask about an amount of money, price, or budget. Common in questions like “Com quanto fica?” (How much does it come to?) or “Você está com quanto?” (How much money do you have on you?). Literally “with how much,” but in natural English you usually translate it as “how much.”
target_language_example: Com quanto fica tudo isso?
native_language_example: How much does all of that come to?

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something should include all items/options, often in food orders (“all the toppings”) or when you want the complete version of something. It can also mean doing something fully/wholeheartedly (“go all in”).
target_language_example: Eu quero um cachorro-quente com tudo, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot dog with everything, please.

meaning: food and drinks (refreshments), especially at an event.
additional_notes: A common, slightly informal way to talk about the snacks/refreshments served at a party, meeting, or reception. Often used in the plural to refer to what will be available to eat and drink (e.g., “Vai ter comes e bebes?”).
target_language_example: Vai haver comes e bebes depois da reunião.
native_language_example: There will be food and drinks after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used for a woman who works on an airplane taking care of passengers. The male form is "comissário de bordo"; a gender-neutral option is "assistente de bordo". In Portugal, you may also hear "assistente de bordo" more often.
target_language_example: A comissária de bordo pediu que todos apertassem os cintos de segurança.
native_language_example: The flight attendant asked everyone to fasten their seat belts.

meaning: “How come?” / “What do you mean?” / “Wait, what?” (asking for clarification or expressing surprise).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Portuguese. Used when you don’t understand, disagree, or are surprised and want the other person to explain. Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (“What do you mean?”) or sound a bit confrontational (“How come?!”). Often followed by a question or a repetition of what you just heard.
target_language_example: —Vou cancelar a viagem. —Como assim? A gente já comprou as passagens!
native_language_example: —I’m going to cancel the trip. —Wait, what? We already bought the tickets!

additional_notes: Used mostly in Brazilian Portuguese as a short reply to show strong agreement or willingness to do something. Often comes across as upbeat/colloquial, similar to “sure!” or “definitely!”.
target_language_example: —Você pode me ajudar amanhã? —Como não!
native_language_example: “Can you help me tomorrow?” “Of course!”

additional_notes: Used to accept someone’s preference or decision (“OK, your choice”). It can sound polite and neutral, but depending on tone it may also sound a bit dismissive (“fine, whatever you want”).
target_language_example: — Podemos marcar para amanhã? — Como queira.
native_language_example: — Can we schedule it for tomorrow? — As you wish.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unreal, hypothetical, or doubtful comparison. Very often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "como se fosse", "como se tivesse"). It can also appear in set phrases like "como se não bastasse" (as if that weren’t enough).
target_language_example: Ele fala comigo como se fosse meu chefe.
native_language_example: He talks to me as if he were my boss.

meaning: “how do you say … ?” (used to ask for a word or expression).
additional_notes: Used when you’re searching for the correct word/phrase in Portuguese. Often followed by the thing you want to translate: “Como se diz ‘receipt’ em português?” You can also use it alone (with a gesture or pointing) when you don’t know the word. More formal alternatives include “Como se chama…?” (“What is it called…?”).
target_language_example: Como se diz “receipt” em português?
native_language_example: How do you say “receipt” in Portuguese?

additional_notes: Very informal/colloquial, common in texting or casual chat. It drops the accent and the apostrophe/space you’d see in standard writing (e.g., “como estás?” or in Brazil often “como tá?”). Use with friends; in more polite contexts use “Como está?” (formal) or “Tudo bem?”.
target_language_example: Oi! Como tas?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: Common greeting (often written without the accent as “como vai?”, though the standard spelling is “Como vai?”). It literally means “how goes (it)” and is usually followed by “tudo bem?” (“all good?”) or a reply like “Vou bem, e você?” (“I’m well, and you?”). Can be used with “o senhor / a senhora” for more formality: “Como vai o senhor?”
target_language_example: Oi, como vai?
native_language_example: Hi, how are you?

additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese to ask someone to repeat or to show you didn’t understand. It can also be used to challenge what someone said (“How is that?”), depending on tone. Often followed by a repeat of what you heard: “Como é que é? Você disse o quê?”
target_language_example: Como é que é? Não ouvi o que você disse.
native_language_example: What? I didn’t hear what you said.

meaning: roommate (a person you share a room with).
additional_notes: Used for someone who shares the same bedroom with you (e.g., in a dorm/hostel). In many everyday situations, Brazilians/Portuguese speakers also say “colega de quarto” for the same idea. If you share the same apartment/house (not necessarily the same bedroom), the more common term is “companheiro de apartamento/casa” or simply “colega de apartamento/casa.”
target_language_example: Meu companheiro de quarto ronca muito.
native_language_example: My roommate snores a lot.

additional_notes: A chemistry term for a compound based on carbon (often containing hydrogen, and possibly oxygen, nitrogen, etc.). Common in science classes, labels, and news about chemicals. Not the same as "orgânico" meaning "organic" in food/farming (produced without certain pesticides, etc.), though the word is related.
target_language_example: O etanol é um composto orgânico usado como combustível.
native_language_example: Ethanol is an organic compound used as fuel.

additional_notes: Used for an account you have at a bank to deposit, withdraw, and manage money. Common in formal and everyday contexts (e.g., opening an account, giving your account details). Also appears without the accent sometimes in informal writing: "conta bancaria".
target_language_example: Preciso abrir uma conta bancária.
native_language_example: I need to open a bank account.

additional_notes: Used to set a requirement/condition for something to happen. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive: e.g., “contanto que você venha” (“as long as you come”). Common in both spoken and written Portuguese. Similar to “desde que” in many contexts.
target_language_example: Você pode sair mais cedo, contanto que termine o trabalho.
native_language_example: You can leave early, as long as you finish the work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about looking directly into someone’s eyes (or maintaining a direct look). Common in everyday conversation and in advice/instructions (e.g., interviews, presentations). Often used with the verb "fazer" (fazer contato visual) or "manter" (manter contato visual).
target_language_example: Tente manter contato visual quando estiver falando.
native_language_example: Try to maintain eye contact when you’re speaking.

additional_notes: A common phrase for traditional children’s stories with magic, princesses, witches, etc. Often used literally (a story) or figuratively to mean something unreal or too perfect to be true ("isso é conto de fadas"). Plural: "contos de fadas".
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, minha avó me contava contos de fadas antes de dormir.
native_language_example: When I was a child, my grandmother told me fairy tales before bed.

meaning: remote control (for a TV, AC, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for the handheld device you use to control an appliance from a distance, especially a TV ("controle remoto da TV"). In Brazil people often shorten it to "o controle" when context is clear. Plural: "controles remotos".
target_language_example: Você viu o controle remoto da TV?
native_language_example: Have you seen the TV remote control?

additional_notes: Usually refers to talk that isn’t serious, reliable, or useful (e.g., excuses, gossip, or promises with no real substance). Common in expressions like "Isso é conversa fiada" ("That’s nonsense") and "Não vem com conversa fiada" ("Don’t give me that nonsense").
target_language_example: Não acredito nisso — é conversa fiada.
native_language_example: I don’t believe that — it’s nonsense.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is pink. In European Portuguese, “cor-de-rosa” is often hyphenated, especially before a noun (e.g., “um vestido cor-de-rosa”). You can also hear “rosa” used alone to mean “pink,” but “cor de rosa” is very common and clear for beginners.
target_language_example: Comprei uma camisola cor de rosa.
native_language_example: I bought a pink sweater.

additional_notes: Common adjective for something that is pink. It agrees in gender and number: cor-de-rosa (m./f. singular) and cores-de-rosa (plural). Often used after the noun: "uma camisa cor-de-rosa". Also appears in the expression "ver tudo cor-de-rosa" (“to see everything through rose-colored glasses”).
target_language_example: Comprei uma blusa cor-de-rosa para a festa.
native_language_example: I bought a pink blouse for the party.

additional_notes: Used to talk about emotional pain, especially after a breakup or unrequited love. Often appears with the verb "estar" (estar de coração partido = to be heartbroken) or "ficar" (ficar de coração partido = to end up heartbroken). Literal meaning: "broken heart."
target_language_example: Depois do término, ela ficou de coração partido.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she was heartbroken.

meaning: to chase after; to go after (try hard to get something).
additional_notes: Often used both literally (running after someone/something) and figuratively (making an effort to achieve or obtain something). Common pattern: “correr atrás de + noun/pronoun” (e.g., correr atrás de um sonho, correr atrás do prejuízo). In Brazil, the figurative meaning (“go after it”, “hustle for it”) is very common.
target_language_example: Eu vou correr atrás de um emprego melhor.
native_language_example: I’m going to go after a better job.

meaning: to believe that; to think that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief, opinion, or assumption: "Eu creio que...". "Crer" is a bit more formal/literary than "achar" (to think) and often slightly stronger than "achar"; in everyday speech many people use "achar que" more often. Common variants: "creio que" (I believe that), "não creio que" (I don't believe that).
target_language_example: Eu creio que ele já saiu.
native_language_example: I believe that he has already left.

additional_notes: A formal legal/political term for extremely serious crimes committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against civilians (e.g., murder, deportation, torture). Often used in news, history, and international law contexts; plural: "crimes contra a humanidade".
target_language_example: O tribunal investigou o caso como crime contra a humanidade.
native_language_example: The court investigated the case as a crime against humanity.

meaning: 'to take care of' / 'to look after'; also 'to handle/deal with' (a task).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: cuidar de alguém/alguma coisa. Often means caring for a person/animal (feeding, helping, watching), but it can also mean taking responsibility for a matter or task ("I’ll take care of it"). In Portuguese, you normally say "cuidar de" (not just "cuidar" by itself) before the thing/person you’re taking care of.
target_language_example: Eu cuido das crianças enquanto você faz o jantar.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the kids while you make dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how expensive it is to live in a place (rent, food, transportation, etc.). Often appears with comparisons (mais alto/mais baixo), and with verbs like “aumentar” (to go up) and “diminuir” (to go down).
target_language_example: O custo de vida em Lisboa aumentou muito nos últimos anos.
native_language_example: The cost of living in Lisbon has increased a lot in recent years.

additional_notes: Used to specify a still-photo camera (as opposed to a video camera). In everyday speech, people often just say "câmera" or "máquina fotográfica". Article and gender: "a câmera fotográfica" (feminine).
target_language_example: Levei a câmera fotográfica para tirar fotos da viagem.
native_language_example: I took the camera to take photos on the trip.

additional_notes: A medical term meaning cancer in the lungs. Very commonly used with the verb "ter" (to have) and in health-related contexts. In Brazil, you may also see the spelling "cancro do pulmão" in European Portuguese.
target_language_example: Meu avô teve câncer de pulmão e fez tratamento por vários meses.
native_language_example: My grandfather had lung cancer and underwent treatment for several months.

additional_notes: A simple noun + adjective phrase (Portuguese often puts the adjective after the noun). You can use it literally to talk about the weather or scenery; it can also sound poetic when describing a nice day.
target_language_example: Hoje o céu azul está lindo.
native_language_example: Today the blue sky is beautiful.

additional_notes: Very informal Brazilian Portuguese. It’s a contracted form of “você que sabe” and is used when you don’t have a preference or want the other person to choose. Often said neutrally, but depending on tone it can sound a bit dismissive (like “whatever you want”).
target_language_example: — Vamos comer pizza ou hambúrguer? — Cê que sabe.
native_language_example: — Should we eat pizza or burgers? — It’s up to you.

additional_notes: Very informal Brazilian Portuguese. “cê” is a reduced form of “você” (“you”), common in speech and casual texting. Often used to show surprise, disbelief, or mild scolding; depending on tone it can be playful or rude. More neutral: “Você é louco?”
target_language_example: Cê é louco? Você pagou quanto nisso?
native_language_example: Are you crazy? How much did you pay for that?

additional_notes: Used for the square scannable code you scan with your phone (camera or an app) to open a link, see a menu, pay, check in, etc. Often appears as: “Ler/Escanear o código QR” (read/scan the QR code) or “Aponte a câmera para o código QR” (point the camera at the QR code).
target_language_example: Você pode escanear o código QR para ver o cardápio?
native_language_example: Can you scan the QR code to see the menu?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the communication system that uses dots and dashes to represent letters and numbers. Common in technical or historical contexts; often appears with the verb “aprender” (to learn) or “transmitir” (to transmit).
target_language_example: Ele aprendeu código morse no exército.
native_language_example: He learned Morse code in the army.

additional_notes: Informal expression used mainly in Brazil to praise something (a movie, idea, place, person, etc.). It often follows the verb "ser" (e.g., "é da hora"). Not usually understood as a literal "of the hour" meaning.
target_language_example: Esse filme é da hora!
native_language_example: This movie is awesome!

additional_notes: Most often used after a noun to mean “of one’s life,” usually with an article/possessive: “da minha vida” (of my life), “da vida dele/dela” (of his/her life). It can also appear in a more general sense meaning “in life” or “in someone’s life,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Foi o melhor dia da vida dela.
native_language_example: It was the best day of her life.

additional_notes: Used mainly in wedding contexts. In Portugal and Brazil, it can refer to any bridesmaid, but it’s also commonly used for the main bridesmaid (maid/matron of honor) depending on the wedding. Plural: "damas de honra".
target_language_example: A minha irmã vai ser minha dama de honra no casamento.
native_language_example: My sister is going to be my bridesmaid/maid of honor at the wedding.

meaning: “Screw it.” / “To hell with it.” (strong, rude dismissal).
additional_notes: Very informal and considered profanity. Used to show anger, frustration, or that you don’t care anymore. Often appears as an exclamation (“Dane-se!”). You may also hear “Dane-se isso!” (“Screw that!”). In polite situations, prefer softer options like “deixa pra lá” (let it go) or “não tem problema” (no problem).
target_language_example: Ah, dane-se — eu vou embora.
native_language_example: Ah, screw it — I’m leaving.

meaning: "in" (a period of time); "from now until" (a future time/point).
additional_notes: Used to talk about time starting from now: (1) duration + "daqui a" = "in" (e.g., "daqui a 10 minutos" = "in 10 minutes"); (2) "daqui a" + time/point/event = "until" or "from now to" (e.g., "daqui a amanhã" = "until tomorrow"). Often appears in the fixed expression "daqui a pouco" (in a little while).
target_language_example: Daqui a meia hora eu te ligo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in half an hour.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning “after a short time (from now)”. It can mean “soon” (imprecise) or “later, in a bit.” Often used to say you’ll do something shortly: “Eu já volto daqui a pouco” (I’ll be right back). Less immediate than “já” (right now) and similar to “daqui a um pouco” or “daqui a uns minutos” (in a few minutes).
target_language_example: Daqui a pouco eu te ligo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in a little while.

meaning: to hold hands; to give a hand (help).
additional_notes: Literally “to give the hand.” Commonly used as “dar a mão a alguém” (to hold someone’s hand), often with kids or in romantic contexts. In a broader sense it can also mean to help/support someone, similar to “dar uma mão” (give a hand). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Pode me dar a mão para atravessar a rua?
native_language_example: Can you hold my hand to cross the street?

meaning: to give someone the floor; to let someone speak.
additional_notes: Used in meetings, classes, or discussions when a moderator/teacher invites someone to speak (e.g., “Vou dar a palavra ao João.”). It can also mean “to give your word” (to promise), especially in “dar a palavra (de) que…”, though “dar a sua palavra” is clearer for that sense.
target_language_example: Agora vou dar a palavra à Maria para ela explicar o projeto.
native_language_example: Now I’m going to give Maria the floor so she can explain the project.

additional_notes: Used with the general meaning “to teach,” especially in school/university contexts. Often followed by the subject: “dar aula de matemática” (teach math). You can also specify where: “dar aula na escola/universidade” (teach at the school/university). In Portuguese you say “dar” (to give) + “aula” (class/lesson), not *fazer aula*.
target_language_example: Ela dá aula de inglês na universidade.
native_language_example: She teaches English at the university.

meaning: to pay attention to; to show interest (often romantically).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese and informal. Often used with "para/em alguém" meaning you pay attention to someone or flirt/show interest in them. In the negative, "não dar bola" means to ignore someone/something.
target_language_example: Ela não deu bola pra ele na festa.
native_language_example: She didn’t pay attention to him at the party.

meaning: to call the shots; to be the one in control.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning someone has the power to decide what happens (they set the rules). It comes from card games, where the person who deals the cards controls the start of the round. Can also be used about a person/company that dominates a market or situation.
target_language_example: Na negociação, quem dá cartas é o cliente.
native_language_example: In the negotiation, the client is the one calling the shots.

meaning: to manage/handle (to be able to cope).
additional_notes: Very common with "de": "dar conta de + noun/verb" = to be able to do/handle something (often used in the negative: "não dou conta"). It can also mean "to notice/realize" ("Dei conta de que..." = I realized that...) and, in some contexts, "to finish/consume" (food/drink).
target_language_example: Não dou conta de tudo sozinho.
native_language_example: I can’t handle everything by myself.

meaning: to work hard; to put in a lot of effort.
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used for sustained effort at work, studying, training, or pursuing a goal. Often appears as "dar duro no trabalho" (work hard at work) or "dar duro pra passar" (work hard to pass). Conjugates with "dar": eu dou duro, você/ele dá duro, nós damos duro, eles dão duro.
target_language_example: Tenho dado duro no trabalho para conseguir uma promoção.
native_language_example: I’ve been working hard at work to get a promotion.

meaning: to hit on (someone); to come on to (someone).
additional_notes: Informal. Usually used as "dar em cima de alguém" (to flirt with someone / make a pass at someone). Can sound a bit forward depending on context. In other contexts, "dar em cima" can also mean to confront or put pressure on someone, but the most common everyday use is romantic/sexual interest.
target_language_example: Ele ficou dando em cima dela a noite toda.
native_language_example: He kept hitting on her all night.

meaning: to get on someone’s nerves; to drive someone crazy (annoy).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, noise, or situation is really annoying you. Common in everyday speech. Often used with an indirect object: “dar-me/te/lhe nos nervos” (to get on my/your/his/her nerves). You can also use “isso dá-me nos nervos” (that gets on my nerves).
target_language_example: Esse barulho está a dar-me nos nervos.
native_language_example: That noise is getting on my nerves.

meaning: to leave (often abruptly); to get out of here.
additional_notes: Informal expression. Often used as an imperative: "Dá o fora!" = "Get out!" It can also mean to leave a place/party quickly: "dei o fora". Conjugates like "dar": eu dou / você dá / ele dá; past: eu dei. Similar idea to "ir embora" but more abrupt/colloquial.
target_language_example: Está tarde — vou dar o fora.
native_language_example: It’s late — I’m going to head out.

meaning: to listen (to) / to pay attention to (someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used with "a" + a person/thing ("dar ouvidos a alguém"). It often implies choosing to take someone seriously or follow their advice (or refusing to): "Não dê ouvidos" = “Don’t listen to them / don’t pay attention.”
target_language_example: Não dê ouvidos ao que eles dizem.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to what they say.

meaning: to be possible; to be enough / fit for.
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often followed by an infinitive to mean “it’s possible to…” (e.g., Dá para fazer isso hoje? = Can we do that today?). It can also mean something is enough for a purpose (e.g., Isso dá para duas pessoas = That’s enough for two people) or that something fits/works for a situation (e.g., Esta chave dá para esta porta = This key works/fit for this door).
target_language_example: Dá para ir a pé até lá?
native_language_example: Is it possible to walk there?

meaning: to find a way; to fix/solve something (somehow).
additional_notes: Very common everyday expression meaning you’ll manage to solve a problem or make something work, often with some improvisation. It can mean “fix” (a situation/object) or “sort it out” (an issue). Often used as: “Eu dou um jeito” (I’ll handle it / I’ll find a way) or “Dá um jeito!” (Figure it out!). Related: “dar um jeito em (algo)” = to fix/sort out (something).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, eu vou dar um jeito nisso.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll find a way to sort this out.

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used to say someone is putting on an attitude/role or trying to seem like something (often with a mildly critical or teasing tone). It’s usually followed by a noun or adjective: "dar uma de esperto" (act smart), "dar uma de vítima" (play the victim), "dar uma de chefe" (act like the boss). Often used as "dar uma de + [role]" or "dar uma de + [adjective]".
target_language_example: Ele deu uma de esperto, mas não sabia do que estava falando.
native_language_example: He acted smart, but he didn’t know what he was talking about.

meaning: to help (someone); to give a hand.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression meaning to assist someone with a task. Often used with “para” + infinitive: “dar uma mão para + verb” (to help to do something). You can also say “dar uma mão a alguém” (to help someone).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma mão com as malas?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?

meaning: to value; to appreciate; to give importance to.
additional_notes: Used when talking about appreciating someone/something or treating it as important. Common patterns: "dar valor a" (to value/appreciate), and "dar valor a si mesmo" (to value yourself). In the negative, it can mean not paying attention to someone: "não dar valor".
target_language_example: Você precisa dar valor ao que tem.
native_language_example: You need to appreciate what you have.

meaning: to go around; to take a quick walk/ride (often: “dar uma volta”).
additional_notes: Usually used as “dar uma volta” (take a short walk/drive) or “dar a volta” (go around something / take the long way around). It can be literal (walking/driving around a place) or more general (go out for a bit).
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma volta no quarteirão depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s take a walk around the block after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about childbirth. Literally “to give to the light,” but in Portuguese it simply means “to give birth.” You’ll often see it with a direct object (the baby): “dar à luz um menino/uma menina.”
target_language_example: Ela deu à luz uma menina ontem.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a baby girl yesterday.

meaning: old-school; from back in the day.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to describe something in an old-fashioned, nostalgic, or traditional style (music, clothes, habits, places). Often used with "estilo" or after a noun: "som das antigas" (old-school sound), "bar das antigas" (old-style bar). Similar idea to "à moda antiga" (more neutral/formal: 'in the old-fashioned way').
target_language_example: Eu gosto de música das antigas.
native_language_example: I like old-school music.

meaning: “of Jesus”; used in names and set phrases.
additional_notes: Literally means “of Jesus.” Common in Portuguese personal names (especially in Brazil/Portugal) as a religious family-name element (e.g., Maria de Jesus). It can also appear in expressions like “Igreja de Jesus” (“Church of Jesus”). In names, it’s usually not translated; you typically keep it as part of the person’s full name.
target_language_example: O nome dela é Maria de Jesus.
native_language_example: Her name is Maria de Jesus.

additional_notes: Used after a first name (often “Fulano”) to refer to an unknown, unnamed, or unimportant person: “Fulano de tal”. It’s common in speech and informal writing, and can sound slightly dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Quem te ligou foi o João de tal.
native_language_example: The one who called you was so-and-so João.

meaning: in agreement; OK / agreed; according to.
additional_notes: Common in expressions like "estar de acordo" (to agree), "de acordo?" (OK?/Agreed?), and "de acordo com" (according to). As a short reply, it’s a neutral way to say you agree or accept instructions.
target_language_example: Tudo bem, estou de acordo com você.
native_language_example: All right, I agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a source, reference, rule, or opinion (a person, document, law, report, schedule, etc.). Very common in formal and neutral contexts. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: "de acordo com o médico" (according to the doctor), "de acordo com a lei" (according to the law).
target_language_example: De acordo com o relatório, as vendas aumentaram este mês.
native_language_example: According to the report, sales increased this month.

meaning: from now on; from this point forward.
additional_notes: Used to mark a change starting at the present moment, often after a decision, rule, or new situation. It can refer to “from now on” in time, and also “from here on out” in a conversation or document (e.g., introducing a new term or rule).
target_language_example: De agora em diante, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m going to study Portuguese every day.

additional_notes: Common in expressions like “uma pessoa de bem” (a decent/straightforward person) and “ficar/estar de bem com alguém” (to be on good terms with someone). Often suggests being peaceful, friendly, and not looking for trouble.
target_language_example: Ele é uma pessoa de bem e está de bem com todo mundo.
native_language_example: He’s a decent person and is on good terms with everyone.

additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese slang. Used to say you’re fine/okay, calm, relaxed, or that something is not a problem (similar to “it’s cool” or “no big deal”). Common in replies like “Tô de boa” (I’m good) or “Fica de boa” (Relax / Don’t worry).
target_language_example: Fica de boa, eu resolvo isso depois.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of that later.

meaning: willingly; gladly; of one’s own free will.
additional_notes: Used to say you do something because you want to (not because you’re forced). Often comes with verbs like "fazer" (to do) or "ajudar" (to help): "Eu faço de boa vontade." It can also politely accept a request: "De boa vontade" = "Sure / gladly."
target_language_example: Eu te ajudo de boa vontade.
native_language_example: I’ll help you gladly.

meaning: chill; relaxed; no worries; it’s all good.
additional_notes: Common Brazilian Portuguese slang. Used to say you’re fine/okay with something (“I’m cool with it”) or that things are calm/relaxed. Often appears with verbs like “ficar” (to stay/be) or “estar” (to be): “Tô de boas.”
target_language_example: Pode deixar, eu tô de boas com isso.
native_language_example: No worries, I’m cool with that.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe a smaller, portable version of something: "livro de bolso" (paperback/pocket book), "dicionário de bolso" (pocket dictionary), "guia de bolso" (pocket guide). It can also mean "for pocket/money" in some contexts (e.g., "dinheiro de bolso" = pocket money), but the most common beginner use is "pocket-sized".
target_language_example: Comprei um dicionário de bolso para levar na viagem.
native_language_example: I bought a pocket dictionary to take on the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something with pleasure or without hesitation. Often appears with verbs like "fazer" (to do), "aceitar" (to accept), "ajudar" (to help): "Eu aceito de bom grado". Slightly formal/literary in everyday conversation; in casual speech you might also hear "de boa" (Brazil) or simply "com prazer" depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu aceito de bom grado o seu convite.
native_language_example: I gladly accept your invitation.

additional_notes: Used to describe a position where someone is lying with their belly on the ground/bed and their face turned downward. Common with verbs like "ficar" (to stay), "deitar" (to lie down), "cair" (to fall), and "dormir" (to sleep): "ficar/deitar-se de bruços".
target_language_example: Ele caiu de bruços no chão.
native_language_example: He fell face down on the floor.

additional_notes: Used when you can say/recite something without looking (no notes, no phone, no book): “saber de cabeça” = to know by heart. It can also mean “headfirst” or “fully/wholeheartedly” in expressions like “mergulhar de cabeça” (to dive in headfirst / to throw yourself into something).
target_language_example: Eu sei esse poema de cabeça.
native_language_example: I know this poem by heart.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is inverted (orientation flipped). It can be literal (an object turned over) or sometimes figurative (a situation is chaotic or “turned upside down”). Often used with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/become): "Está/Ficou de cabeça para baixo."
target_language_example: O quadro está de cabeça para baixo.
native_language_example: The picture frame is upside down.

meaning: from beginning to end; all the way through.
additional_notes: Means doing/reading/watching something completely, without skipping anything. Often used with verbs like "ler" (to read), "assistir" (to watch), "ouvir" (to listen), and "conhecer" (to know).
target_language_example: Li o livro de cabo a rabo.
native_language_example: I read the book from beginning to end.

meaning: in bed; bedridden (staying in bed because you’re sick).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ficar" or "estar" to say someone is (staying) in bed, often due to illness or recovery. Common phrases: "ficar de cama" (to be stuck in bed / bedridden) and "estar de cama" (to be in bed, typically because you’re unwell).
target_language_example: Estou de cama desde ontem com gripe.
native_language_example: I’ve been in bed since yesterday with the flu.

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in everyday speech. Often used with verbs like "saber" (to know), "perceber" (to notice), "ver" (to see): "Percebi de cara" = "I noticed right away." It can also mean "at first glance" depending on context: "De cara, achei estranho" = "At first, I found it strange."
target_language_example: Eu percebi de cara que ele estava nervoso.
native_language_example: I noticed right away that he was nervous.

meaning: 'in a way' / 'in some way' (to some extent).
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or show partial agreement: you’re saying something is true or makes sense, but not completely or not in every case. Very common in conversation and writing. Often appears with verbs like "ser", "entender", "concordar": "De certa forma, eu concordo."
target_language_example: De certa forma, ele tem razão, mas não é tão simples assim.
native_language_example: In a way, he’s right, but it’s not that simple.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty or a confident assumption. In everyday Portuguese it often sounds a bit formal/literary, and it can also mean “most likely / probably” depending on context. Commonly appears in the phrase “de certo que …” (“surely/most likely …”).
target_language_example: Ele de certo já chegou em casa.
native_language_example: He’s probably already arrived home.

additional_notes: Used when you know something so well you can say it without looking (a poem, song lyrics, a phone number, etc.). Common with verbs like "saber" and "decorar": "saber de cor" = to know by heart. Also appears as one word in spelling: "decor".
target_language_example: Eu sei essa música de cor.
native_language_example: I know that song by heart.

additional_notes: Means something is habitual or customary. Very common in the fixed expression "como de costume" (“as usual”). It often appears at the end of a sentence ("..., de costume") or after "como". Note: despite containing "costume", it generally does NOT mean “in costume/dressed up”.
target_language_example: Ela tomou café, como de costume, antes de sair.
native_language_example: She had coffee, as usual, before leaving.

meaning: during the day; in the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens in daylight hours (as opposed to "de noite" = at night). Common with verbs like "trabalhar" (to work), "dormir" (to sleep), "sair" (to go out), and "estar aberto" (to be open).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho de dia e estudo à noite.
native_language_example: I work during the day and study at night.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true or real, often to correct, confirm, or add emphasis. Similar to "na verdade" in many contexts. Can also appear as "de facto" (more formal/Latinized spelling) in some texts.
target_language_example: Eu achava que ele era brasileiro, mas ele é, de fato, português.
native_language_example: I thought he was Brazilian, but he is, in fact, Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny something or refuse a request. It’s common in polite speech when paired with “não” (e.g., “Não, de forma alguma.”). It can also mean “by no means” in statements. The tone is emphatic but not slang.
target_language_example: —Você se importa se eu abrir a janela? —Não, de forma alguma.
native_language_example: —Do you mind if I open the window? —No, not at all.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs nothing. It can also mean “for nothing / in vain” in some contexts (e.g., effort that doesn’t help). Often used with verbs like ser/estar (“é/está de graça”), conseguir (“consegui de graça”), or dar (“me deram de graça”).
target_language_example: A entrada é de graça, mas precisa reservar online.
native_language_example: Entry is free, but you need to book online.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will be different starting at this moment (or from today forward). Often used when making a decision, setting a new rule, or changing a habit. Similar to “a partir de agora”.
target_language_example: De hoje em diante, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m going to study Portuguese every day.

meaning: "of honor" / "honorary" (used to indicate something prestigious or ceremonial).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show it is connected to honor or is an honorary/ceremonial role or distinction. Common in set phrases and titles like "menção de honra" (honorable mention), "código de honra" (code of honor), and "dama de honra" (maid of honor). Meaning depends on the noun it follows.
target_language_example: Ela recebeu uma menção de honra pelo trabalho.
native_language_example: She received an honorable mention for her work.

additional_notes: Used after a number to say someone’s age: "Tenho 20 anos de idade" (I’m 20 years old). Often optional because "anos" alone is enough ("Tenho 20 anos"). Can also be used more generally to mean "of age" or "aged" in descriptions, especially in formal contexts (e.g., "menores de 18 anos de idade" = minors under 18).
target_language_example: Ela tem 30 anos de idade.
native_language_example: She is 30 years old.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be done correctly or in an appropriate manner (often after a verb: fazer de jeito, arrumar de jeito). It also appears in fixed expressions like “de jeito nenhum” (“no way / not at all”).
target_language_example: Faz isso de jeito, por favor.
native_language_example: Do that properly, please.

meaning: No way; not at all; absolutely not.
additional_notes: Strong, emphatic negation used to refuse, deny, or emphasize that something is impossible. Common in everyday speech; can sound blunt depending on tone. Often used as a short standalone answer (like “No way!”) or to reinforce another negative (e.g., “Não vou, de jeito nenhum.”).
target_language_example: Você vai contar para alguém? — De jeito nenhum!
native_language_example: Are you going to tell anyone? — No way!

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "estar": "estar de lua". It means someone’s mood changes a lot, or they’re in a particular (often unpredictable) mood at the moment. Common in informal speech.
target_language_example: Hoje ele está de lua; melhor não falar com ele agora.
native_language_example: He’s in a mood today; better not talk to him right now.

meaning: in mourning; wearing mourning (after someone dies).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to say someone is mourning: "estar de luto". It can also describe clothing (often black) traditionally worn after a death. Commonly followed by "por" + the person who died: "de luto por alguém".
target_language_example: Ela está de luto pela avó.
native_language_example: She is in mourning for her grandmother.

additional_notes: Used especially in Brazil to say someone is legally an adult (usually 18 or older), often contrasting with "de menor" (a minor). Common in everyday speech and also understood in formal contexts (e.g., rules, age restrictions).
target_language_example: Ele já é de maior, então pode assinar o contrato.
native_language_example: He’s already an adult (of legal age), so he can sign the contract.

meaning: on bad terms; upset/angry (with someone) (usually in "estar de mal (com)").
additional_notes: Most common in the expression "estar de mal com alguém" = to be upset with someone / not speaking / not getting along. You can also see it in "de mal a pior" = from bad to worse, but "de mal" alone is typically part of a larger expression.
target_language_example: Eu estou de mal com o João desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’m upset with João since yesterday.

additional_notes: A strong, emphatic way to say “no” or “not at all,” often used to reject a suggestion, deny something, or reassure someone (like “Absolutely not”). Can also appear after a negative statement for emphasis. Typically comes at the end of the sentence or right after what it negates.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu conte para eles? De maneira alguma!
native_language_example: Do you want me to tell them? No way!

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something without looking at notes or a text (e.g., reciting, singing, giving information). Often appears after verbs like “saber” (to know) or “recitar” (to recite): “saber de memória” = “to know by heart.”
target_language_example: Eu sei essa música de memória.
native_language_example: I know that song by heart.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is not genuine (e.g., "um relógio de mentira" = a fake watch). It can also describe something imaginary/pretend, especially with kids or in games ("de mentirinha" is a common, more playful variant).
target_language_example: Ele comprou um relógio de mentira na feira.
native_language_example: He bought a fake watch at the market.

meaning: “shitty” / “of shit” (vulgar; used to insult or show strong frustration).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used after a noun to strongly criticize it: “um trabalho de merda” (“a shitty job”), “um carro de merda” (“a crappy car”). Also common in fixed phrases like “Que dia de merda!” (“What a shitty day!”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Esse serviço é de merda.
native_language_example: This service is shitty.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or refuse something (often as a stand-alone answer). It sounds firm and can be emphatic, but it isn’t slang. Commonly appears after a negative statement (e.g., “Não quero, de modo algum.”) or in replies (“— Você fez isso? — De modo algum!”).
target_language_example: — Você está com raiva de mim? — De modo algum!
native_language_example: — Are you mad at me? — Not at all!

meaning: soaking; also (informally) sidelined/out of action (because of illness or injury).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like “deixar” or “pôr” when talking about food in liquid: “Deixe o feijão de molho” (leave the beans soaking). In everyday speech, “ficar de molho” means to be stuck resting/recovering and not able to do your usual activities (often at home).
target_language_example: Fiquei de molho com gripe a semana toda.
native_language_example: I was out of action with the flu all week.

additional_notes: Used to describe two people physically holding hands (often a romantic or affectionate image). It can also be used figuratively to mean things go together or happen together ("hand in hand"). Common with verbs like "andar" (to walk), "ir" (to go), and "ficar" (to be/stay).
target_language_example: Eles estavam andando de mãos dadas no parque.
native_language_example: They were walking hand in hand in the park.

meaning: empty-handed; with nothing to bring/show for it.
additional_notes: Used when someone arrives or leaves without bringing anything (e.g., not bringing a gift or items requested), or when someone fails to obtain anything after an effort (e.g., searching/shopping and finding nothing). Often used with verbs like "chegar" (to arrive), "vir" (to come), "voltar" (to return), "sair" (to leave).
target_language_example: Não vá de mãos vazias para a festa; leve um vinho.
native_language_example: Don’t go to the party empty-handed; bring a bottle of wine.

additional_notes: Common reply after someone says “obrigado/obrigada” (“thank you”). Literally “of nothing,” meaning “it was nothing.” Neutral and very frequent in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: —Obrigado pela ajuda! —De nada!
native_language_example: —Thanks for the help! —You’re welcome!

additional_notes: Used after a noun/adjective to indicate something is true because of someone’s birth or since they were born (not acquired later). Common in phrases like “português de nascença” (Portuguese by birth) or “cego de nascença” (blind from birth).
target_language_example: Ela é brasileira de nascença, mas mora no Canadá desde criança.
native_language_example: She is Brazilian by birth, but she has lived in Canada since she was a child.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the night period. Very common in everyday speech. Often contrasts with "de dia" (during the day). In European Portuguese, you may also see "à noite" used very frequently with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho de noite e durmo de dia.
native_language_example: I work at night and sleep during the day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens another time or you’re restarting something. Often placed after the verb: “começar de novo” (start again), “tentar de novo” (try again). In everyday speech you may hear redundant combinations like “repetir de novo” (“repeat again”), but “repetir” already implies “again.”
target_language_example: Vamos começar de novo.
native_language_example: Let’s start again.

meaning: keeping an eye on; watching; on the lookout.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ficar" or "estar" to mean paying attention, monitoring, or being alert (often to prevent a problem or not miss something): "ficar de olho em" (keep an eye on / watch), "estar de olho" (be watching / be on the lookout).
target_language_example: Fica de olho nas suas coisas no metrô.
native_language_example: Keep an eye on your things on the subway.

meaning: “of gold”; “golden” (made of gold or figuratively very valuable).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something made of gold (um anel de ouro = a gold ring). It’s also common in figurative expressions like “idade de ouro” (golden age) or “regra de ouro” (golden rule).
target_language_example: Ela usa um anel de ouro.
native_language_example: She wears a gold ring.

additional_notes: Used to say you are physically close to something/someone ("up close") or that you are monitoring something carefully ("closely"). Often appears with verbs like ver (to see), olhar (to look), conhecer (to get to know), acompanhar (to follow/track), observar (to observe). Common contrast: de longe (from far away).
target_language_example: Quero ver isso de perto.
native_language_example: I want to see that up close.

additional_notes: Used to describe something modern, advanced, and among the best available (technology, research, equipment, services, professionals). Common in phrases like “tecnologia de ponta” (cutting-edge technology) and “equipamento de ponta” (state-of-the-art equipment).
target_language_example: O hospital tem equipamentos de ponta.
native_language_example: The hospital has state-of-the-art equipment.

meaning: upside down; turned over; in disorder.
additional_notes: Used to describe something literally inverted (e.g., a picture, a shirt) or figuratively thrown into chaos (e.g., plans, life). Often used with verbs like "ficar" (to end up/become) and "virar" (to turn). Also written "de ponta cabeça" (without hyphen) in everyday writing.
target_language_example: Meu quarto ficou de ponta-cabeça depois da mudança.
native_language_example: My room was upside down (a total mess) after the move.

meaning: not very talkative; a person of few words.
additional_notes: Describes someone who speaks little or is very concise (often implying they are quiet, reserved, or to-the-point). Commonly used after "ser" ("Ele é de poucas palavras") or as a descriptor in a sentence. Not necessarily negative; it can be neutral or even complimentary depending on context.
target_language_example: Meu pai é de poucas palavras, mas sempre me ajuda quando preciso.
native_language_example: My dad is a man of few words, but he always helps me when I need it.

meaning: on the first try; straight away (also: top-notch).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say something worked immediately or was done successfully on the first attempt: "passar de primeira" (to pass on the first try), "funcionar de primeira" (to work right away). In some contexts it can also mean "excellent / first-class" (similar to "de primeira qualidade"), though the “first try” meaning is very frequent in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O carro pegou de primeira.
native_language_example: The car started on the first try.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is ready to act immediately or is available if needed (often with verbs like estar/ficar/manter-se). Common in professional, emergency, or formal contexts: “estar de prontidão” = to be on call/on standby.
target_language_example: A equipe médica ficou de prontidão durante o evento.
native_language_example: The medical team stayed on standby during the event.

additional_notes: Used to say something was done deliberately (often implying it wasn’t an accident). Common with verbs like "fazer" and "dizer": "fez de propósito" (did it on purpose). In European Portuguese you’ll also hear "de propósito" meaning "by the way" when introducing a new topic (e.g., "De propósito, amanhã não posso").
target_language_example: Ele fez isso de propósito.
native_language_example: He did that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like estar/ficar (“to be/to remain”) to describe someone’s posture: estar de pé = “to be standing.” It can also describe doing something while standing (e.g., comer de pé = “to eat standing up”) or being “on foot” (ir de pé = “to go on foot”).
target_language_example: Eu estava de pé na fila quando você chegou.
native_language_example: I was standing in line when you arrived.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe that something is well-made or reliable: "um produto de qualidade". It’s also common with "boa" for emphasis: "de boa qualidade" (= of good quality). In some contexts it can be closer to “quality” as a category/standard (e.g., "controle de qualidade" = quality control), but as an adjective phrase it usually means “high-quality.”
target_language_example: Quero um café de qualidade.
native_language_example: I want a high-quality coffee.

additional_notes: Used to change topic, wrap up a point, or say something is true regardless of what was just mentioned. Often comes at the beginning of a sentence (“De qualquer forma, …”) or after a pause. Similar in tone to “anyway” in English and works in both speech and writing.
target_language_example: De qualquer forma, vamos sair às oito.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’re going out at eight.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese. Often means “anyway / regardless” to move on in a conversation (similar to “anyway…”). It can also describe doing something without care or in a messy/quick way (“any old way”), which can sound critical depending on tone and context. Sometimes interchangeable with “de qualquer forma / de todo jeito,” though “de qualquer jeito” can feel a bit more informal and can imply sloppiness when describing how something is done.
target_language_example: Estou cansado, mas vou de qualquer jeito.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but I’m going anyway.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation forward, show that something is true regardless of other details, or change topics. Often appears at the start of a sentence ("De qualquer maneira, ...") and can sound slightly dismissive depending on tone. Close to "de qualquer forma".
target_language_example: De qualquer maneira, vamos sair às oito.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’re going to leave at eight.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation on, conclude a topic, or emphasize that something remains true regardless of circumstances. Similar in tone to “anyway” in English; it can sound slightly dismissive depending on context. Also appears as “de qualquer maneira” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: De qualquer modo, vamos embora porque já está tarde.
native_language_example: Anyway, let’s go because it’s already late.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person or animal positioned with both hands (or front legs) and knees (or back legs) on the ground. It’s common in everyday speech (e.g., babies crawling, looking for something on the floor). In some contexts it can also refer to a sexual position, so tone and situation matter.
target_language_example: O bebê ficou de quatro e começou a engatinhar.
native_language_example: The baby got on all fours and started crawling.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the manner, method, or way something is done or happens. It’s slightly more formal than just "como" and often appears in questions (direct or indirect). Can also be used to ask for clarification about steps or procedures.
target_language_example: De que forma posso pagar?
native_language_example: How can I pay?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the method or manner of doing something. It’s similar to “como?”, but can sound a bit more specific or emphatic (asking “in what way exactly?”). Common in conversation, including in Brazil.
target_language_example: De que jeito eu faço isso?
native_language_example: How do I do this?

meaning: “how” / “in what way” (asking about the manner or method).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the way something is done or happens. Often interchangeable with "como", but "de que maneira" can sound a bit more formal or emphatic. Common in questions and indirect questions (e.g., "Não sei de que maneira...").
target_language_example: De que maneira você resolveu esse problema?
native_language_example: How did you solve that problem?

additional_notes: Used after the preposition **de** when asking what something is about or what someone needs/likes/is talking about. Common with verbs that take **de** (e.g., *falar de* = to talk about, *gostar de* = to like, *precisar de* = to need). Spelling note: **de quê** (with an accent) is typical when it comes at the end of the question: *Você está falando de quê?*; **de que** (no accent) is common when it’s followed by more words: *De que você está falando?*
target_language_example: Você está falando de quê?
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

meaning: suddenly; all of a sudden (sometimes: maybe).
additional_notes: Most commonly means something happens unexpectedly: "De repente, começou a chover" (“Suddenly, it started to rain”). In Brazilian Portuguese, it can also be used to mean “maybe / perhaps,” often shortened to "de repente" in suggestions: "A gente pode, de repente, ir amanhã" (“We could maybe go tomorrow”).
target_language_example: De repente, ele ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: Suddenly, he went silent.

meaning: otherwise; apart from that; as for the rest.
additional_notes: Used to add a final comment meaning “besides that / other than that.” Common in European Portuguese, often after stating an exception: “De resto, está tudo bem.” It can also mean “as for the rest (of it/them)” depending on context.
target_language_example: O hotel é bom; de resto, fica um pouco longe do centro.
native_language_example: The hotel is good; otherwise, it’s a bit far from the city center.

additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say you’ve had enough of a situation or someone’s behavior. Common patterns: "Estou de saco cheio" (I’m fed up) and "Estou de saco cheio de + [noun/verb]" (I’m fed up with…).
target_language_example: Estou de saco cheio de esperar; vamos embora.
native_language_example: I’m sick and tired of waiting; let’s go.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase after a noun. Common meanings: (1) “secondhand/used” when talking about items (roupa de segunda, carro de segunda). (2) “second-rate/inferior” when talking about quality or status (produto de segunda, time de segunda). Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Comprei um casaco de segunda, mas está em ótimo estado.
native_language_example: I bought a secondhand coat, but it’s in great condition.

meaning: as always; the same as usual; longstanding.
additional_notes: Used to describe something habitual or unchanged over time, or something/someone that has been around for a long time ("the usual/longtime one"). Common in phrases like "como de sempre" (as always) and "o de sempre" (the usual thing/person). Often appears after a noun: "amigos de sempre" = lifelong/longtime friends.
target_language_example: Ele chegou atrasado, como de sempre.
native_language_example: He arrived late, as always.

additional_notes: Used to say there is more than is needed (quantity, time, money, etc.) or that something remains after using what was needed. Common with verbs like “ter” (to have), “sobrar” (to be left over), “dar” (to be enough), and “chegar” (to be enough). Example: “Tenho tempo de sobra” = I have plenty of time.
target_language_example: Temos comida de sobra para todo mundo.
native_language_example: We have more than enough food for everyone.

meaning: from time to time; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally, not regularly. Common in both European and Brazilian Portuguese. Similar options: "de vez em quando" (every now and then).
target_language_example: De tempos em tempos, eu vou ao cinema com meus amigos.
native_language_example: From time to time, I go to the movies with my friends.

meaning: completely; entirely (often: “not at all” in negatives).
additional_notes: Used mainly as an adverb meaning “completely/entirely.” Very common in the negative structure “não … de todo” to mean “not at all / not completely” depending on context (often European Portuguese).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi de todo o que ele disse.
