native_language_example: I didn’t understand at all what he said.

additional_notes: Used to move on from a detail or objection, or to say the conclusion stays the same regardless of circumstances. Similar to “de qualquer forma/jeito”. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: De todo modo, vou falar com ela amanhã.
native_language_example: Anyway, I’ll talk to her tomorrow.

meaning: once and for all; all at once.
additional_notes: Used to mean doing something definitively ("once and for all") or doing something in a single go/at the same time ("all at once"). Often appears as "de uma vez por todas" for extra emphasis ("once and for all"). In everyday speech you may also hear it in complaints/urging someone: "Faz isso de uma vez!" = "Just do it already!"
target_language_example: Vamos resolver isso de uma vez por todas.
native_language_example: Let’s solve this once and for all.

meaning: once and for all; for good (finally, definitively).
additional_notes: Used to say you want something settled permanently, so it won’t happen again or won’t need to be discussed again. Often used with verbs like "resolver" (to solve), "acabar" (to put an end to), "decidir" (to decide), "parar" (to stop), and can sound emphatic/firm depending on tone.
target_language_example: Vamos resolver isso de uma vez por todas.
native_language_example: Let’s settle this once and for all.

additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize that something is genuine or serious, or to strengthen what you’re saying. Often comes after what it modifies: "É de verdade" (It’s real). It can also be used in questions to confirm: "De verdade?" (Really?/For real?). Similar in meaning to "mesmo" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Você gostou de verdade do filme?
native_language_example: Did you really like the movie?

meaning: for good; once and for all (permanently).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like parar, deixar, acabar to mean doing something permanently: “parar de vez” = “stop for good.” It also appears in longer expressions: “de uma vez (por todas)” = “once and for all,” and “de vez em quando” = “from time to time.”
target_language_example: Eu vou parar de fumar de vez.
native_language_example: I’m going to quit smoking for good.

meaning: every now and then; from time to time.
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase meaning something happens occasionally (not regularly). Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: "De vez em quando, ..." / "..., de vez em quando."
target_language_example: De vez em quando, eu vou ao cinema com meus amigos.
native_language_example: Every now and then, I go to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to a place or state. Common with verbs like “voltar” (to return) and “estar” (to be): “voltar de volta” is usually redundant—most often you just say “voltar”. It can also mean something coming back (e.g., a symptom, a feeling).
target_language_example: Estou de volta amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll be back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally “finger of the foot.” Use it to refer to any toe; for “big toe,” you can say “dedão do pé.” In everyday speech, people also say “dedo do pé” when they mean “toe” in general, even though “dedo” alone often means “finger.”
target_language_example: Eu bati o dedo do pé na quina da mesa.
native_language_example: I banged my toe on the corner of the table.

meaning: to stop (doing something); to no longer do.
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive verb: "deixar de + infinitive". Often means stopping an action/habit ("Deixei de fumar" = I stopped smoking) or not doing something anymore/this time ("Ele deixou de ir" = he stopped going / he didn’t go anymore). In negative commands it can mean “don’t (do it)” in the sense of “stop it”: "Não deixa de falar" = Stop talking (you can also hear "Deixa de..." as a direct command).
target_language_example: Eu deixei de tomar café à noite.
native_language_example: I stopped drinking coffee at night.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to let (someone) be.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to stop bothering/interfering or to stop talking to someone. It can be directed at a person (Deixa-me em paz.) or used with an object pronoun (Deixa-o/a em paz.). Often implies “stop pestering” rather than just physical distance; tone can be polite or annoyed depending on context.
target_language_example: Por favor, deixa-me em paz — preciso de pensar.
native_language_example: Please leave me alone — I need to think.

meaning: to let escape; to let slip (e.g., a secret or a chance).
additional_notes: Used when someone unintentionally (or carelessly) lets something go out or be revealed. Common with things like “um segredo” (a secret), “um comentário” (a comment), “um suspiro” (a sigh), or “uma oportunidade” (an opportunity/chance). Often implies it happened by accident: “Deixei escapar…” = “I let slip…”.
target_language_example: Ela deixou escapar um segredo sem querer.
native_language_example: She accidentally let a secret slip.

meaning: to let it go; to drop it (stop worrying/talking about it).
additional_notes: Used when you decide not to deal with something now, or to stop insisting/arguing about it. Depending on tone, it can sound calm (“forget it”) or slightly dismissive (“whatever, leave it”). Often said as a suggestion or decision: “Deixa/Deixe para lá.”
target_language_example: Ah, deixa para lá — não vale a pena discutir.
native_language_example: Oh, let it go — it’s not worth arguing.

meaning: to let (someone/something) pass; to let something go by / miss (an opportunity).
additional_notes: Common in everyday situations: letting a person or car go ahead ("deixa passar"), letting something through (security, a gate), or missing/letting an opportunity slip by ("não vou deixar passar essa chance"). In the imperative, "Deixa passar!" means "Let (them/it) through!"
target_language_example: Não vou deixar passar essa oportunidade.
native_language_example: I’m not going to miss that opportunity.

meaning: 'to leave it alone' / 'to let it be'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop touching, bothering, or insisting on something, or to stop interfering. It can sound firm depending on tone (similar to 'Just leave it alone'). Also used as advice: better not to get involved or to drop the subject.
target_language_example: Deixa isso quieto e vamos embora.
native_language_example: Leave that alone and let’s go.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the local police station/precinct where you file a report (fazer um boletim de ocorrência) or go to speak with an officer. In Brazil, you may also see “delegacia” used alone to mean the police station.
target_language_example: Preciso ir à delegacia de polícia para registrar um boletim de ocorrência.
native_language_example: I need to go to the police station to file a police report.

meaning: inside; within (a place, time limit, or range).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location (inside something) or a deadline/range (within a certain amount of time). Common in phrases like "dentro de casa" (inside the house), "dentro de um carro" (inside a car), and "dentro de dois dias" (within two days). With time, it often implies a limit before the time runs out.
target_language_example: Vou te ligar dentro de dez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll call you within ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens later than another event: "depois de + noun" (depois de jantar = after dinner) or "depois de + infinitive" (depois de comer = after eating). You can also use it before a clause with a verb: "Depois de eu chegar, ..." (After I arrive, ...). Often contrasts with "antes de" (before).
target_language_example: Depois de jantar, vamos dar uma volta.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a date two days from today. Common in scheduling and making plans. Often used without an article (e.g., "Até depois de amanhã" = "See you the day after tomorrow").
target_language_example: A reunião é depois de amanhã às 10h.
native_language_example: The meeting is the day after tomorrow at 10 a.m.

meaning: to rest in peace (said about someone who has died).
additional_notes: Used to express condolences or respect for someone who has passed away; often appears as "Descanse em paz" (to one person, formal/neutral) or "Descansem em paz" (plural). Commonly written as "RIP" in Portuguese too ("R.I.P.").
target_language_example: Meu avô faleceu ontem. Que ele descanse em paz.
native_language_example: My grandfather passed away yesterday. May he rest in peace.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a point in the past that was mentioned or is clear from context, and everything that happened after that point up to now (or up to another moment). Common in storytelling and explanations of changes over time.
target_language_example: Mudei de cidade em 2020 e, desde então, fiz muitos amigos.
native_language_example: I moved to another city in 2020 and, since then, I’ve made many friends.

additional_notes: Used to ask from what point in time something has been true. Often expresses surprise, doubt, or a challenge (“Since when is that true?”). You’ll also see it in indirect questions: “Não sei desde quando…” (“I don’t know since when…”).
target_language_example: Desde quando você mora aqui?
native_language_example: Since when have you lived here?

meaning: "since" (from the time that) / "as long as" (on the condition that).
additional_notes: Common with the subjunctive when it means a condition ("as long as"): "Você pode ir, desde que chegue cedo." When it means time ("since"), it often refers to a starting point in the past: "Desde que mudei para cá..." Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Você pode sair, desde que volte antes da meia-noite.
native_language_example: You can go out, as long as you come back before midnight.

additional_notes: A common everyday term for animated TV shows and movies. In Portuguese, it literally means “animated drawing.” You’ll often hear it with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch): “assistir a um desenho animado.” The plural is “desenhos animados.”
target_language_example: As crianças estão assistindo a um desenho animado na TV.
native_language_example: The kids are watching a cartoon on TV.

meaning: homework (school assignment to do at home).
additional_notes: Common in Brazil; in European Portuguese, "trabalhos de casa" is very common. Usually used with "fazer" (to do): "fazer o dever de casa". It can also be used figuratively to mean "do your homework" (prepare/research) before something.
target_language_example: Tenho muito dever de casa para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of homework to do today.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason/cause for something, typically in neutral or formal contexts (common in writing and announcements). It’s followed by a noun or noun phrase: "devido ao trânsito" (due to traffic). With a verb, Portuguese usually uses "devido a" + infinitive: "devido a chover" (due to it raining) or more commonly "por causa de" + noun/infinitive in everyday speech. Note the contraction with the definite article: devido a + o = devido ao; devido a + a = devido à; devido a + os = devido aos; devido a + as = devido às.
target_language_example: O voo foi cancelado devido ao mau tempo.
native_language_example: The flight was canceled due to bad weather.

additional_notes: Used to talk about daily life, routine, or the ordinary things that happen regularly. Often appears with verbs like "viver" (to live), "lidar com" (to deal with), or "no" (in the): "no dia a dia" = "in daily life".
target_language_example: No dia a dia, eu vou de ônibus para o trabalho.
native_language_example: In my day-to-day life, I take the bus to work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the holiday known as Thanksgiving. In Brazil it’s not a widely celebrated holiday, but the term is common in translations, media, or when talking about the US/Canada. Also appears as "Dia de Ação de Graças" (capitalized as a holiday name) and often without "dia": "Ação de Graças".
target_language_example: Nos Estados Unidos, o Dia de Ação de Graças é comemorado em novembro.
native_language_example: In the United States, Thanksgiving Day is celebrated in November.

meaning: day and night; all the time (continuously).
additional_notes: Literally “day and night.” Used to emphasize that something happens constantly or without stopping (often about work, noise, worry, care, etc.). Common in phrases like “trabalhar dia e noite” (to work day and night).
target_language_example: Ela trabalha dia e noite para terminar o projeto.
native_language_example: She works day and night to finish the project.

meaning: 'in front of' / 'before' (in the presence of; faced with).
additional_notes: Preposition used (1) for physical position: something is located in front of something else, and (2) for situations: 'faced with' a fact/problem or 'in light of' something. Often followed by a noun or infinitive phrase (e.g., diante de tudo, diante de um problema, diante de saber disso).
target_language_example: Diante de tantas dificuldades, continuamos tentando.
native_language_example: Faced with so many difficulties, we kept trying.

meaning: “let it be said / that is to say / mind you” (used as a parenthetical aside).
additional_notes: Used in writing and formal speech as a comment inserted into a sentence, often to add clarification, emphasis, or a “by the way” remark. Common patterns: “diga-se de passagem” (“by the way”) and “diga-se, aliás,” (“in fact / mind you”). Usually set off by commas.
target_language_example: Ele aceitou o trabalho, diga-se, sem negociar o salário.
native_language_example: He accepted the job, mind you, without negotiating the salary.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying, suggest an approximation, or introduce a rephrasing. Often comes mid-sentence or at the end as a hedging expression. Common in both European and Brazilian Portuguese in casual and neutral speech.
target_language_example: Ele é, digamos assim, um pouco teimoso.
native_language_example: He is, let’s say, a bit stubborn.

additional_notes: Used to talk about basic rights that every person should have (often in law, politics, and news). Commonly appears in the plural: "direitos humanos" (human rights). Can also be used in phrases like "violação de direitos humanos" (human rights violation) and "defender os direitos humanos" (to defend human rights).
target_language_example: A liberdade de expressão é um direito humano fundamental.
native_language_example: Freedom of expression is a fundamental human right.

additional_notes: Used for a computer’s data storage device. In everyday speech, people may also say "HD". Can refer to an internal drive or an external one ("disco rígido externo").
target_language_example: Preciso de um disco rígido externo para fazer backup dos meus arquivos.
native_language_example: I need an external hard drive to back up my files.

additional_notes: Common in science and environmental contexts (climate change, pollution) and also when talking about drinks (carbonated beverages). Often written as “CO₂”. The structure is compositional: “dióxido” (dioxide) + “de” (of) + “carbono” (carbon).
target_language_example: As plantas absorvem dióxido de carbono e libertam oxigénio.
native_language_example: Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

additional_notes: "Do" is the contraction of "de" (of/from/about) + "o" (the, masculine singular). "Do amor" is used to link something to love: "história do amor" (a love story / the story of love), "dia do amor" (Valentine’s Day / day of love), "a dor do amor" (the pain of love). Depending on context, "de" can mean "of", "about", or sometimes "from".
target_language_example: Ele contou a história do amor deles.
native_language_example: He told the story of their love.

meaning: inside out; the wrong way round.
additional_notes: Used mainly to describe clothing or something turned the opposite way (e.g., a shirt worn inside out). It can also be used figuratively to mean something is reversed, mixed up, or not as it should be (e.g., your schedule/life is “upside down”). Often appears with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/get): "A camiseta está do avesso."
target_language_example: A tua camisola está do avesso.
native_language_example: Your sweater is inside out.

meaning: (vulgar slang) “fucking awesome” / “amazing” (sometimes: “fucking terrible,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Very vulgar in Brazil because it refers to male genitalia. Most commonly used as an intensifier meaning “really/very,” often in compliments: “muito/foda do caralho” = “so damn good.” It can also express anger/negativity (“um dia do caralho” = “a shitty day”). Avoid in polite/company situations; among friends it can be emphatic and common in informal speech.
target_language_example: Esse show foi do caralho!
native_language_example: That show was fucking awesome!

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" = "do". Used to express that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to the world in general. Very common in superlatives like "o melhor do mundo" (the best in the world) and expressions like "todo mundo" (everyone).
target_language_example: Este é o melhor café do mundo.
native_language_example: This is the best coffee in the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unexpectedly, with no warning or obvious reason. Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence. Literally “from (the) nothing,” but in English it’s usually “out of nowhere,” not “from nothing.”
target_language_example: Do nada, começou a chover.
native_language_example: Out of nowhere, it started to rain.

meaning: “than” (in comparisons); also “of/about what” (after verbs that use de).
additional_notes: Do que is a contraction of de + o + que. Most commonly, it’s used after comparatives: mais/menos/melhor/pior/maior/menor + do que (“more/less/better/worse/bigger/smaller than”). It can also appear when a verb/expression requires the preposition de, meaning “of/about what/that”: e.g., Não sei do que você está falando (“I don’t know what you’re talking about”).
target_language_example: Ela é mais alta do que eu.
native_language_example: She is taller than me.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o quê". Used when the verb or expression normally takes the preposition "de" (e.g., "ter medo de", "gostar de", "precisar de"). Common in questions like "Você tem medo do quê?" It can also be used on its own as a surprised follow-up question: "Do quê?!" (“Of what?!” / “What for?!”).
target_language_example: Você está com medo do quê?
native_language_example: What are you afraid of?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re starting something with nothing prepared or with no previous progress (no experience, no materials, no plan). Common with verbs like "começar" (to start), "fazer" (to do/make), "aprender" (to learn), and "criar" (to create). Literal sense is “from zero.”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: podemos começar do zero.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we can start from scratch.

meaning: “two brothers” (often used as a place name: “Dois Irmãos”).
additional_notes: Literally means “two brothers” (dois = two; irmãos = brothers). With capital letters (Dois Irmãos), it’s commonly a proper noun in Brazil (e.g., Morro Dois Irmãos in Rio de Janeiro; cities or parks named Dois Irmãos). In running text, if it’s just the general phrase (not a name), it’s usually written in lowercase: dois irmãos.
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar no Morro Dois Irmãos no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to hike Morro Dois Irmãos this weekend.

meaning: housewife; homemaker (a woman who manages the home).
additional_notes: Refers to a woman whose main role is taking care of the household (cleaning, cooking, childcare, etc.). It can be a neutral description, but it may feel traditional or gendered; for a more inclusive/neutral option you may hear "pessoa que cuida da casa" (person who takes care of the home).
target_language_example: Minha mãe é dona de casa e cuida das crianças.
native_language_example: My mom is a homemaker and takes care of the kids.

additional_notes: Common way to say you have a headache: "Estou com dor de cabeça" (Brazil) / also understood in Portugal. Literally "pain of head." Can also be used figuratively to mean "a hassle/problem" (e.g., paperwork can be "uma dor de cabeça").
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache since yesterday.

additional_notes: “Dos” is the contraction of “de + os” (“of the” / “from the”). “dos Reis” is most often seen in proper names (e.g., surnames like “Maria dos Reis”) or place names, and in references to “Dia de Reis” (Epiphany/Three Kings’ Day). Capitalization (“Reis”) often indicates it’s part of a name/title.
target_language_example: A Maria dos Reis mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: Maria dos Reis lives nearby.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that a list or series continues without mentioning every item. Common in both speech and writing, similar to “etc.” You can also say “e por aí vai” (more informal) with the same idea.
target_language_example: Precisamos comprar arroz, feijão, legumes e assim por diante.
native_language_example: We need to buy rice, beans, vegetables, and so on.

additional_notes: Very common in informal conversation. As a greeting, it’s like “Hey, what’s up?” As a follow-up question, it asks what happened next or what the other person thinks/decided (“So, what now?”). Often used alone, or with a person: “E aí, tudo bem?”
target_language_example: E aí, tudo bem?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s up—everything good?

additional_notes: Literally “and how.” Common in two main uses: (1) In questions to add a follow-up: “E como foi?” = “And how was it?” (2) As an emphatic reply, often with an exclamation: “E como!” = “And how!” / “You bet!” / “Definitely!” (agreeing strongly with what was just said).
target_language_example: —Você está cansado? —E como!
native_language_example: —Are you tired? —And how!/You bet!

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) as a dismissive reaction meaning “so what?” or “who cares?” (can sound rude/defiant depending on tone). (2) as a follow-up question meaning “and then?” to keep a story going. Often said on its own, or after a statement: “Eu errei. E daí?”
target_language_example: Eu não vou. — E daí?
native_language_example: I’m not going. — So what?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical situation, possibility, or suggestion. Often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "E se a gente fosse…?" = "What if we went…?") or by a present-tense question when thinking out loud ("E se chove?" = "What if it rains?").
target_language_example: E se a gente fosse ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: What if we went to the movies today?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a list or description to mean “and similar things,” often to avoid listing everything. Very common in casual speech; in writing, “etc.” is more formal. Often appears as “e tal” or “e tal e coisa” in informal conversation.
target_language_example: Comprei pão, leite, frutas e tal.
native_language_example: I bought bread, milk, fruit, and so on.

meaning: “and so on; etc.” (and other things like that).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a list to mean “and other similar things,” like English “and so on / and stuff.” It’s more common in casual speech, often alongside similar fillers like “e tal” or “e tudo.”
target_language_example: Falamos de trabalho, família, planos e tanto.
native_language_example: We talked about work, family, plans, and so on.

additional_notes: Literally means “and everything,” but in conversation it’s often used at the end of a list to mean “and so on / and stuff,” similar to “e tudo mais.” It can also simply mean “and everything” in a literal sense, depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu levei comida, água, roupas, e tudo.
native_language_example: I brought food, water, clothes, and everything.

additional_notes: Used like in English. In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll also hear/see "email" (without the hyphen) and the plural "e-mails". Common with verbs like "enviar" (to send) and "mandar" (to send).
target_language_example: Vou te mandar um e-mail ainda hoje.
native_language_example: I’ll send you an email later today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the astronomical event when the Moon darkens because Earth blocks sunlight. Very common in news, science, and casual conversation. Plural: "eclipses lunares". Related: "eclipse solar" (solar eclipse).
target_language_example: Hoje à noite vai ter um eclipse lunar visível em várias regiões.
native_language_example: Tonight there will be a lunar eclipse visible in several regions.

additional_notes: Used mostly in medical/pharmacy contexts for an unintended effect of a medicine or treatment (can be negative or just unexpected). Also used more generally for an indirect, unintended consequence of an action or decision.
target_language_example: Este remédio pode causar efeitos colaterais, como sonolência.
native_language_example: This medicine can cause side effects, such as drowsiness.

additional_notes: A literal noun phrase: "elefante" (elephant) + "africano" (African). Used to refer to the African elephant species in general, or to an individual animal. Adjectives like "africano" typically come after the noun in Portuguese. Plural: "elefantes africanos".
target_language_example: O elefante africano é o maior mamífero terrestre.
native_language_example: The African elephant is the largest land mammal.

additional_notes: Used in science contexts (chemistry, physics) to refer to a pure substance made of only one type of atom (e.g., oxygen, iron). Often appears with the verb “ser” (to be) or in definitions and explanations: “X é um elemento químico…”.
target_language_example: O oxigênio é um elemento químico essencial para a vida.
native_language_example: Oxygen is a chemical element essential for life.

additional_notes: Used to say something is currently happening or being processed (a project, investigation, construction, order, etc.). Common in formal and everyday contexts. Often appears after a noun: "projeto em andamento", "obra em andamento", "pedido em andamento".
target_language_example: A reforma está em andamento e deve terminar no mês que vem.
native_language_example: The renovation is in progress and should finish next month.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position or direction. Common in phrases like "lá em baixo" (down there) and "aqui em baixo" (down here). It can also mean "downstairs" depending on context. Often contrasts with "em cima" (up/above).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica lá em baixo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is downstairs (down there).

meaning: in good hands (safe; well taken care of).
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a person or thing is being cared for by someone competent or trustworthy. Common with verbs like estar/ficar (e.g., "Está em boas mãos"). Can also be used about a project, pet, or responsibility.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, seu filho está em boas mãos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, your son is in good hands.

additional_notes: Used for forms, spaces, or fields that are not filled in ("deixar em branco" = to leave blank). It can also mean "without anything written/recorded" or "with no content" (e.g., a blank page). In some contexts, "ficar em branco" means your mind goes blank (you forget what to say).
target_language_example: Você pode deixar essa parte em branco.
native_language_example: You can leave that part blank.

additional_notes: Common in announcements, messages, and formal writing to mean something will happen in a short time (often translated as “coming soon”). Less specific than “daqui a pouco,” and not as immediate as “já já.”
target_language_example: Voltarei em breve.
native_language_example: I’ll be back soon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being at home or going/staying home. Common with verbs like estar (to be), ficar (to stay), and ir/voltar (to go/come back): "Estou em casa" (I’m at home), "Vou ficar em casa" (I’m going to stay home). It can also mean being comfortable/familiar in a place or situation: "Sinto-me em casa aqui" (I feel at home here).
target_language_example: Hoje vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate position: (1) literally on top of something (often with "de": "em cima da mesa" = on the table), (2) location upstairs: "lá em cima" = up there/upstairs, and (3) being above/over something: "em cima de mim" = above me/over me. It can also appear in fixed expressions like "em cima da hora" (at the last minute) or "em cima disso" (on top of that).
target_language_example: O livro está em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: The book is on top of the table.

meaning: on top of; above; over; (also) right after / following.
additional_notes: Common preposition meaning physical position (on/over/above) and, in some contexts, sequence in time (right after). Often used with articles: “em cima da/do/das/dos”. Can also be used figuratively to mean “on (a topic)” as in “falar em cima de algo” = talk about something.
target_language_example: O livro está em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: The book is on top of the table.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people or things share the same characteristic, interest, or element. Common patterns: "ter algo em comum" (to have something in common) and "em comum com" (in common with).
target_language_example: Acho que temos muito em comum.
native_language_example: I think we have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Common in shopping/price contexts, often after a noun: "um hotel em conta" / "uma opção em conta". Similar idea to "barato", but "em conta" suggests “good value / within budget” rather than “cheap.” Note: in other expressions like "levar em conta", it means "to take into account" (different meaning).
target_language_example: Queremos um hotel em conta perto do centro.
native_language_example: We want an affordable hotel near downtown/the city center.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like explicar (to explain), descrever (to describe), contar (to tell), falar (to talk) to say you want more complete, specific information. Often appears as "em detalhes" or "com detalhes" with very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso em detalhes?
native_language_example: Can you explain that in detail?

meaning: up to date; current; (payments) up to date.
additional_notes: Used to say something is current/updated (informação em dia) or that obligations like bills, rent, or documents are not overdue (contas em dia, pagamentos em dia, documentos em dia). Often appears with verbs like estar/manter: "Está tudo em dia" (everything is up to date) or "manter as contas em dia" (keep bills paid on time).
target_language_example: Estou com as contas em dia e meus documentos estão em dia.
native_language_example: My bills are paid up and my documents are up to date.

additional_notes: Used to indicate continuation from a point in time (“a partir de agora”) or movement/progress forward (“para a frente”). Often appears after a time expression (“de hoje em diante” = “from today on”) or after a point in a sequence (“do capítulo 3 em diante” = “from chapter 3 onward”).
target_language_example: De hoje em diante, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From today on, I’m going to study Portuguese every day.

additional_notes: Used to highlight one person/thing within a broader group. Often appears after a general statement to add emphasis (e.g., “..., em especial X”). Similar to “especialmente,” but “em especial” is very common in writing and formal speech.
target_language_example: Gosto de frutas, em especial de morango.
native_language_example: I like fruit, especially strawberries.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location or position facing something/someone. Often followed by an article: "em frente ao" (masc. sing.), "em frente à" (fem. sing.), "em frente aos/às" (plural). Common with "ficar" or "estar" to describe where something is. Don’t confuse with "em frente" alone, which can mean "straight ahead".
target_language_example: O banco fica em frente ao supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is in front of the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something in a broad, general way (not in every single case). It can go at the beginning of the sentence or after the subject: “Em geral, ...” / “As pessoas, em geral, ...”. Similar in meaning to “normalmente” (usually), but “em geral” emphasizes a general trend or overview.
target_language_example: Em geral, o transporte público aqui é bom.
native_language_example: In general, public transportation here is good.

meaning: on guard; alert and ready (to react).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be cautious or vigilant (often as an exclamation: “Em guarda!”). It can also be used more generally to mean being watchful or ready for something.
target_language_example: Em guarda! Tem um carro vindo.
native_language_example: On guard! There’s a car coming.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is on the line or being decided in a situation (e.g., a result, money, your reputation). In sports, it can also mean the ball is “in play” (the game is actively happening).
target_language_example: Há muito dinheiro em jogo nesta negociação.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of money at stake in this negotiation.

meaning: en masse; in large numbers; all at once (as a group).
additional_notes: Used to say many people do something together/collectively, often emphasizing that it happens at the same time or in large quantity. Common in news and everyday speech (e.g., buying, leaving, resigning, protesting).
target_language_example: Muitas pessoas começaram a comprar ingressos em massa.
native_language_example: Many people started buying tickets en masse.

additional_notes: Used to say you physically have something (documents, a phone, a product) or that something is under your responsibility/control. Common with verbs like “ter” (to have) and “estar” (to be): “Tenho o documento em mãos” = “I have the document in hand.” Can also be used more figuratively: “O caso está em boas mãos” = “The case is in good hands.”
target_language_example: Já tenho os documentos em mãos.
native_language_example: I already have the documents in hand.

additional_notes: Used to indicate representation or acting for someone/something (e.g., speaking for a group, signing for a company), or to justify an action by invoking a principle/cause (e.g., "in the name of justice"). It’s common in formal contexts (letters, announcements, speeches): "Em nome da empresa..." / "Em nome de todos nós...". It can be followed by a person, organization, or abstract idea (em nome da lei, da paz, da justiça).
target_language_example: Estou aqui em nome da minha equipe para agradecer a todos.
native_language_example: I’m here on behalf of my team to thank everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say something is organized/correct (“in order”) or that everything is fine/acceptable (“OK”). Common in confirmations and status updates: “Está tudo em ordem?” (Is everything OK?) / “Tudo em ordem.” (Everything’s fine.)
target_language_example: Está tudo em ordem com a sua reserva?
native_language_example: Is everything OK with your reservation?

meaning: “in other words”; used to rephrase or clarify.
additional_notes: Used to restate something more clearly or simply, often after giving an explanation or idea. Common in both speech and writing. Similar to “ou seja” (“that is / i.e.”).
target_language_example: Eu não posso sair hoje; em outras palavras, vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; in other words, I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to say something is only true/possible to a certain extent, not completely. Common in explanations and polite disagreement (often with verbs like "concordar" / "entender"): "Concordo em parte" = "I partly agree."
target_language_example: Eu concordo em parte com você, mas acho que precisamos de mais tempo.
native_language_example: I partly agree with you, but I think we need more time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize physical presence (not by phone/online) or that someone did something themselves. Common after verbs like “ir” (to go), “vir” (to come), “falar” (to speak), “conhecer” (to meet/know), and “entregar” (to deliver).
target_language_example: Prefiro falar com você em pessoa.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to you in person.

meaning: exactly (at a specific time); “on the dot.”
additional_notes: Used mainly with clock times to say something happens at the exact hour/minute, not earlier or later. Very common in schedules and appointments: “às 8 em ponto” = “at 8:00 exactly.”
target_language_example: O trem sai às sete em ponto.
native_language_example: The train leaves at seven o’clock sharp.

meaning: first; first of all (to introduce the first point).
additional_notes: Used to organize what you’re saying, especially in explanations, lists, arguments, or presentations. Often followed by a comma and then the first reason/step. Common pairings: “em segundo lugar” (second), “por último” (last/finally).
target_language_example: Em primeiro lugar, precisamos confirmar a data da reunião.
native_language_example: First of all, we need to confirm the date of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person’s position (standing up) or something upright/vertical. Also used in set phrases like “ficar em pé” (to stand up / stay standing), “levantar-se e ficar em pé” (to get up and stand), and “ir a pé” (to go on foot, i.e., walking).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei em pé no ônibus porque não havia lugares sentados.
native_language_example: I stood on the bus because there were no seats.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that comes as a powder rather than liquid or solid pieces. Common with foods and household products: "leite em pó" (powdered milk), "café em pó" (ground coffee), "sabão em pó" (laundry detergent powder). Often contrasts with "líquido" (liquid) or "em tabletes" (in tablets).
target_language_example: Você prefere leite em pó ou leite líquido?
native_language_example: Do you prefer powdered milk or liquid milk?

meaning: 'in how much?' / 'for how much?' (asking the price or amount).
additional_notes: Used mainly in questions about cost, value, or an amount. In everyday Portuguese, many speakers prefer forms like “Por quanto?” or “Quanto custa?”, and the very common word “enquanto” (written together) is different—it means “while.”
target_language_example: Em quanto fica este casaco?
native_language_example: How much is this coat?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re referring to, especially in more formal or written Portuguese. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause: “em relação ao/à” + noun (contracts with articles: ao = a + o, à = a + a). Similar alternatives: “sobre” (about), “quanto a” (as for).
target_language_example: Em relação ao seu pedido, precisamos de mais informações.
native_language_example: Regarding your request, we need more information.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the next step in a sequence or something that happens immediately after something else. Common in instructions, narratives, and formal speech/writing. Similar in meaning to “depois” (“after/later”), but often feels more immediate and step-by-step.
target_language_example: Primeiro, lave as mãos e, em seguida, prepare o jantar.
native_language_example: First, wash your hands and then prepare dinner.

meaning: in time; on time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened early enough (not too late), often in contexts like arriving, meeting a deadline, or preventing a problem. Common with verbs like “chegar” (to arrive) and “entregar” (to submit/hand in). Depending on context, it can overlap with “a tempo” (in time) and “na hora” (right on time/at the exact time).
target_language_example: Ainda chegamos em tempo de ver o filme.
native_language_example: We still got there in time to see the movie.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation forward, often after mentioning a possibility or uncertainty. Similar to "anyway" when changing focus or concluding: it can mean “regardless of what happens/what is true” or “either way.” Often appears at the start of a sentence: "Em todo caso, ...".
target_language_example: Em todo caso, podemos falar amanhã.
native_language_example: In any case, we can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a replacement/substitution: doing one thing in place of another. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun or an infinitive verb (e.g., “em vez de sair…” = “instead of going out…”). Common contrast: “em vez de” (instead of) vs. “ao invés de” (often used the same way in everyday speech, but can imply “the opposite of” in more formal usage).
target_language_example: Em vez de pegar o ônibus, vou a pé.
native_language_example: Instead of taking the bus, I’m going on foot.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or factor that should be taken into account, similar to “considering…” or “given…”. Common in more formal writing and speech. It is often followed by a noun or an infinitive phrase: “em vista do atraso” (given the delay) / “em vista de reduzir custos” (in order to reduce costs). Note the common variant “em vista disso” = “in view of that / given that.”
target_language_example: Em vista do mau tempo, o evento foi cancelado.
native_language_example: Given the bad weather, the event was canceled.

additional_notes: Used mainly to talk about being positioned around something ("as pessoas em volta" = the people around) or moving in a circular way ("dar uma volta" / "andar em volta" = to take a lap / walk around). Often appears with "de": "em volta de" = around (something).
target_language_example: Há muitas pessoas em volta do palco.
native_language_example: There are many people around the stage.

additional_notes: Used either for physical position/movement around something (often with verbs like andar/passear/olhar) or for approximate quantities/time (similar to “about/around”). With time: "em volta das 3" = around 3 o’clock; with numbers: "em volta de 20" = around 20. Note: "em volta" alone can mean “around (it)” depending on context (e.g., "Olhe em volta" = Look around).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar em volta das 3 e caminhar em volta do parque.
native_language_example: Let’s meet around 3 and walk around the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken so others can hear it (not silently/in your head). Common in instructions and requests: "Leia em voz alta" (Read out loud) or "Fala em voz alta" (Speak up). Often contrasts with "em silêncio" (silently) or "na minha cabeça" (in my head).
target_language_example: Você pode ler em voz alta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you read out loud, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an effort was useless or didn’t produce the desired outcome. Often appears with verbs like "tentar" (to try), "procurar" (to look for), "esperar" (to hope/wait), and "ser" (to be): "Foi em vão" = "It was in vain." Also common in the phrase "em vão" meaning "pointlessly".
target_language_example: Tentei ligar várias vezes, mas foi em vão.
native_language_example: I tried calling several times, but it was in vain.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position: something is under something else. Very common with places and objects (e.g., under the table, under the bed). Often interchangeable with "debaixo de" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O gato está embaixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

meaning: to annoy (someone); to be really irritating. Also: to be fed up.
additional_notes: Very common Brazilian Portuguese slang (can be rude depending on tone). Used as (1) “Isso enche o saco.” = “That’s annoying.” (2) “Você está enchendo o saco.” = “You’re bugging me.” (3) “Não enche o saco!” = “Stop annoying me!” Not literal (literally “to fill the bag”).
target_language_example: Para de encher o saco e me deixa trabalhar.
native_language_example: Stop annoying me and let me work.

additional_notes: Used in science/news contexts to talk about energy produced from nuclear reactions (especially fission), often in discussions of power plants, safety, or policy. In everyday conversation, "energia nuclear" is also very common and often interchangeable.
target_language_example: O governo está debatendo o uso de energia atômica para gerar eletricidade.
native_language_example: The government is debating the use of atomic energy to generate electricity.

meaning: nuclear energy (energy produced from nuclear reactions, especially in power plants).
additional_notes: Used in news and science contexts to talk about nuclear power and electricity production. Often appears in discussions about alternative energy sources, safety, waste, and climate policy. Related terms: "usina nuclear" (nuclear power plant), "energia atômica" (atomic energy; near-synonym), "energia renovável" (renewable energy).
target_language_example: Muitos países investem em energia nuclear para reduzir as emissões de carbono.
native_language_example: Many countries invest in nuclear energy to reduce carbon emissions.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the time another event is happening or being dealt with. Often comes at the start of a sentence to switch focus: "Enquanto isso, ..." It can also appear mid-sentence after a pause.
target_language_example: Estou a cozinhar; enquanto isso, podes pôr a mesa.
native_language_example: I’m cooking; meanwhile, you can set the table.

additional_notes: In Brazil, this refers to compulsory basic schooling (typically from 1st to 9th grade). In Portugal you may also hear it, but the more common term is "ensino básico". Used in education contexts (schools, résumés, government services).
target_language_example: Ela cursou o ensino fundamental em uma escola pública.
native_language_example: She attended elementary school at a public school.

additional_notes: Used in Brazil to refer to the final stage of basic education, typically after “ensino fundamental” and before university/college (“faculdade”/“universidade”). In Portugal, a similar idea is often expressed as “ensino secundário.”
target_language_example: Eu terminei o ensino médio no ano passado.
native_language_example: I finished high school last year.

meaning: to enter; to go into; to join (a place, vehicle, organization, etc.).
additional_notes: Common preposition combo: "entrar" + "em" + definite article usually contracts (em + o = no, em + a = na, em + os = nos, em + as = nas). Used for entering places (entrar no prédio), getting into vehicles (entrar no carro/ônibus), and joining or starting participation in something (entrar no time/na empresa). With some nouns it can mean "to begin" or "to come into" a state/topic (e.g., entrar em vigor = come into effect; entrar em contato = get in touch; entrar em detalhes = go into details).
target_language_example: Você pode entrar no ônibus pela porta da frente.
native_language_example: You can get on the bus through the front door.

meaning: to panic; to go into a panic.
additional_notes: Used for the moment someone suddenly becomes very anxious or loses calm (often because of fear, stress, or an emergency). Common with verbs like "não" (to say someone didn’t panic) or with a cause introduced by "com"/"por causa de". You can also say "Entrou em pânico" to describe what happened.
target_language_example: Quando vi que tinha perdido o passaporte, entrei em pânico.
native_language_example: When I saw that I had lost my passport, I panicked.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a list is not complete (like “etc.”). It often follows examples: “X, Y e Z, entre outros.” You can use it for people or things; for things you may also hear “entre outras coisas.”
target_language_example: Gosto de viajar para Portugal, Espanha e Itália, entre outros países.
native_language_example: I like traveling to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, among other countries.

meaning: Common Era (CE) — the era used in modern dating of years (same as AD, but non-religious).
additional_notes: Used mainly in academic, historical, or formal contexts to date years without using “d.C.” (depois de Cristo). Often appears as “Era Comum (EC)” and contrasts with “antes da era comum (AEC)” = BCE.
target_language_example: O Império Romano caiu no ano 476 da Era Comum (EC).
native_language_example: The Roman Empire fell in the year 476 Common Era (CE).

additional_notes: Fixed storytelling opening, especially in fairy tales and children’s stories. Literally “it was one time” (imperfect of *ser*: *era*), used to set the scene in the past. Often followed by *um/uma...* (“Era uma vez um rei...”).
target_language_example: Era uma vez uma menina que morava na floresta.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a girl who lived in the forest.

additional_notes: Used for plants that grow where you don’t want them (in a garden, lawn, or field). Often appears in the plural: "ervas daninhas". "Erva" = herb/grass/plant; "daninha" = harmful/noxious, meaning it’s not desirable in that place.
target_language_example: Precisamos arrancar as ervas daninhas do jardim.
native_language_example: We need to pull the weeds out of the garden.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun phrase for the object used to brush your teeth. Often used with articles/possessives: “a escova de dentes” (the/a toothbrush), “minha escova de dentes” (my toothbrush).
target_language_example: Esqueci a minha escova de dentes no hotel.
native_language_example: I forgot my toothbrush at the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pause or stop briefly, often in conversation (e.g., on the phone or when you’re about to explain something). It can sound a bit abrupt depending on tone; you can soften it with “por favor” or by using “espera aí” (very common in speech).
target_language_example: Espera aí um segundo, já te digo.
native_language_example: Hold on a second, I’ll tell you in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the recent period around now, often implying a temporary trend or situation. Common in phrases like “Ando/Estou + ... esses dias” (“I’ve been ... lately”) and “Nesses/Esses dias” (“these days”).
target_language_example: Ando muito cansado esses dias.
native_language_example: I’ve been really tired these days / lately.

meaning: to feel like (doing something); to be up for it; (also) to be interested in someone.
additional_notes: Informal, especially in Brazil. Often used with "de" + infinitive: "estar a fim de + verb" (= be in the mood to / feel like doing). It can also mean being romantically interested in someone: "estar a fim de alguém".
target_language_example: Hoje eu não estou a fim de sair, mas acho que ele está a fim de você.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel like going out, but I think he’s into you.

meaning: to be about to (do something); to be intended/ready for (something).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an infinitive to say something is about to happen: "Estou para sair" = "I’m about to leave." It can also mean something is intended or destined for someone/something (more context-dependent): "Isto é para você" = "This is for you" (often just "ser para" / "é para" in everyday speech). With "estar para" + noun, it can suggest readiness/availability: "Estou para trabalho" = "I’m ready/available to work" (less common).
target_language_example: Eu estou para sair, só vou pegar minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave; I’m just going to grab my keys.

meaning: to be hanging by a thread (very close to failing/ending).
additional_notes: An idiom used for situations that are very fragile or about to collapse—relationships, health, plans, a job, a business, etc. Often appears with things like "a relação", "a vida", "o emprego", "o acordo". You can also say "ficar por um fio" (to end up in that fragile state).
target_language_example: Depois da discussão, a relação deles está por um fio.
native_language_example: After the argument, their relationship is hanging by a thread.

additional_notes: Used for places where you take/arrive by train. In Brazil, "trem" is common; you may also hear "estação de trem" or "estação ferroviária" (more formal). In Portugal, people often say "estação de comboio" (train station).
target_language_example: Onde fica a estação de trem mais próxima?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest train station?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s habits and daily routines (diet, exercise, work-life balance, etc.). Often appears with adjectives like “saudável” (healthy) or “sedentário” (sedentary), and with verbs like “ter” (to have) or “mudar” (to change): “ter um estilo de vida saudável”, “mudar o estilo de vida”.
target_language_example: Ela quer mudar o estilo de vida e fazer mais exercício.
native_language_example: She wants to change her lifestyle and exercise more.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the bright streak you see in the sky when a small space rock burns up in the atmosphere. In everyday speech, it’s also linked to the idea of making a wish when you see one. Literal meaning: “falling star,” even though it isn’t actually a star.
target_language_example: Olha, uma estrela cadente! Pede um desejo.
native_language_example: Look, a shooting star! Make a wish.

additional_notes: Used to agree/accept something (“OK.”), to reassure (“It’s fine.”), or to check that something is OK (“Is it all right?”). Common in conversation and can sound a bit formal compared to “tá bem”. Often appears as a response on its own: “Está bem.”
target_language_example: — Podemos marcar para amanhã? — Está bem.
native_language_example: — Can we schedule it for tomorrow? — OK.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. It can simply approve/accept something (“OK, that works”), or it can be used to stop something (“OK, that’s enough”). Often said as a response in conversation; in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear it meaning “Sounds good” after a plan is suggested. Intonation matters: neutral = agreement; firmer tone = asking someone to stop.
target_language_example: —Posso desligar o rádio? —Está bom.
native_language_example: —Can I turn off the radio? —OK / All right.

additional_notes: Used to say you deserve something (good or bad), often with an implied object: Eu mereço isso. Can also be used alone to emphasize that you’ve earned something, e.g., after hard work or as a complaint. Verb: merecer (to deserve).
target_language_example: Depois de tanto trabalhar, eu mereço um descanso.
native_language_example: After working so much, I deserve a rest.

additional_notes: Common phrase to say you don’t understand what someone said or what is happening. You can soften it by adding “desculpe” (Sorry) or follow it with a clarification request like “Pode repetir?” (Can you repeat?). Word-by-word: eu (I) + não (not) + entendo (I understand).
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu não entendo. Pode repetir, por favor?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat, please?

additional_notes: A direct, romantic way to say “I love you.” In Brazil it’s common; in Portugal you’ll also hear “amo-te.” For a lighter/less intense option (often for friends and family), people may say “gosto de você” (Brazil) / “gosto de ti” (Portugal) (“I like you/I care about you”). Word order and pronouns can vary (e.g., “eu amo você”).
target_language_example: Eu te amo muito.
native_language_example: I love you a lot.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission to speak or to introduce a question politely. Often shortened in conversation to “Tenho uma pergunta” (dropping “eu”). You can also use “Eu tenho uma dúvida” when you mean a doubt/uncertainty rather than a specific question.
target_language_example: Com licença, eu tenho uma pergunta: onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman someone used to date. The prefix "ex-" means "former" and is often written with a hyphen (ex-namorado/ex-namorada). It can be used possessively ("minha ex-namorada" = "my ex-girlfriend") and is generally neutral, though the context can make it sound sensitive.
target_language_example: Eu vi minha ex-namorada ontem no supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw my ex-girlfriend yesterday at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone you used to date. In Portuguese, the prefix “ex-” means “former” and is commonly used with relationship words (ex-namorado/ex-namorada, ex-marido/ex-mulher). It’s typically written with a hyphen: “ex-namorado”.
target_language_example: Meu ex-namorado mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My ex-boyfriend lives in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used for the portable device that puts out small fires. Common in signs/instructions and safety contexts. Often appears with the verb "usar" (to use) or "haver/ter" (to have): "Onde fica o extintor de incêndio?".
target_language_example: Tem um extintor de incêndio perto da porta.
native_language_example: There is a fire extinguisher near the door.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used casually to invite someone to speak (“Go on, tell me”) or as a friendly opener meaning something like “What’s up?/So, what is it?”. Often said to friends; can sound too casual in formal situations.
target_language_example: E aí, fala aí: o que aconteceu?
native_language_example: So, tell me—what happened?

additional_notes: From the verb "falar" (to speak) + "inglês" (English). It can be a question or a statement depending on intonation/context. Often used as "Você fala inglês?" (Do you speak English?) or with other subjects: "Eu falo inglês" (I speak English), "Ele/Ela fala inglês" (He/She speaks English).
target_language_example: Você fala inglês?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech. Often used as a reaction to something surprising, annoying, or hard to believe. It can sound playful among friends or rude if said sharply. You can also hear it as an instruction meaning “be serious” (literally “speak seriously”).
target_language_example: Fala sério, você esqueceu de novo?
native_language_example: Seriously, you forgot again?

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman who grew up speaking a language from childhood. For a man, say "falante nativo"; for a group/mixed gender, "falantes nativos". Often used with "de" + language (e.g., "falante nativa de português"). In everyday conversation, you may also hear "nativa" alone or "falante"/"pessoa" + "nativa", but "falante nativa" is clear and common in language-learning contexts.
target_language_example: Ela é falante nativa de português e pode te ajudar com a pronúncia.
native_language_example: She is a native Portuguese speaker and can help you with pronunciation.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who learned a language from childhood as their first language (e.g., "um falante nativo de português"). You’ll also see the plural "falantes nativos". Common in language-learning, education, and job contexts.
target_language_example: Ela é falante nativa de português, mas fala inglês muito bem.
native_language_example: She is a native Portuguese speaker, but she speaks English very well.

meaning: to speak badly of (someone/something); to badmouth.
additional_notes: Often used to mean criticizing someone (sometimes behind their back), gossiping, or saying negative things. It can take a direct object: "falar mal de alguém" (to speak badly of someone). Note: "falar mal" can also literally mean "to speak poorly" (e.g., not speaking a language well), but in everyday conversation it very often means "to badmouth".
target_language_example: Ele vive falando mal dos colegas no trabalho.
native_language_example: He’s always badmouthing his coworkers at work.

meaning: to be serious; to talk seriously.
additional_notes: Used to say you mean what you’re saying or to ask someone to stop joking. Common as an interjection: “Fala sério!” = “Seriously?!” / “Come on!” You can also use it with a subject: “Estou falando sério.” (I’m serious.)
target_language_example: Fala sério! Você vai embora amanhã?
native_language_example: Seriously?! You’re leaving tomorrow?

meaning: “Do you speak Portuguese?” / “You speak Portuguese.” (informal “tu” form).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "falar" (to speak) in the 2nd person singular: "tu falas". Commonly said as a question to someone you’re addressing with "tu" (friends, kids, people your age in many contexts). In Brazil, people more often say "Você fala português?"; in Portugal, "Falas português?" is very common in informal situations.
target_language_example: Falas português? Posso fazer-te uma pergunta.
native_language_example: Do you speak Portuguese? Can I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Common, slightly informal way to say "please" in European Portuguese, often used in requests. Frequently appears as "faz favor de + infinitive" (e.g., faz favor de esperar) or on its own as a polite prompt (e.g., Faz favor!). It comes from the longer phrase "faz (o) favor".
target_language_example: Faz favor de fechar a porta.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: a handyman; a jack-of-all-trades (someone who does many different tasks).
additional_notes: Often used as a noun to describe a person who can fix/build/handle many small jobs (especially around the house or workplace). Can also describe something “multi-purpose” (e.g., a cleaner or tool). Colloquial/commonly spoken; you may also see it hyphenated as “faz-tudo.”
target_language_example: Ele é o faz tudo do prédio: arruma torneiras, troca lâmpadas e conserta portas.
native_language_example: He’s the building’s handyman: he fixes faucets, changes light bulbs, and repairs doors.

additional_notes: Common everyday expression meaning to remove facial hair, usually with a razor. You can specify whose beard with a possessive: "fazer a barba" (shave), "fazer a barba dele" (shave his beard). Also used for grooming in general before going out: "Preciso fazer a barba".
target_language_example: Vou fazer a barba antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’m going to shave before going out.

additional_notes: Common daily-routine phrase. It literally means “to do the bed,” but in Portuguese it’s the normal way to say “make the bed” (tidy the sheets/blankets after sleeping).
target_language_example: Eu sempre faço a cama antes de sair de casa.
native_language_example: I always make the bed before leaving the house.

meaning: to have a great time; to party (a lot).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone really enjoyed themselves at a party/event (sometimes implying drinking, dancing, and staying out late). Depending on context, it can also mean “to throw/host a party,” but it more often means “to party hard / have a blast.”
target_language_example: No casamento, eles fizeram a festa até de madrugada.
native_language_example: At the wedding, they partied until dawn.

meaning: to make love; to have sex (romantic/soft).
additional_notes: Common, fairly neutral expression for having sex, often with a romantic or affectionate tone. In the present tense you might see/hear "fazemos amor" (we make love). It’s compositional from "fazer" (to do/make) + "amor" (love), and it can be translated literally as "make love" in English. Use with care in polite conversation; for a more clinical term, Portuguese also has "ter relações sexuais".
target_language_example: Eles disseram que fizeram amor pela primeira vez.
native_language_example: They said they made love for the first time.

meaning: to have a birthday (to turn an age).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s birthday date or the act of turning a certain age. Often followed by a time expression (hoje, amanhã, no mês que vem) or an age: “fazer 18 anos”. You can also ask: “Quando você faz aniversário?” = “When is your birthday?”
target_language_example: Eu faço aniversário em março e este ano faço 30 anos.
native_language_example: My birthday is in March, and this year I’m turning 30.

meaning: to have a birthday (to turn X years old).
additional_notes: Used to say that it’s someone’s birthday or that they are turning a certain age. Very common with a time expression ("hoje", "amanhã") or an age: "Faço 30 anos" = "I’m turning 30". Literally "to make years" (not the natural English phrasing).
target_language_example: Hoje eu faço 25 anos.
native_language_example: Today I turn 25.

meaning: to make up; to reconcile (after an argument).
additional_notes: Used when people stop being angry at each other and become friends again after a fight or disagreement. Common with "com": "fazer as pazes com alguém" (make up with someone). Also used with "voltar a" to mean "to make up again".
target_language_example: Depois da briga, eles fizeram as pazes.
native_language_example: After the fight, they made up.

meaning: to do good; to be good for (someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two ways: (1) general idea of benefiting someone/something: "Isso faz bem (para você)" = "That’s good for you." (2) with an indirect object pronoun to mean it does someone good (often emotionally): "Faz-me bem" / "Faz bem a ela" = "It does me/her good." Can also be used as "fazer bem a + noun" ("fazer bem ao coração" = "be good for the heart").
target_language_example: Caminhar todos os dias faz bem à saúde.
native_language_example: Walking every day is good for your health.

meaning: to make a face; to grimace.
additional_notes: Used when someone changes their facial expression to show disgust, pain, embarrassment, or to tease/joke. Often said to kids (e.g., “Não faz careta!”). Also common with “para” (“fazer careta para alguém” = to pull faces at someone).
target_language_example: Ele fez careta quando provou o remédio.
native_language_example: He made a face when he tasted the medicine.

meaning: to poop; to have a bowel movement.
additional_notes: Common, child-friendly, and mildly informal way to talk about going to the bathroom (number two). In more formal contexts you might hear "defecar" (very formal/medical) or "evacuar". Often used with "precisar" (to need): "Preciso fazer cocô."
target_language_example: Eu preciso fazer cocô. Onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: I need to poop. Where is the bathroom?

meaning: to keep someone company; to accompany someone.
additional_notes: Used when you stay with someone so they are not alone (at home, in the hospital, on a trip, etc.). It commonly takes an indirect object with “a”: “fazer companhia a alguém” (to keep someone company). You can also use it without saying who, if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Posso fazer companhia à minha avó esta tarde.
native_language_example: I can keep my grandma company this afternoon.

additional_notes: Commonly used with “que” + a clause: “fazer de conta que …” (= “pretend that …”). Often refers to acting as if something were true, sometimes to ignore something on purpose (“fazer de conta que não viu” = pretend you didn’t see). Also used with children’s play (“Vamos fazer de conta!” = “Let’s play pretend!”).
target_language_example: Ele fez de conta que não me viu.
native_language_example: He pretended he didn’t see me.

meaning: to do everything (possible); to do whatever it takes.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize making a big effort to achieve something, help someone, or solve a problem. Often followed by a clause with “para” (to) or “por” (for): “Vou fazer de tudo para…”. In many contexts it implies “do anything/everything I can,” rather than literally doing every single thing.
target_language_example: Vou fazer de tudo para chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re doing/making is masculine (or when a masculine noun is implied but not said). Often you’ll hear it with an explicit noun: “fazer esse trabalho” (do this job), “fazer esse pedido” (place/make this order). If the noun is feminine, you usually use “fazer essa”.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer esse trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s do this work today.

meaning: to be missing; to be needed; to miss (someone/something).
additional_notes: Very common expression. It often means “to miss” in the sense of feeling someone/something’s absence: “Você me faz falta” = “I miss you.” It can also mean something is needed: “Faz falta dinheiro/tempo” = “Money/Time is needed,” and in context it can mean something wasn’t present/available: “Senti que fez falta” = “I felt it was missing.” Structure: “fazer falta a + alguém” (to be missed by someone) and “fazer falta” + noun (to need/lack something).
target_language_example: Você me faz falta desde que se mudou.
native_language_example: I’ve missed you since you moved.

meaning: to border (to share a border with).
additional_notes: Used with "com" to say that one place shares a border with another: "X faz fronteira com Y". It’s common in geography and travel contexts. The literal idea is “to make a border,” but in English you usually say “to border / to share a border with.”
target_language_example: Portugal faz fronteira com a Espanha.
native_language_example: Portugal borders Spain.

meaning: to kill time; to wait around (often while stalling).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used when you have nothing to do and you’re just passing the time, or when you’re deliberately stalling (e.g., before an appointment). Related: “fazer hora com alguém” means “to tease/make fun of someone,” but that usually needs “com alguém.”
target_language_example: Cheguei cedo e fiquei fazendo hora no café até a reunião começar.
native_language_example: I arrived early and killed time at the café until the meeting started.

meaning: to work extra hours; to do overtime.
additional_notes: Often said as "fazer horas extra(s)" (to do overtime). Common in work contexts to talk about staying after your scheduled shift to finish tasks or meet deadlines.
target_language_example: Esta semana vou ter de fazer horas extra para acabar o projeto.
native_language_example: This week I’m going to have to work overtime to finish the project.

meaning: to have an idea; (usually in the negative) to have no idea.
additional_notes: Very common in everyday speech, especially as “não fazer ideia” = “to have no idea / not have a clue.” Often followed by “de” + noun or clause: “não faço ideia do que…” / “não faço ideia de como…”. More formal alternatives: “não sei” (I don’t know), “não tenho ideia” (I have no idea).
target_language_example: Não faço ideia de onde ele mora.
native_language_example: I have no idea where he lives.

meaning: to be bad for; to harm; to make (someone) feel sick.
additional_notes: Used to say something is harmful to someone’s health or wellbeing, or that it makes you feel unwell (often after eating/drinking). Common patterns: "X faz mal (para/a) Y" (X is bad for Y) and "Isso/Algo me faz mal" (That/Something makes me feel sick). Not the same as "fazer o mal" (to do evil).
target_language_example: Leite me faz mal, então eu não tomo.
native_language_example: Milk makes me feel sick, so I don’t drink it.

meaning: to screw up; to do something stupid (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used when someone makes a mess, makes a bad mistake, or causes trouble. Often said as a warning (Não vai fazer merda!) or as a confession/regret (Eu fiz merda.). In more polite speech, use "fazer besteira" (to do something silly/stupid) or "fazer bobagem".
target_language_example: Se você mexer nisso sem saber, vai fazer merda.
native_language_example: If you mess with that without knowing what you’re doing, you’ll screw up.

meaning: “what can you do?” / “what else can we do?” (resigned acceptance).
additional_notes: Often used as a standalone comment after something bad or unavoidable happens, to show resignation (similar to “oh well”). It can also appear as a question like “E agora, fazer o quê?” meaning “So what do we do now?” More common in casual conversation; in more formal contexts you might say “O que podemos fazer?”
target_language_example: Chegamos atrasados e a loja já fechou — fazer o quê?
native_language_example: We got there late and the store is already closed—what can you do?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is a member or component of a group, organization, or whole. It’s usually followed by "de" (fazer parte de + noun). You can also use it with "não" to say someone/something is not included: "não faz parte de...".
target_language_example: Ela faz parte da equipe de marketing.
native_language_example: She is part of the marketing team.

meaning: to belittle / make fun of (someone); to treat (something) as unimportant.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "fazer pouco de" + person/thing: "fazer pouco de mim/de você/de alguém". It can mean mocking someone, looking down on them, or minimizing something (not taking it seriously). In a literal, non-idiomatic sense, "fazer pouco" can also mean "to do little / not do much," but the "belittle" meaning is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Não faça pouco de mim.
native_language_example: Don’t make fun of me / Don’t belittle me.

meaning: to insist on; to make a point of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is important to you and you won’t skip it. Very common with "de" + noun ("fazer questão de silêncio" = to insist on quiet) or "de" + infinitive ("fazer questão de pagar" = to insist on paying). In the negative, it can mean you don’t care: "Não faço questão" = I don’t mind / It’s not important to me.
target_language_example: Eu faço questão de pagar a conta.
native_language_example: I insist on paying the bill.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical, understandable, or reasonable. Often appears in questions or negatives: “Faz sentido?” (Does that make sense?), “Não faz sentido.” (That doesn’t make sense). In the past: “Fazia sentido.” (It made sense).
target_language_example: Isso não faz sentido.
native_language_example: That doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Common, straightforward way to talk about having sex. Neutral but explicit; in formal/medical contexts you may also hear "ter relações sexuais". Conjugates like "fazer": "fiz sexo" (I had sex), "vai fazer sexo" (will have sex). Often used with "com" + person: "fazer sexo com alguém".
target_language_example: Eles disseram que não vão fazer sexo antes do casamento.
native_language_example: They said they won’t have sex before marriage.

meaning: to act like; to pretend (often to look cool, innocent, etc.).
additional_notes: Informal (common in Brazil). Used when someone is putting on an attitude or pretending to be/feel something. Often followed by “de” + noun/adjective ("fazer tipo de rico" = act like a rich person) or by a clause with “que” ("fazer tipo que não viu" = pretend you didn’t see).
target_language_example: Ele fez tipo que não ouviu e continuou andando.
native_language_example: He acted like he didn’t hear and kept walking.

additional_notes: Very common, child-friendly/euphemistic way to say you need to urinate. Used with “precisar” or “ter que”: “Preciso fazer xixi.” More formal alternatives: “urinar” (medical/formal) or “ir ao banheiro” (neutral: go to the bathroom).
target_language_example: Desculpa, preciso fazer xixi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to pee.

additional_notes: Literally “do (me/us) a favor.” Common in Portugal (often as “Faça favor” or “Faz favor” informally). Used to make polite requests (like “please”) or to invite someone to proceed (like “go ahead”). In Brazil, “por favor” is more common.
target_language_example: Faça favor de esperar um momento.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment.

additional_notes: A common holiday greeting used around December 25. Capitalization varies (often written “Feliz Natal”). You can also say it with a wish: “Desejo-lhe/te um feliz Natal” (“I wish you a Merry Christmas”).
target_language_example: Feliz Natal para você e sua família!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used to поздравить someone on their birthday. You can say it on its own, or add the person’s name (e.g., “Feliz aniversário, Ana!”). In Brazil it’s also common to say “Parabéns!” alongside it. Literally “happy anniversary/birthday,” but in everyday use it means “happy birthday.”
target_language_example: Feliz aniversário, João! Tudo de bom pra você!
native_language_example: Happy birthday, João! All the best to you!

additional_notes: A common greeting used around New Year’s (before and after midnight on New Year’s Eve). Often said or written on cards/messages. You may also see it with an article: “Feliz Ano Novo!” (more formal capitalization) or “Um feliz ano novo!” (“A happy new year!”).
target_language_example: Feliz Ano Novo! Que este ano traga muita saúde e paz.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! May this year bring lots of health and peace.

additional_notes: Used for the appliance that you use to iron clothes. Often appears as “ferro de passar roupa” (clothes iron). Related verb: “passar a ferro” = to iron (clothes).
target_language_example: Preciso do ferro de passar para tirar as rugas da camisa.
native_language_example: I need the iron to remove the wrinkles from the shirt.

meaning: to be alert; to watch out (wise up).
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to warn someone to pay attention, be cautious, or not be fooled. Literally “to become smart/clever,” but it often means “stay sharp” or “be on your guard,” especially after a mistake or when there’s risk of being tricked.
target_language_example: Fica esperto com esses e-mails falsos.
native_language_example: Watch out for those fake emails.

meaning: to stay behind; to fall behind.
additional_notes: Used when someone/something remains behind physically (doesn’t go with the group) or lags behind in progress (e.g., in school, work, a schedule). Often used with pronouns: “Eu fiquei para trás”, “Ela ficou para trás”.
target_language_example: Se você parar, vai ficar para trás.
native_language_example: If you stop, you’ll fall behind.

additional_notes: Used to name the genre in books, movies, TV shows, etc. Often shortened to "sci-fi" in English; in Portuguese you’ll usually say the full phrase (or "ficção" if the context is clear).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de filmes de ficção científica.
native_language_example: I like science fiction movies.

meaning: a very offensive insult: “bitch” / “son of a bitch” (said about a woman).
additional_notes: Strong profanity and highly insulting; avoid in polite conversation. Literally means “daughter of a whore” and is used to insult someone or express intense anger. (Male form: “filho da puta”.)
target_language_example: Ele me chamou de filha da puta.
native_language_example: He called me a bitch / a son of a bitch.

meaning: “son of a mother” → “son of a bitch” / “(that) bastard” (insult).
