additional_notes: A strong insult used to express anger or contempt, directed at a person (often said as an exclamation). It can be joking among close friends in some contexts, but it’s still rude and risky with strangers. Literally it means “son of the mother,” which is a euphemistic/less explicit version of “filho da puta.”
target_language_example: Aquele filho da mãe me enganou!
native_language_example: That bastard tricked me!

meaning: a very offensive insult: “son of a bitch” / “motherf***er.”
additional_notes: Strong vulgar profanity used to insult someone or express anger. Not appropriate in polite conversation; can escalate conflict. Literally “son of a whore,” and it’s often used as a standalone insult (“Seu filho da puta!”).
target_language_example: Seu filho da puta, sai daqui agora!
native_language_example: You motherf***er, get out of here now!

additional_notes: Common in Christian/religious contexts. “Filho” is masculine (“son”); “filha de Deus” is feminine (“daughter of God”). You may also hear the plural “filhos de Deus” (“children of God”). Can be used literally (religious belief/title) or more generally to mean a person as a creation of God.
target_language_example: Na igreja, ele disse que todos nós somos filhos de Deus.
native_language_example: At church, he said that all of us are children of God.

meaning: only child (a person with no siblings).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is their parents’ only child. It agrees with the person’s gender/number: "filho único" (male), "filha única" (female). Plural: "filhos únicos" / "filhas únicas". Often used with "ser": "Eu sou filho único".
target_language_example: Ela é filha única.
native_language_example: She is an only child.

meaning: “son of a bitch” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar/offensive profanity in Portuguese. Used to insult someone (noun) or as an intensifier/adjective (e.g., “um trânsito filho-da-puta” = “a horrible/awful traffic jam”). Often written with hyphens when used as a single insult, but you may also see it without hyphens (“filho da puta”). Avoid in polite situations; it can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: Ele me chamou de filho-da-puta.
native_language_example: He called me a son of a bitch.

additional_notes: Common everyday term meaning Saturday and Sunday. Often used with "no" (on/at the weekend) and with verbs like "passar" (to spend): "No fim de semana" = "on the weekend"; "passar o fim de semana" = "spend the weekend". Also used in greetings: "Bom fim de semana!" (Have a good weekend!).
target_language_example: O que você vai fazer no fim de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do on the weekend?

meaning: "the end of the world"; also a very remote, out-of-the-way place.
additional_notes: Literally means “end of the world.” Besides the literal/apocalyptic meaning, it’s very commonly used to mean somewhere extremely far away, hard to get to, or isolated (often with a complaining tone): "mora no fim do mundo" (“he/she lives in the middle of nowhere”). Often used with verbs like ficar (to be located), morar (to live), or ir (to go).
target_language_example: A casa dela fica no fim do mundo, leva duas horas pra chegar.
native_language_example: Her house is in the middle of nowhere; it takes two hours to get there.

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese you’ll more often see/hear "fim de semana" (usually without hyphens). Often used with prepositions like "no/ao" (on the weekend) and "de" (at the weekend): "no fim-de-semana", "ao fim-de-semana".
target_language_example: O que vais fazer no fim-de-semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do on the weekend?

additional_notes: Common Brazilian Portuguese term for Saturday and Sunday (similar to “fim de semana”). Often used with prepositions: “no final de semana” = “on/over the weekend”; “neste final de semana” = “this weekend”; “no próximo final de semana” = “next weekend.”
target_language_example: O que você vai fazer no final de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do on the weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about stories, films, books, relationships, or situations that end well. Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "dar" (to give/turn out), e.g., "ter um final feliz" = "to have a happy ending."
target_language_example: Eu adoro filmes que têm um final feliz.
native_language_example: I love movies that have a happy ending.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for the thin thread used to clean between your teeth. Often used with verbs like "usar" (to use), "passar" (to floss/run it between teeth), and "comprar" (to buy).
target_language_example: Eu uso fio dental todos os dias.
native_language_example: I use dental floss every day.

additional_notes: Common general term for tape that sticks, used for wrapping, sealing boxes, quick fixes, and crafts. In Brazil, people also say "fita crepe" (masking tape) and "fita isolante" (electrical tape) for specific types. In Portugal, you may also hear "fita-cola" for sticky tape.
target_language_example: Você tem fita adesiva para fechar essa caixa?
native_language_example: Do you have adhesive tape to close this box?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about tropical regions with hot climates and lots of rain (e.g., the Amazon). Often used with the definite article: “a floresta tropical” (the tropical rainforest/forest). In Portuguese, “floresta” is feminine, so adjectives agree: “tropical” stays the same for masculine/feminine.
target_language_example: A Amazônia é uma grande floresta tropical.
native_language_example: The Amazon is a large tropical rainforest.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive in many contexts. Used to show anger, frustration, defiance, or indifference (similar to “screw it” but much stronger). You may also hear it directed at someone as an insult (“fuck you”), depending on tone and context. Best avoided in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ah, foda-se, eu vou embora.
native_language_example: Ah, fuck it, I’m leaving.

additional_notes: Used for fireworks in general, especially for celebrations. In Brazilian Portuguese it’s very common in the plural: "fogos de artifício" (fireworks). In European Portuguese, you may also hear "fogo de artifício" as a mass noun. It’s also used figuratively for a flashy display meant to impress ("just for show").
target_language_example: Na virada do ano, teve muitos fogos de artifício na praia.
native_language_example: On New Year’s Eve, there were lots of fireworks on the beach.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to apologize for a small mistake or inconvenience. Literally “it was bad,” but it’s used like “my bad” or “sorry about that.” Often said quickly in conversation; you can also hear “foi mal aí” (“sorry about that / my bad there”).
target_language_example: Foi mal, eu te interrompi.
native_language_example: My bad, I interrupted you.

additional_notes: Common term in Brazil for devices you listen with. Often shortened to just "fone" in casual speech. You may also hear "fones de ouvido" (plural) for a pair, or "fone de ouvido sem fio" for wireless. In Portugal, "auscultadores" is more common.
target_language_example: Esqueci meu fone de ouvido em casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my headphones at home.

additional_notes: Common preposition meaning 'outside' a place (fora de casa = outside the house) or 'out of' a limit/condition (fora de controle = out of control). It can also mean 'except for'/'apart from' (fora de você, ninguém sabe = apart from you, nobody knows). Often followed by a noun; with infinitive, it can introduce an exception: fora de brincadeira = no kidding / seriously.
target_language_example: Isso está fora de controle.
native_language_example: This is out of control.

additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, emotion, behavior, or event that is no longer being managed or kept within limits. Common with verbs like "ficar" (to become): "ficou fora de controle". Can also describe something literally unmanageable (a fire, a crowd) or figuratively (anger, spending).
target_language_example: A situação ficou fora de controle muito rápido.
native_language_example: The situation got out of control very quickly.

additional_notes: Most often means a "way of life" (a lifestyle or how people live), especially in phrases like "um modo/uma forma de vida". It can also mean a "life form" in biology/ecology (a type of living organism). The meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Eles defendem uma forma de vida mais simples.
native_language_example: They support a simpler way of life.

meaning: willpower; self-control to keep doing something.
additional_notes: Used to talk about mental strength and determination to resist temptations or persist with a goal. Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "precisar de" (to need): "ter força de vontade", "precisar de força de vontade".
target_language_example: Preciso de força de vontade para parar de comer doces.
native_language_example: I need willpower to stop eating sweets.

additional_notes: Common preposition used for physical location (in front of something) and for figurative situations meaning "in the face of"/"when confronted with". It can also introduce a comparison, similar to "compared to" (especially in writing or formal speech). Often used with a noun or pronoun: "frente ao/à" (a + o/a) or "frente aos/às".
target_language_example: Frente ao banco, há uma farmácia.
native_language_example: In front of the bank, there is a pharmacy.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural as "frutos do mar" to mean seafood in general (shrimp, clams, squid, etc.). You’ll see it on menus and in dish names, similar to English "seafood".
target_language_example: Hoje vou pedir uma massa com frutos do mar.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to order pasta with seafood.

meaning: to smoke one (usually a cigarette or a joint).
additional_notes: An informal, incomplete phrase where the object is implied by context (e.g., “um cigarro” or “um baseado”). Common in speech, often used as a suggestion/invitation: “Vamos fumar um?” = “Wanna smoke one?”
target_language_example: Vamos lá fora fumar um?
native_language_example: Shall we go outside to smoke one?

meaning: rock bottom; the lowest point (in a bad situation).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation that has become as bad as it can get, often emotionally, financially, or in someone’s life. It can refer to a person (“chegar ao fundo do poço” = to hit rock bottom) or to a situation (“estar no fundo do poço” = to be at rock bottom). Literally “bottom of the well,” and it’s commonly used in a serious tone.
target_language_example: Depois de perder o emprego e terminar o namoro, ele chegou ao fundo do poço.
native_language_example: After losing his job and ending the relationship, he hit rock bottom.

additional_notes: Used to talk about local time differences between places. Often appears with a location ("no fuso horário de Lisboa") or with "diferença de fuso horário" (time difference). Plural: "fusos horários".
target_language_example: O Brasil tem vários fusos horários.
native_language_example: Brazil has several time zones.

additional_notes: Used to refer specifically to the U.S. sport with helmets and an oval ball, to distinguish it from "futebol" (soccer). In Brazil, "futebol" usually means soccer, so "americano" clarifies which sport you mean.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de assistir a futebol americano aos domingos.
native_language_example: I like watching American football on Sundays.

meaning: to earn a living; to make a living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone supports themselves financially (their job or way of earning money). Often used with “como” (how/doing what) or “a” + profession: “ganhar a vida como professor” (make a living as a teacher). Literal meaning is “to win/earn the life,” but in Portuguese it’s the fixed expression for earning a living.
target_language_example: Ela ganha a vida como tradutora.
native_language_example: She makes a living as a translator.

meaning: nice people; a good/nice person (friendly, decent).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. "Gente" can mean "people" or refer to a person informally, and "boa" means "good"—together it describes someone as friendly, trustworthy, and pleasant to be around. You can use it about a group (plural idea) or about one person: "Ele é gente boa."
target_language_example: A Maria é gente boa — sempre ajuda todo mundo.
native_language_example: Maria is a nice person — she always helps everyone.

meaning: a classy, very nice person; “good people.”
additional_notes: Common in Brazil as a compliment. Often used about someone’s character/vibe: “Ele é gente fina” = “He’s a really nice/cool guy.” Can also be plural: “Eles são gente fina.”
target_language_example: A Ana é gente fina; sempre ajuda todo mundo.
native_language_example: Ana is a really nice person; she always helps everyone.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something or show you’re unimpressed. Often comes as an exclamation or short reply: “Grande coisa!” or “Ah, grande coisa…”. Can also appear in phrases like “não é grande coisa” (“it’s nothing special / not a big deal”).
target_language_example: Ele comprou um carro novo? Grande coisa!
native_language_example: He bought a new car? Big deal!

additional_notes: Used to indicate a cause. Often positive (“thanks to”), but it can also be neutral/negative (“due to/because of”), depending on context. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive: graças a você (thanks to you), graças ao trânsito (due to traffic), graças a ter estudado (thanks to having studied). Note the contraction with masculine singular: graças a + o → graças ao; plural: graças aos; feminine: graças à / graças às.
target_language_example: Cheguei a tempo graças ao metrô.
native_language_example: I arrived on time thanks to the subway.

meaning: “thank God” / “thanks to God” (said to express relief or gratitude).
additional_notes: Common exclamation in Brazilian and European Portuguese. You can say it alone (“Graças a Deus!”) to show relief, or use it before a clause to mean “thankfully” (e.g., “Graças a Deus, deu tudo certo.”). More religious-sounding than neutral options like “ainda bem,” but also used casually.
target_language_example: Graças a Deus, você chegou bem.
native_language_example: Thank God, you arrived safely.

meaning: Ancient Greek (the Greek language from antiquity).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical language of Ancient Greece, especially in school/university, linguistics, history, and classical literature. It contrasts with "grego moderno" (Modern Greek). Capitalization varies, but in Portuguese it’s common to keep it lowercase in running text unless part of a title.
target_language_example: Na universidade, ela estuda grego antigo e latim.
native_language_example: At the university, she studies Ancient Greek and Latin.

meaning: Modern Greek (the modern form of the Greek language).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the contemporary Greek language (as opposed to older forms like "grego antigo" = Ancient Greek). Often appears in language-learning contexts, classes, and descriptions of what languages someone speaks.
target_language_example: Estou a aprender grego moderno para a minha viagem à Grécia.
native_language_example: I’m learning Modern Greek for my trip to Greece.

additional_notes: A formal/historical title used for certain rulers or members of royal families in some European contexts. Commonly appears in history texts and proper names; plural: grãos-príncipes.
target_language_example: Ele era o grão-príncipe de um pequeno território.
native_language_example: He was the grand prince of a small territory.

additional_notes: Refers to a person hired to protect someone (often a celebrity, politician, or VIP). It’s a common noun; plural is usually “guarda-costas” (invariable in practice).
target_language_example: O cantor chegou com dois guarda-costas.
native_language_example: The singer arrived with two bodyguards.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a wardrobe/closet where you store clothes. It can also refer to the clothes you own as a group (your “wardrobe”), depending on context. Literally “clothes-keeper” (guardar = to keep/store + roupa = clothes). In Brazil it’s very common; in some contexts you may also hear “armário” for a closet/cabinet.
target_language_example: Vou colocar as roupas no guarda-roupa.
native_language_example: I’m going to put the clothes in the wardrobe/closet.

additional_notes: Used to describe a war fought within the same country (between groups of citizens), often in historical or news contexts. Plural: "guerras civis".
target_language_example: A guerra civil durou vários anos.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a war involving many countries. Often appears with an article ("a guerra mundial") or with an ordinal to specify a historical event: "Primeira Guerra Mundial" (World War I) and "Segunda Guerra Mundial" (World War II).
target_language_example: A Segunda Guerra Mundial terminou em 1945.
native_language_example: World War II ended in 1945.

meaning: to have to; to be supposed to (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express obligation/necessity or something expected to happen: “Hei de estudar” (I must/will study), “Hás de ver” (you’ll see). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “ter de/ter que” is more common; “haver de” can sound more formal, literary, or emphatic (and it’s also common in European Portuguese). Conjugates like “haver” (hei, hás, há, havemos, haveis, hão) + de + infinitive.
target_language_example: Tenho de sair agora, mas hei de voltar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I have to leave now, but I will/must come back later.

additional_notes: Geography term for the half of the Earth north of the Equator. Often used when talking about seasons and climate differences (e.g., summer in the Northern Hemisphere is winter in the Southern Hemisphere). Usually written in lowercase in Portuguese unless part of a proper name or at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: No hemisfério norte, o verão começa em junho.
native_language_example: In the Northern Hemisphere, summer begins in June.

additional_notes: Geography term for the half of the Earth south of the Equator. Used in weather/season talk (seasons are opposite to the Northern Hemisphere). Often appears in phrases like "no hemisfério sul" (in the Southern Hemisphere).
target_language_example: No hemisfério sul, o verão começa em dezembro.
native_language_example: In the Southern Hemisphere, summer starts in December.

additional_notes: Used for a country’s official anthem, especially in formal or ceremonial contexts (sports events, official ceremonies). In Brazil and Portugal, you’ll commonly hear it with a definite article: “o hino nacional”.
target_language_example: Antes do jogo, todos cantaram o hino nacional.
native_language_example: Before the match, everyone sang the national anthem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the present time in general (current habits, trends, or how things are now), often contrasted with the past (e.g., antigamente). It’s common at the start of a sentence: “Hoje em dia, …”.
target_language_example: Hoje em dia, muita gente trabalha de casa.
native_language_example: Nowadays, a lot of people work from home.

meaning: businessman; a man who works in business.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a man who works in commerce/business, often implying an executive or entrepreneur. Plural: homens de negócios. Feminine equivalent: mulher de negócios (or empresária, depending on context). In European Portuguese, you may also hear homem de negócios; in Brazilian Portuguese, homem de negócios is understood, but empresário is very common.
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de negócios muito bem-sucedido.
native_language_example: He is a very successful businessman.

additional_notes: Used mainly in work contexts to talk about working beyond your normal schedule. It can refer to a single extra hour or overtime in general; the plural is “horas extras.” Common with the verb “fazer” (to do/work): “fazer hora extra.”
target_language_example: Hoje vou fazer hora extra para terminar o relatório.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work overtime to finish the report.

meaning: “how long ago” / “for how long” (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Used with the verb haver (há) to ask about elapsed time. 
- Past point (“how long ago”): Há quanto tempo você chegou? (You arrived some time ago.)
- Duration up to now (“for how long”): Há quanto tempo você mora aqui? (You’ve been living here up to now.)
Common answers use “há + time”: Há dois anos. (Two years ago / for two years, depending on the question.)
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você mora aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you lived here?

meaning: a long time ago; for a long time (already).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to indicate elapsed time, similar to "ago" or "for" in English. Common with the imperfect tense to talk about something that has been true for a while ("Há tempos que..."). In speech it often implies “quite a while,” not a precise duration.
target_language_example: Não te vejo há tempos.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in ages.

additional_notes: Used to refer to any language that is not your native language (e.g., English is an "idioma estrangeiro" for a Portuguese speaker). Common in school/work contexts ("aulas de idioma estrangeiro", "curso de idioma estrangeiro"). Similar meaning to "língua estrangeira"; "idioma" and "língua" are often interchangeable in everyday Portuguese.
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo um idioma estrangeiro para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language for work.

meaning: equal to; the same as; like (similar to).
additional_notes: Used mainly for comparisons and equality. Common patterns: "X é igual a Y" (X is the same as Y) and "igual a + noun/pronoun" (like/similar to). In math and measurements it means "equal to" (e.g., "dois mais dois é igual a quatro").
target_language_example: Isso é igual a ontem: está chovendo de novo.
native_language_example: It’s the same as yesterday: it’s raining again.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “fingerprint” (used for identification, police records, unlocking a phone, etc.). It can also mean a “digital impression/print” in technical contexts (like dentistry or 3D scanning). In everyday speech, to specify the sense clearly, you may hear “impressão digital do dedo” (fingerprint).
target_language_example: Para fazer o documento, preciso da sua impressão digital.
native_language_example: To make the document, I need your fingerprint.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about instruments in general. Usually preceded by an article (um/uma, o/a) and can be pluralized: instrumento(s) musical(is). Often used with the verb “tocar” (to play): tocar um instrumento musical.
target_language_example: Ela toca um instrumento musical desde criança.
native_language_example: She has played a musical instrument since she was a child.

additional_notes: Used to refer to computer systems or software that can perform tasks that seem to require human intelligence (e.g., learning, recognizing images/voices, generating text). Often abbreviated as “IA” in Portuguese. Common in tech, business, and everyday news.
target_language_example: A inteligência artificial está mudando a forma como trabalhamos.
native_language_example: Artificial intelligence is changing the way we work.

additional_notes: Very commonly spelled and used as **em vez de** (standard form). It introduces an alternative: do one thing **instead of** another, followed by a noun or an infinitive verb (e.g., *em vez de estudar* = instead of studying). You may also see **ao invés de**, but **em vez de** is the safest, most general choice.
target_language_example: Em vez de sair, vamos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Instead of going out, let’s stay at home.

meaning: to go after; to pursue; to look for (something/someone).
additional_notes: Often used with "de": "ir atrás de" + noun/pronoun. It means trying to get something, chasing a goal, or actively looking for someone/something (not literally walking behind). Common in everyday speech, similar to "to go after" or "to chase down" in English.
target_language_example: Vou ir atrás de um emprego melhor.
native_language_example: I’m going to go after a better job.

meaning: to go ahead; to move forward; to continue.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to proceed ("Go ahead") or to describe continuing despite a pause/difficulty ("carry on"). Very common in conversation and instructions. Often appears as a command: "Vai em frente!"
target_language_example: Pode ir em frente, eu já vou atrás.
native_language_example: You can go ahead; I’ll come right behind.

additional_notes: A very common way to say you’re leaving a place (often “to go home” is implied by context). You can conjugate ir (vou, vai, vamos, etc.) and keep embora: “Eu vou embora.” It can also describe something going away/disappearing: “A dor foi embora” (“The pain went away”).
target_language_example: Já está tarde, vou embora.
native_language_example: It’s already late; I’m leaving.

additional_notes: Used for the action of going to bed (usually to sleep). Often appears as "vou para a cama" (I’m going to bed) or in the past: "fui para a cama" (I went to bed). You can also hear "ir pra cama" in casual speech/writing (dropping the "a").
target_language_example: Estou cansado(a); vou para a cama cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to bed early today.

meaning: to go to jail; to get arrested (end up in jail).
additional_notes: Literally “to go (be) jailed.” Used for someone being arrested or going to prison/jail as a result. Often appears in the past: “Ele foi preso” (“He was arrested”). You can also say “ser preso” (to be arrested).
target_language_example: Se ele fizer isso de novo, vai preso.
native_language_example: If he does that again, he’ll go to jail.

additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going to bathe, often implying “I’m going to go (now) and take a shower.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, tomar banho usually means “to take a shower,” though it can also mean “to take a bath” depending on context. Uses ir + infinitive to express a near-future plan/intention; often appears as Vou tomar banho (“I’m going to take a shower”).
target_language_example: Vou tomar banho agora, já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a shower now; I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: A strong, offensive way to tell someone to go away or express anger. Most often used in the imperative: “Vai à merda!” (you, informal singular) or “Vão à merda!” (you all). Avoid in polite situations; it’s harsher than “vai embora” (go away).
target_language_example: Vai à merda! Não quero falar com você.
native_language_example: Fuck off! I don’t want to talk to you.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for going out to buy groceries, clothes, etc. Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + "às" (= a + as, "to the") + "compras" (purchases/shopping). Often used with a time expression: "Vou às compras amanhã" (I’m going shopping tomorrow).
target_language_example: Vou às compras depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going shopping after work.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese. Often used to point to something (“that one there”), to agree/confirm (“that’s it”, “exactly”), or to react to something just said (“right on / that’s the idea”). “Aí” adds an informal, conversational sense of “there/like that”.
target_language_example: É isso aí! Vamos embora.
native_language_example: That’s it! Let’s go.

additional_notes: Used to clarify or restate what you just said, often to give a more precise explanation or a correction. In writing it’s commonly used like “isto é,” and is equivalent to “ou seja” in many contexts.
target_language_example: Podemos ir amanhã, isto é, se você estiver livre.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow, that is, if you’re free.

additional_notes: Used for the first stage of school before primary school, typically for young children. In Brazil, it often refers to early childhood education (especially ages ~4–5), but usage can overlap with “pré-escola”. In Portugal, “jardim de infância” commonly refers to preschool (roughly ages 3–5/6).
target_language_example: Minha filha vai para o jardim de infância no ano que vem.
native_language_example: My daughter is going to kindergarten/preschool next year.

additional_notes: The standard, neutral term for a zoo. Often shortened to “zoológico” in everyday speech. Commonly used with the verb “ir ao” (to go to): “ir ao jardim zoológico / ir ao zoológico.”
target_language_example: Vamos ao jardim zoológico no sábado?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the zoo on Saturday?

meaning: to play soccer/football; to play ball (in general).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “to play soccer” in Brazil. It can also mean playing ball sports more generally, depending on context. Literally “to play ball,” and it’s a common everyday phrase.
target_language_example: No domingo, a gente vai jogar bola no parque.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we’re going to play soccer in the park.

additional_notes: Common with objects you no longer want or that are unusable. It can also mean "to waste" (time/money/chances) depending on context. In European Portuguese you may also hear "deitar fora" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vou jogar fora essas caixas velhas.
native_language_example: I'm going to throw away those old boxes.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about games played on a computer (PC/Mac), as opposed to "jogo de videogame" (console video game) or "jogo de celular" (mobile game). Plural: "jogos de computador". You can also say "jogo para computador" (game for computer).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de jogar jogos de computador no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I like to play computer games on the weekend.

meaning: next to; close to; with (in the care of / in the possession of).
additional_notes: Commonly indicates physical proximity ("next to") or being near something ("close to"). It can also mean "with" in the sense of being kept/left in someone’s care or possession, especially in more formal contexts (e.g., "deixei junto ao porteiro" = left with the doorman). Often appears after nouns like "ao lado" or in phrases like "junto a mim/ti/ele" (close to me/you/him).
target_language_example: O banco fica junto ao supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is next to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is in the company of, accompanied by, or included with someone/something else. Common in everyday speech and writing. Often followed by a noun/pronoun: "junto com a minha irmã" (together with my sister). Similar in meaning to "com" (with), but "junto com" emphasizes being together/alongside.
target_language_example: Vou ao mercado junto com a minha mãe.
native_language_example: I’m going to the market together with my mom.

meaning: to swear to God (to insist something is true).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you’re telling the truth or making a serious promise. It can sound intense, religious, or overly dramatic depending on context; in some settings it may be considered inappropriate. Common patterns: "Eu juro por Deus (que...)" and "Jura por Deus!" (asking someone to swear).
target_language_example: Eu juro por Deus que não fui eu.
native_language_example: I swear to God it wasn’t me.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve had enough and want something to stop (complaining, noise, teasing, an argument, etc.). Can sound firm or irritated depending on tone. Often appears as a standalone exclamation: “Já basta!”
target_language_example: Já basta! Para com isso agora.
native_language_example: That’s enough! Stop it now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something or that you’ve had enough. Often said firmly (sometimes annoyed), similar to “Enough already!” You can also use it when something is sufficient: “Já chega de comida” (“That’s enough food”).
target_language_example: Já chega! Para com isso.
native_language_example: That’s enough! Stop it.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese as an informal way to say something is finished, lost, or no longer possible (similar to “that’s it” or “game over”). Literally it looks like “already was,” but the idiomatic meaning is usually “it’s over/too late.” Tone can be resigned (“oh well”) or emphatic (“no chance”).
target_language_example: Tentei comprar o ingresso, mas esgotou — já era.
native_language_example: I tried to buy the ticket, but it sold out — it’s over (too late now).

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening later than expected (often with impatience, relief, or mild criticism). Common in conversation. Literally “it was already time,” and it can be followed by “de + infinitive”: “Já era hora de ir.”
target_language_example: Já era hora de você chegar!
native_language_example: It was about time you arrived!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or justification that the listener is expected to accept (often like “since…, then…”). Common in spoken and written Portuguese. It can also mean “now that” when referring to a change in situation.
target_language_example: Já que você está aqui, pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: Since you’re here, can you help me?

additional_notes: Used to show you understand, remember, or have figured something out. Often said as a quick response in conversation (like “OK, I know” or “Got it”). Can also be used to mean “I know!” when you suddenly remember something or get an idea. Tone depends on context: it can sound neutral, reassuring, or impatient if said sharply.
target_language_example: Tá bem, já sei — vou fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: OK, I know / I’ve got it — I’ll do that now.

additional_notes: Common, casual way to say you’re leaving briefly and will return soon. You can also say it when stepping away from a conversation, desk, or shop counter. Variations you may hear: “já volto” / “já já eu volto” (even sooner) / “já volto aí” (I’ll be right there/back there).
target_language_example: Espera um minuto, já volto.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Made of já (“already/now”) + é (“is”). Often used to emphasize that something is already the case or that a small achievement still counts (similar to “at least it’s something”). In speech it can appear alone as a short comment: “Já é.”
target_language_example: Não é muito, mas já é alguma coisa.
native_language_example: It’s not much, but it’s already something (at least it’s something).

meaning: side by side; next to each other.
additional_notes: Used for things (or people) positioned close together in a line or at the same level. It can also be used figuratively to mean doing something together or in agreement (e.g., working side by side). Often used with verbs like ficar/estar (to be) or caminhar (to walk).
target_language_example: As duas casas ficam lado a lado.
native_language_example: The two houses are side by side.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the exterior of something or being outside (not inside). Often appears with prepositions: "do lado de fora" = "on the outside" / "outside"; "ficar do lado de fora" = "to stay outside"; "do lado de fora da casa" = "outside the house". Also common in contrasts like "por dentro" (inside) vs. "por fora / do lado de fora" (outside).
target_language_example: Deixa os sapatos do lado de fora, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the shoes outside, please.

additional_notes: A formal/legal term for hiding the illegal origin of money by moving it through businesses or bank transactions to make it seem legitimate. Common in news, law, and finance contexts.
target_language_example: A polícia está investigando um caso de lavagem de dinheiro.
native_language_example: The police are investigating a money laundering case.

meaning: to wash your hands; (figuratively) to refuse responsibility.
additional_notes: Literally means washing your hands. Figuratively, it’s used when someone “washes their hands of” a problem—i.e., says it’s not their responsibility anymore and won’t get involved (often with a negative tone). Conjugates like a regular verb phrase: “Eu lavei as mãos”, “Ele vai lavar as mãos”.
target_language_example: O chefe lavou as mãos e disse que não era problema dele.
native_language_example: The boss washed his hands of it and said it wasn’t his problem.

meaning: deathbed; the bed (or final period) before someone dies.
additional_notes: Used in literal and figurative contexts. Literal: someone is very ill and close to dying (often in hospitals or at home). Figurative: the final stage of something (e.g., an institution, a project). "Leito" means "bed" (more formal than "cama" in some contexts), so the phrase is fairly transparent.
target_language_example: Ele fez um último pedido no leito de morte.
native_language_example: He made one last request on his deathbed.

additional_notes: Used for a single contact lens; the plural is "lentes de contato". In Brazil you’ll also hear "lente de contacto" in Portugal (European Portuguese spelling). Often used with "usar" (to wear/use): "Eu uso lentes de contato."
target_language_example: Esqueci minha lente de contato em casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my contact lens at home.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Used when you mean you will consider a factor/information before deciding or judging something. Very common in everyday and formal contexts. Often followed by "que" + clause ("Leve em conta que...") or by a noun phrase ("levar em conta o preço"). Conjugates like the verb "levar" (eu levo, você leva, nós levamos).
target_language_example: Temos que levar em conta o trânsito antes de sair.
native_language_example: We have to take traffic into account before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity/process needs a certain amount of time. Common patterns: "Leva tempo" (It takes time), "Leva muito/pouco tempo" (It takes a lot/little time), and "Leva X minutos/horas" (It takes X minutes/hours). Often followed by an infinitive: "Leva tempo para + infinitive" (It takes time to...).
target_language_example: Leva tempo para aprender português.
native_language_example: It takes time to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: A formal phrase used in politics, law, journalism, and everyday discussion to talk about the right to express opinions and ideas. Often appears with verbs like "defender" (to defend), "garantir" (to guarantee), and "respeitar" (to respect). Also commonly said as "liberdade de expressão e de imprensa" (freedom of expression and of the press).
target_language_example: A liberdade de expressão é um direito fundamental.
native_language_example: Freedom of expression is a fundamental right.

additional_notes: Used to talk about computer languages used to write code (e.g., Python, Java, C++). Often appears with the verb “usar” (to use) or “aprender” (to learn): “usar uma linguagem de programação”, “aprender uma linguagem de programação”. You can also say “linguagem de programação (X)” to specify one: “linguagem de programação Python”.
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo uma linguagem de programação para criar aplicativos.
native_language_example: I’m learning a programming language to create apps.

meaning: major home appliances (“white goods”), like fridges, stoves, and washing machines.
additional_notes: Common in Brazil, especially in retail/e-commerce. Refers to large kitchen/laundry appliances traditionally made in white (geladeira, fogão, máquina de lavar, freezer). Not used to mean a literal “white line.”
target_language_example: A loja está com promoção de linha branca: geladeiras e máquinas de lavar com desconto.
native_language_example: The store is having a sale on major appliances: refrigerators and washing machines are discounted.

additional_notes: Used for a book designed for teaching/learning a subject (school or language courses). Plural: "livros didáticos". You may also hear "material didático" for teaching materials in general.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar o livro didático de português para o semestre.
native_language_example: I need to buy the Portuguese textbook for the semester.

additional_notes: Used for schoolwork you do at home (school assignment). Often said as "fazer a lição de casa" (to do homework). You may also hear "dever de casa" in some places with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Tenho muita lição de casa para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of homework to do today.

meaning: as soon as; once; right when.
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive to express something that will happen immediately after another event in the future (similar to "as soon as"). Common in Brazilian Portuguese in the pattern: "logo que" + present subjunctive (e.g., "logo que eu puder", "logo que ele chegar"). In European Portuguese, you may also hear "logo que" (and very commonly "assim que") with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu te ligo logo que eu puder.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I can.

additional_notes: A small shop (often open late or 24/7) that sells everyday items like snacks, drinks, and basic essentials. Also commonly called "loja de conveniência" at gas stations ("posto de gasolina"). Plural: "lojas de conveniência".
target_language_example: Vou passar na loja de conveniência para comprar água e um lanche.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop by the convenience store to buy water and a snack.

additional_notes: A large store divided into sections (“departamentos”) for different types of products (clothes, home goods, electronics, etc.). Common collocation: "loja de departamentos" (plural) is also widely used. Often used with verbs like "ir a" (to go to) and "comprar" (to buy).
target_language_example: Vou à loja de departamento para comprar roupas.
native_language_example: I’m going to the department store to buy clothes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the lunar phase (often in weather/astronomy contexts or in storytelling/romantic descriptions). It’s a noun phrase: "a lua cheia" = "the full moon"; "na lua cheia" = "during the full moon". Also common in dates/events: "na noite de lua cheia" (on a full-moon night).
target_language_example: Hoje à noite vai ter lua cheia.
native_language_example: Tonight there will be a full moon.

additional_notes: Refers to the trip or period right after getting married (or a romantic post-wedding vacation). Often used with the verb "ir" (to go) or "estar" (to be): "ir para a lua de mel" / "estar em lua de mel". Common collocation: "viagem de lua de mel" (honeymoon trip).
target_language_example: Eles vão para a lua de mel na Bahia na semana que vem.
native_language_example: They’re going to Bahia for their honeymoon next week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a language that was deliberately created rather than naturally developed (e.g., Esperanto). In everyday conversation, people more often say "língua construída" or "idioma construído"; "língua artificial" can sound more technical.
target_language_example: O esperanto é uma língua artificial criada no século XIX.
native_language_example: Esperanto is an artificial language created in the 19th century.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a sign language in general or a specific one (e.g., Língua Gestual Portuguesa / Língua Brasileira de Sinais). Often appears in phrases like “aprender língua de sinais” (to learn sign language) and “intérprete de língua de sinais” (sign language interpreter).
target_language_example: Ela está a aprender língua de sinais para se comunicar melhor.
native_language_example: She is learning sign language to communicate better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language (your "língua materna"). Very common in school/work contexts and when discussing learning languages. Plural: "línguas estrangeiras".
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo português como língua estrangeira.
native_language_example: I’m learning Portuguese as a foreign language.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the first language someone learned (often the language spoken at home while growing up). Common in school, language-learning, and official contexts (forms, surveys): "Qual é a sua língua materna?" It can also be used more generally for someone’s primary language.
target_language_example: A minha língua materna é o inglês.
native_language_example: My native language is English.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the language(s) legally recognized by a country/region, or the official language of an organization. Often used with a possessive or a preposition: "a língua oficial do Brasil" (Brazil’s official language), "línguas oficiais" (plural).
target_language_example: O português é a língua oficial do Brasil.
native_language_example: Portuguese is the official language of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to compare size, quantity, importance, or age. It’s the comparative form of "grande" (big/great): "maior" + "que" (than). Often appears in basic comparisons like "X é maior que Y". For age, it means "older than": "Ele é maior que ela."
target_language_example: Este apartamento é maior que o outro.
native_language_example: This apartment is bigger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is bound to happen at some point in the future (even if you don’t know when). You can also use it about doing something eventually: "Tenho que fazer isso mais cedo ou mais tarde" (I have to do that sooner or later).
target_language_example: Mais cedo ou mais tarde, você vai precisar tomar uma decisão.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, you’ll need to make a decision.

additional_notes: Used before numbers, amounts, or measures to indicate something exceeds that amount: "mais de 10" = "more than 10". Common with time, money, distance, and quantities. Compare: "mais" = "more" (as an adverb) and "mais do que" = "more ... than" for comparisons (e.g., "mais alto do que" = "taller than").
target_language_example: Tenho mais de 20 anos.
native_language_example: I’m over 20 years old.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, numbers, or degrees: “mais do que X” = “more than X.” It can also compare two things with “mais … do que …” (“more … than …”). Often followed by numbers or time expressions (e.g., “mais do que 10 euros”, “mais do que uma hora”).
target_language_example: Ele ganha mais do que eu.
native_language_example: He earns more than I do.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number/amount/time (“around/about”) or to give a non-enthusiastic, mixed answer to “How are you?/How was it?” It can also soften a statement (not completely yes/no).
target_language_example: —Como você está? —Mais ou menos. Acho que vou melhorar amanhã.
native_language_example: —How are you? —So-so. I think I’ll feel better tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, numbers, or degrees: "mais que X" = more than X. Often appears with numbers ("mais que dez") or in comparisons ("mais que isso"). In European Portuguese, you may hear "mais do que" as a very common variant with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Este livro custa mais que vinte euros.
native_language_example: This book costs more than twenty euros.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a later time in the day or in the future. Common in phrases like “Até mais tarde” (“See you later”) and “Falamos mais tarde” (“We’ll talk later”). It can also mean “later than” in comparisons: “Ele chegou mais tarde do que eu” (“He arrived later than me”).
target_language_example: Não posso agora; ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t right now; I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used mainly in restaurants to describe how cooked you want meat: "bem passado" (well-done), "ao ponto" (medium), "mal passado" (rare). It agrees with the noun: "um bife mal passado". Not a literal translation into English.
target_language_example: Queria um bife mal passado, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a rare steak, please.

meaning: “I can’t wait” (I’m really looking forward to it).
additional_notes: Used to express excitement/anticipation about something that will happen soon. Literally “I can barely wait,” with *mal* meaning “barely/hardly” here. Often followed by *para* + infinitive (*mal posso esperar para ver…*) or *por* + noun (*mal posso esperar pelo fim de semana*).
target_language_example: Mal posso esperar para ver você amanhã!
native_language_example: I can’t wait to see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Describes a person’s behavior as lacking good manners (not “poorly educated” in the academic sense). Used as an adjective: "Ele é mal-educado" (He’s rude). You can also use it about an action: "Foi mal-educado da sua parte" (That was rude of you). Feminine form: "mal-educada"; plural: "mal-educados / mal-educadas".
target_language_example: Achei mal-educado ele falar no telefone durante a reunião.
native_language_example: I thought it was rude of him to talk on the phone during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about confusion or miscommunication. Often appears with the verbs "haver"/"acontecer" (to be/to happen) or "esclarecer" (to clear up): "Houve um mal-entendido" / "Vamos esclarecer o mal-entendido". Plural: "mal-entendidos".
target_language_example: Desculpe, acho que houve um mal-entendido.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think there was a misunderstanding.

meaning: bad-tempered; grumpy; in a bad mood.
additional_notes: An adjective describing someone’s mood/temper. Often used with "estar" for a temporary mood ("Ele está mal-humorado hoje"), but it can also describe a person’s general disposition ("Ele é mal-humorado"). Agree it with the person: mal-humorada (f.), mal-humorados (m. pl.), mal-humoradas (f. pl.). Common opposite: "bem-humorado" (good-humored).
target_language_example: Ela está mal-humorada porque dormiu pouco.
native_language_example: She’s grumpy because she slept little.

additional_notes: Often used to tell someone to leave (“mandar embora”) or to talk about being fired from a job (“ser mandado(a) embora”). In Brazil it’s common in everyday speech; in Portugal, “despedir” is more common for firing. With a direct object: “mandar alguém embora” = to send someone away.
target_language_example: O chefe mandou o funcionário embora.
native_language_example: The boss fired the employee.

meaning: to go for it; to go ahead and do it (often: do it confidently).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Used to encourage someone to start or continue, or to give permission/approval (“Go ahead!”). It can also mean to do something with energy or intensity (e.g., eating, working). Usually informal; the exact nuance depends on context and tone.
target_language_example: Se você está pronto, manda ver!
native_language_example: If you’re ready, go for it!

additional_notes: Common food item; literally “butter of peanut.” You’ll see it on grocery labels and in recipes. In Brazil, “pasta de amendoim” is also very common (often used for fitness/high-protein products).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de torrada com manteiga de amendoim no café da manhã.
native_language_example: I like toast with peanut butter for breakfast.

additional_notes: Common in Brazil. Used when someone deliberately doesn’t go to a class they’re supposed to attend. Literally “to kill class,” but it just means to miss class on purpose. Often used with "hoje" (today) or "vamos" (let’s): "Vamos matar aula".
target_language_example: Hoje eu matei aula porque não estava me sentindo bem.
native_language_example: Today I skipped class because I wasn’t feeling well.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (while waiting).
additional_notes: Common expression for doing something to make time go by, especially when you’re waiting (e.g., at the airport, before an appointment). Usually used with “para” + infinitive ("para matar o tempo") or in the past ("matei o tempo"). It does not mean literally killing time.
target_language_example: Vou ler um pouco para matar o tempo enquanto espero o ônibus.
native_language_example: I’m going to read a bit to kill time while I wait for the bus.

additional_notes: Brazilian Portuguese internet/slang expression (imperative). Literally “miss me” (from *errar* = to miss a target), used to tell someone to go away, stop talking to you, or stop being annoying (similar to “get lost” / “bye”). Usually written casually in messages and comments.
target_language_example: Ah, me erra, eu não tô com paciência hoje.
native_language_example: Ugh, leave me alone, I don’t have patience today.

additional_notes: Used for the prize for first place in sports and competitions. Also used figuratively to mean “the best” or “top quality” (e.g., a “gold-medal performance”).
target_language_example: Ela ganhou a medalha de ouro nos 100 metros.
native_language_example: She won the gold medal in the 100 meters.

meaning: half a dozen (six); also: a few.
additional_notes: Literally “half (of a) dozen.” Besides meaning exactly six, it’s often used loosely to mean “a few / several,” especially in casual speech (e.g., “meia dúzia de pessoas” = “a few people”). Common pattern: “meia dúzia de + noun.”
target_language_example: Só vieram meia dúzia de pessoas à reunião.
native_language_example: Only a few people came to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration or waiting time. Often appears with prepositions: "em meia hora" (in half an hour), "daqui a meia hora" (in half an hour/from now), "por meia hora" (for half an hour). Can also be used with "e" to tell time: "duas e meia" = 2:30.
target_language_example: Daqui a meia hora eu te ligo.
native_language_example: In half an hour I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used for a sister you share only one parent with (same mother or same father). Feminine form; masculine is "meio-irmão". Commonly used with a possessive ("minha meia-irmã").
target_language_example: A minha meia-irmã mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My half-sister lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time (00:00) or the start of a new day. Common in schedules and expressions like "à meia-noite" (at midnight) and "depois da meia-noite" (after midnight).
target_language_example: O voo chega à meia-noite.
native_language_example: The flight arrives at midnight.

additional_notes: Common in news, school, and public signs when talking about nature, pollution, conservation, climate, and sustainability. Often appears in phrases like "proteção do meio ambiente" (environmental protection) and "preservar o meio ambiente" (to preserve the environment).
target_language_example: Precisamos proteger o meio ambiente.
native_language_example: We need to protect the environment.

additional_notes: Used to describe a very remote place, far from towns or other people. Common after verbs like ficar/morar/estar (to be/live/stay). Often appears with prepositions like no/num: “no meio do nada” or “em pleno meio do nada.”
target_language_example: O hotel fica no meio do nada, então é melhor alugar um carro.
native_language_example: The hotel is in the middle of nowhere, so it’s better to rent a car.

additional_notes: Used to refer to 12:00 in the daytime. You’ll often see it in time expressions with articles or prepositions: “ao meio-dia” (at noon), “até meio-dia” (until noon), “depois do meio-dia” (after noon). Can also mean “midday” in a general sense (around lunchtime), depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar ao meio-dia.
native_language_example: Let’s have lunch at noon.

additional_notes: Refers to a male sibling who shares one parent with you (same mother or same father). Feminine form: meio-irmã. Plural: meio-irmãos / meio-irmãs. Often used with the preposition “de”: meio-irmão de pai (same father) / meio-irmão de mãe (same mother).
target_language_example: O Pedro é meu meio-irmão por parte de pai.
native_language_example: Pedro is my half-brother on my father’s side.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, ages, sizes, or values. In math and measurements, it corresponds to the symbol “<”. Common in everyday phrases like “menor que 18 anos” (under 18) and with numbers: “menor que dez” (less than ten).
target_language_example: Este preço é menor que o de ontem.
native_language_example: This price is lower than yesterday’s.

additional_notes: Used for an SMS or any short written message sent by phone. You can also hear just “mensagem” (message) or the verb phrase “mandar/enviar uma mensagem de texto” (to send a text message).
target_language_example: Vou te mandar uma mensagem de texto quando eu chegar.
native_language_example: I’ll send you a text message when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying/selling shares (ações) and how stock prices or the economy are doing. Common in news, finance, and everyday conversations about investing. Plural: “mercados de ações” (stock markets).
target_language_example: O mercado de ações caiu muito hoje.
native_language_example: The stock market fell a lot today.

meaning: “crappy/terrible” (used to insult or complain about something).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used before a noun to express strong annoyance or contempt, similar to “this crappy…” or “this piece of…”. Common in speech: “essa merda de + noun”. Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Estou farto dessa merda de computador!
native_language_example: I’m sick of this crappy computer!

additional_notes: Used for the small table next to a bed, typically where you keep things like a lamp, phone, book, or alarm clock. In Brazil, "criado-mudo" is also common (more informal/old-fashioned and can be considered insensitive by some); in Portugal, "mesa de cabeceira" is the standard term.
target_language_example: Deixei meu celular na mesa de cabeceira.
native_language_example: I left my phone on the bedside table.

additional_notes: Used to say something remains true despite what was just said (a contrast/concession). Often follows a reason or negative point: “Está caro, mas mesmo assim vou comprar.” It can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence; “mesmo assim” is slightly more emphatic than “ainda assim.”
target_language_example: Eu sei que está tarde, mas mesmo assim quero ir.
native_language_example: I know it’s late, but I still want to go.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or contrast. With a condition (“even if”), it commonly triggers the present subjunctive (e.g., mesmo que eu vá). With a fact/contrast (“even though”), it can also be followed by the indicative in some contexts (especially in Brazil). Often interchangeable with "ainda que" (more formal) or "embora" ("although").
target_language_example: Mesmo que chova, vamos ao parque.
native_language_example: Even if it rains, we’re going to the park.

meaning: "even if" (introduces a condition that doesn’t change the result).
additional_notes: Used to present a hypothetical or possible condition that won’t affect what happens next. It’s followed by a verb clause (often in the subjunctive, especially when the condition is uncertain): "mesmo se eu tiver tempo" = "even if I have time". Don’t confuse with "mesmo assim" ("even so / still").
target_language_example: Mesmo se chover, vamos sair.
native_language_example: Even if it rains, we’re going to go out.

meaning: to leave; to get out (often quickly).
additional_notes: Informal. Used when someone decides to go away/leave a place or situation, sometimes with a sense of urgency or annoyance. Often appears as “meter o pé” or “meter o pé fora” (to leave/go out).
target_language_example: Já ficou tarde, vou meter o pé.
native_language_example: It’s gotten late, I’m going to head out.

meaning: "My God!" / "Oh my God!" (an exclamation of surprise, shock, frustration, etc.).
additional_notes: Common interjection in Brazilian and European Portuguese. Depending on tone, it can express amazement, worry, annoyance, or disbelief. It can be said sincerely in a religious sense, but very often it’s just a general reaction (similar to English “Oh my God”). Stronger/emphatic variants include “Meu Deus do céu!” and “Ai, meu Deus!”.
target_language_example: Meu Deus, eu esqueci meu celular em casa!
native_language_example: Oh my God, I forgot my phone at home!

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male sibling. In informal speech, it can also be used as a friendly form of address to a man (similar to “bro,” “buddy,” or “my man”), even if he isn’t your actual brother. Feminine equivalent: “minha irmã” (“my sister”).
target_language_example: Este é o meu irmão, o Pedro.
native_language_example: This is my brother, Pedro.

meaning: to mess with; to deal with; to tease/flirt with (someone).
additional_notes: Very common and broad in everyday Portuguese. With things, it can mean “to handle/tamper with” or “to mess around with” (often: don’t touch). With people, it can mean “to tease,” “to pick on,” or even “to flirt/catcall,” depending on context. It can also mean “to affect” someone emotionally: “Isso mexe comigo” = “That gets to me / affects me.”
target_language_example: Não mexe comigo!
native_language_example: Don’t mess with me!

additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll see this as **micro-ondas** (plural form used as a noun) meaning “a microwave (oven)”: *um micro-ondas*. It’s also used in the adjective phrase **forno micro-ondas** (“microwave oven”).
target_language_example: Esquenta a comida no micro-ondas, por favor.
native_language_example: Heat up the food in the microwave, please.

additional_notes: Used as an interjection to react to surprise, shock, admiration, or disbelief. It’s a shortened form of “minha nossa senhora” (“my Our Lady”), so it can be mildly religious in tone, but it’s very common in everyday speech. Often said with emphasis: “Minha nossa!”
target_language_example: Minha nossa, que susto!
native_language_example: Oh my, what a scare!

additional_notes: A common cooking term for sauce made from tomatoes. Used on pasta, pizza, meat, etc. In Brazil you may also see "molho de tomate" (tomato sauce) vs. "extrato de tomate" (tomato paste).
target_language_example: Vou fazer macarrão com molho de tomate.
native_language_example: I’m going to make pasta with tomato sauce.

additional_notes: A highly offensive, crude way to insult a person or describe something as worthless. Avoid in polite conversation; you may hear it in arguments. Less harsh options include “que porcaria” (“what crap”) or “que droga” (“that sucks”).
target_language_example: Ele é um monte de merda.
native_language_example: He’s a pile of shit.

additional_notes: Literally “to die of hunger,” but it’s most often used as an exaggeration to say you’re extremely hungry. Can also be used literally in serious contexts. Common with the verb estar: “Estou a morrer de fome.”
target_language_example: Estou a morrer de fome — vamos comer alguma coisa?
native_language_example: I’m starving—shall we eat something?

additional_notes: Common phrase in news, science, and everyday conversation. Often used with verbs like “combater” (to fight), “reduzir” (to reduce), and “causar” (to cause). Plural: “mudanças climáticas”.
target_language_example: A mudança climática está afetando o clima em muitas regiões do mundo.
native_language_example: Climate change is affecting the weather in many regions of the world.

additional_notes: Used when someone decides differently from what they previously thought or planned. Often followed by “sobre” (about) + a topic or by “e” + a new decision (e.g., “Mudei de ideia e vou ficar em casa.”). In speech you’ll also hear the imperative “Muda de ideia!” (Change your mind!).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu mudei de ideia sobre ir ao cinema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind about going to the movies.

additional_notes: Often used informally to comment on something extreme, shocking, or unbelievable. Depending on context it can be negative (“that’s insane”) or positive (“that’s awesome/wild”). Literally “very crazy,” and it agrees in gender/number with the noun it describes: muito louco (m.), muito louca (f.), muito loucos (m. pl.), muito loucas (f. pl.).
target_language_example: A festa ontem foi muito louca!
native_language_example: The party yesterday was totally wild!

meaning: "much less" / "let alone" (used to emphasize that the second thing is even less likely/possible).
additional_notes: Used after a negative or limiting statement to strengthen it: if the first thing isn’t true/possible, then the second is even more impossible (similar to English “much less” or “let alone”). Often follows “não” (not) or “nem” (not even).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho tempo para cozinhar, muito menos para fazer sobremesa.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to cook, let alone make dessert.

meaning: “thank you very much” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express strong thanks. A man typically says “muito obrigado.” You can also drop “muito” and just say “obrigada/obrigado” for “thank you.” Commonly used on its own or followed by what you’re thanking someone for (e.g., “Muito obrigada pela ajuda”).
target_language_example: Muito obrigada pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help!

additional_notes: A common, polite way to thank someone. Use “muito obrigado” if the speaker is male; many speakers say “muito obrigada” if the speaker is female. Often used on its own, or followed by “por...” (“for...”), e.g., “Muito obrigado por tudo.”
target_language_example: Muito obrigado pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help!

additional_notes: Common, polite phrase used when you first meet someone (in person or in writing). Often said after introductions. You can also hear it as “Prazer” (more neutral/short) or “Muito prazer em conhecer você” (more explicit).
target_language_example: Oi, eu sou a Ana. Muito prazer!
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Ana. Nice to meet you!

meaning: "the real world" (life outside imagination, fiction, or the internet).
additional_notes: Used to contrast everyday reality with something fictional, virtual, idealized, or theoretical. Often appears with prepositions like "no mundo real" (in the real world) or "voltar ao mundo real" (to come back to the real world).
target_language_example: No mundo real, nem tudo sai como a gente planeja.
native_language_example: In the real world, not everything goes the way we plan.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a machine for sewing fabric (at home or professionally). You may also hear the shorter form “máquina” when the context is clear (e.g., in a sewing/alterations setting).
target_language_example: Comprei uma máquina de costura para fazer ajustes nas minhas roupas.
native_language_example: I bought a sewing machine to make adjustments to my clothes.

additional_notes: A noun phrase for the machine used to type on paper (old-style, not a computer). Often used with the verb "escrever" (to write/type) or "digitar" (to type). The plural is "máquinas de escrever".
target_language_example: Ele encontrou uma máquina de escrever antiga no sótão.
native_language_example: He found an old typewriter in the attic.

additional_notes: Common household item; often shortened to “a máquina” when the context is clear. You may also hear “máquina de lavar roupa” (“clothes washing machine”) for clarity, especially if contrasting with other machines (e.g., “máquina de lavar louça” = dishwasher).
target_language_example: A máquina de lavar está avariada.
native_language_example: The washing machine is broken.

additional_notes: Used for protective masks that filter harmful gases/smoke (e.g., in emergencies, firefighting, or chemical hazards). The plural is “máscaras de gás”.
target_language_example: Em caso de fumaça, coloque a máscara de gás e saia do prédio.
native_language_example: In case of smoke, put on the gas mask and leave the building.

additional_notes: A command telling someone to raise their hands, often said by police/security or used jokingly. Common variant: “Mãos para o alto!” It’s an imperative expression, not used for polite requests.
target_language_example: Polícia! Mãos ao alto!
native_language_example: Police! Hands up!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the genre (e.g., Bach, Mozart). In Portuguese, the adjective usually follows the noun: música (music) + clássica (classical). You may also see “a música clássica” (classical music as a category) or “uma música clássica” (a classical piece/song).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ouvir música clássica enquanto estudo.
native_language_example: I like to listen to classical music while I study.

meaning: in (someone’s) face; right in front (of someone).
additional_notes: Literally “on the face” (na = em + a). Common in phrases like “na cara de alguém” (“in someone’s face”) and “bem na cara” (“right in your face”). Can describe something happening openly/obviously, sometimes in a confrontational way depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ele mentiu na minha cara.
native_language_example: He lied right to my face.

additional_notes: Commonly used for position or direction. Often appears as "na frente de" (in front of) and can also mean "ahead" in a line, race, or progress ("Ele está na frente" = he’s ahead/in the lead).
target_language_example: O carro está na frente da casa.
native_language_example: The car is in front of the house.

additional_notes: Common prepositional phrase used for physical position (standing/sitting in front of something) and for being earlier/leading in a line, sequence, or race. Often used with location verbs like "ficar" (to be located), "estar" (to be), and "parar" (to stop).
target_language_example: O banco fica na frente do supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is in front of the supermarket.

meaning: right away; immediately (also: right on time).
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Most often means “immediately/straight away” (especially with verbs like fazer, resolver, mandar). In some contexts it can also mean “at the exact time” or “on time,” depending on what’s being discussed.
target_language_example: Eu faço isso na hora.
native_language_example: I’ll do that right away.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal viewpoint, often at the start of a sentence: "Na minha opinião, ...". It can also come at the end for emphasis. You can change the possessive to match the speaker: "na tua/sua opinião" (in your opinion), "na nossa opinião" (in our opinion).
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, este restaurante é o melhor do bairro.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

meaning: in the capacity of; as (someone’s role/function).
additional_notes: Common in formal or professional contexts to specify what role someone is acting in (job title, responsibility, legal role). It often comes before a noun phrase: "na qualidade de gerente" (as manager). Less common in casual speech; in everyday Portuguese you might simply use "como" (as).
target_language_example: Estou aqui na qualidade de representante da empresa.
native_language_example: I’m here in the capacity of the company’s representative.

additional_notes: Used to correct or clarify something, introduce the true situation, or contrast with what was previously said or assumed. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence ("Na realidade,...") or after the subject. Similar in meaning to "na verdade".
target_language_example: Na realidade, eu não moro aqui; estou só de visita.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t live here; I’m just visiting.

additional_notes: Common discourse marker used to correct, clarify, or add emphasis (often like English “actually”). It can also introduce a more accurate version of what was just said. Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the part being corrected. In writing it’s often followed by a comma: “Na verdade, ...”.
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

meaning: at the time; back then; in that period.
additional_notes: Used to situate something in a specific past period (often one already understood from context). Common in storytelling and explanations: "Na época, eu morava em Lisboa" (back then, I lived in Lisbon). It can also refer to a particular moment or situation: "Na época do acidente" (at the time of the accident).
target_language_example: Na época, eu não tinha carro.
native_language_example: Back then, I didn’t have a car.

meaning: “nothing to do with it” / “not related” (also: “that makes no sense”).
additional_notes: Very common in informal spoken Portuguese. Used to say two things are unrelated (“não tem nada a ver com…”), or to react when something is illogical or doesn’t match what was said (“Nada a ver!”). Often appears as “não tem nada a ver”.
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com o que eu disse.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what I said.

additional_notes: Common reaction to say something is pretty good or acceptable. Often said as “Nada mau!” on its own, or after a noun/idea: “Nada mau essa ideia.” You can also use it to comment on results, looks, or performance.
target_language_example:
—Consegui um desconto de 20%.
—Nada mau!
native_language_example:
—I got a 20% discount.
—Not bad!

meaning: on (someone’s) back; behind someone; by carrying the burden/blame.
additional_notes: Literally “on the backs.” Common with verbs like carregar/levar (to carry), pôr/colocar (to put), ficar (to be/stand), falar (to speak), and with the pronoun “suas/minhas” implied by context. Can be physical (“carry on your back”) or figurative (“to blame”/“to burden” someone). Also used in the sense of “behind someone’s back” (e.g., falar nas costas).
target_language_example: Ele falou de mim nas costas.
native_language_example: He talked about me behind my back.

meaning: in the hands of; under the control/care of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is someone’s responsibility, control, or care (often about decisions, a situation, or an object being entrusted). It can be literal (physically in someone’s hands) or figurative ("it’s up to them"). Usually followed by a person or organization: "nas mãos do médico", "nas mãos da polícia", "nas mãos dela".
target_language_example: Agora a decisão está nas mãos do diretor.
native_language_example: Now the decision is in the director’s hands.

meaning: sunrise; the rising of the sun.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about the time when the sun appears in the morning. Often appears with verbs like "ver" (to see), "assistir" (to watch), or "acordar" (to wake up) and in expressions like "ao nascer do sol" (at sunrise) or "antes do nascer do sol" (before sunrise).
target_language_example: Acordamos cedo para ver o nascer do sol na praia.
native_language_example: We woke up early to see the sunrise at the beach.

additional_notes: Used for a vehicle designed to travel in space (sci‑fi or real space travel). More formal/technical contexts may prefer “espaçonave,” but “nave espacial” is very common and widely understood.
target_language_example: A nave espacial decolou rumo à Lua.
native_language_example: The spaceship took off toward the Moon.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb estar (or as a short reply) to show indifference or that something doesn’t matter to you. Often appears as “não estar nem aí (para ...)” = “not to care (about ...).” Very informal and can sound dismissive.
target_language_example: Eu não estou nem aí para o que eles pensam.
native_language_example: I don’t care what they think.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen or is not true in the smallest/most surprising case. Often comes right before what is being emphasized: "nem mesmo eu" (not even me). Can also appear with verbs or time phrases: "nem mesmo assim" (not even so / even then).
target_language_example: Nem mesmo eu sei a resposta.
native_language_example: Not even I know the answer.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse or reject an idea (“absolutely not”). Often followed by “em + infinitive”: “Nem pensar em sair!” = “Don’t even think about leaving!” It’s common in everyday speech and can sound blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: —Você vai emprestar seu carro? —Nem pensar!
native_language_example: —Are you going to lend your car? —No way!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something did not happen or is not true at the most basic/minimum level. Common in negative statements: "não... nem sequer" (“not... not even”). It can also appear without an explicit "não" when the negation is clear from context.
target_language_example: Eu nem sequer sabia disso.
native_language_example: I didn’t even know that.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise or disbelief about a fact someone might not expect. Often followed by a clause with “que” (e.g., “Ninguém diria que…” = “No one would guess that…”). The verb is in the conditional (“diria” = “would say”), so it can mean “no one would say” or, more naturally in English, “no one would guess.”
target_language_example: Ninguém diria que ele tem 50 anos.
native_language_example: No one would guess that he is 50 years old.

meaning: on air; live/broadcasting (also: in the air).
additional_notes: Common with TV/radio/streams to mean something is currently being broadcast (often used with verbs like estar/entrar: "Estamos no ar", "Entrar no ar"). It can also literally mean something is in the air (e.g., a smell, tension), depending on context.
target_language_example: O programa já está no ar.
native_language_example: The show is already on air.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said (similar to “but,” “however,” “still”). Common in writing and more formal speech; in casual conversation you’ll often hear “mas” or “só que” instead. Usually comes after a comma: “..., no entanto, ...”.
target_language_example: Eu queria ir, no entanto estou muito cansado.
native_language_example: I wanted to go; however, I’m very tired.

meaning: 'in the end' / 'when all is said and done'.
additional_notes: Common in conversation to introduce the final result, conclusion, or what matters after considering everything. Often used like "No fim das contas, ..." at the start of a sentence. It can also imply "after adding everything up" (accounts, costs, consequences), but it’s usually about the overall outcome.
target_language_example: No fim das contas, decidimos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: In the end, we decided to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement (not about a specific case). Often equivalent to "de modo geral" and can appear at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: No geral, o curso foi muito bom, mas as provas foram difíceis.
native_language_example: Overall, the course was very good, but the exams were difficult.

meaning: right now; at the moment; currently.
