additional_notes: Common time expression meaning “at this moment” or “currently.” Often used to say something is true temporarily or to describe what you’re doing now. Can also appear with negatives (e.g., “não posso no momento” = “I can’t right now”).
target_language_example: No momento, estou trabalhando, mas posso falar mais tarde.
native_language_example: Right now, I’m working, but I can talk later.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit (quantity, time, price, etc.). Often comes after the number/time expression (e.g., "dez minutos, no máximo") or right before it ("no máximo, dez minutos"). Common variant: "no máximo" = "no máximo"; contrast with "pelo menos" (at least).
target_language_example: Chego em dez minutos, no máximo.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in ten minutes, at most.

meaning: on paper; in theory (not necessarily in practice).
additional_notes: Literally means “on the paper.” Commonly used to contrast what is officially written/planned with what actually happens in reality (e.g., rules, plans, agreements). Often appears in phrases like “No papel, tudo parece perfeito, mas...”
target_language_example: No papel, o plano é ótimo, mas na prática é difícil de executar.
native_language_example: On paper, the plan is great, but in practice it’s hard to carry out.

meaning: just right; at the right point (e.g., perfect doneness or timing).
additional_notes: Literally “at the point.” Common in cooking to say food is cooked to the ideal doneness (e.g., steak, pasta). It can also describe timing or readiness: something happened/arrived exactly when it should. In other contexts, it may simply mean “at the stop/spot/point” depending on what “ponto” refers to (bus stop, meeting point, etc.).
target_language_example: A carne está no ponto.
native_language_example: The meat is cooked just right.

meaning: "in what" / "in which"; also "when it comes to" (in terms of).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" + "que". Used to introduce the topic/area you’re talking about ("no que diz respeito a..." = "as far as ... is concerned"), or after verbs/prepositions to mean "in what"/"in which" (more common with "no que" + clause). Sometimes appears with the subjunctive in the set phrase "no que depender de mim" (“as far as it depends on me”).
target_language_example: No que diz respeito ao preço, está tudo certo.
native_language_example: As far as the price is concerned, everything is fine.

meaning: "We’ll see" / "let’s see" (often meaning you’re not sure yet).
additional_notes: Very informal, mostly spoken. It’s a contracted/slurred form of "nós vamos ver" (or sometimes just "vamos ver"). Used to delay a decision, show uncertainty, or say you’ll check later.
target_language_example: Você acha que dá pra ir amanhã? — No vamo ver.
native_language_example: Do you think we can go tomorrow? — We’ll see.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the driver/in control of a vehicle. Literally "on the steering wheel" (volante = steering wheel), but in English the natural equivalent is "behind the wheel" or "driving." Often appears with verbs like estar/ficar (to be), sentar-se (to sit), or assumir (to take over) and can be used figuratively for being in charge.
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou no banco e depois fico no volante para voltar para casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the bank and then I’ll drive back home.

meaning: in the last (one) / on the last (one).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "último". Used before a masculine singular noun that is the final one in a sequence or list (e.g., "no último dia" = "on the last day"). Often appears with time expressions and ordinal contexts. For feminine nouns, use "na última".
target_language_example: No último dia da viagem, fomos à praia.
native_language_example: On the last day of the trip, we went to the beach.

additional_notes: Used for a name that identifies a specific person/place (a proper noun). In everyday forms and conversations, it often means your given/first name (as opposed to your family/last name, "sobrenome" or "apelido" in European Portuguese). Common in questions like "Qual é o seu nome próprio?"
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome próprio e o seu sobrenome?
native_language_example: What is your first name and your last name?

additional_notes: Used as an adjective (e.g., cinema norte-americano) or a noun (um norte-americano). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it often refers specifically to someone from the United States, even though literally it means “North American” (from North America). Feminine form: norte-americana; plural: norte-americanos / norte-americanas.
target_language_example: Ele é norte-americano e mora no Brasil há dois anos.
native_language_example: He is American (from the U.S.) and has lived in Brazil for two years.

additional_notes: Usually written as **Novo Mundo** (capitalized) when referring to the Americas in a historical/geographical sense (contrasted with **Velho Mundo**, “Old World,” meaning Europe/Africa/Asia). In everyday speech, **mundo novo** (lowercase, different word order) more often means “a new world” in a general/figurative sense.
target_language_example: Os europeus chamavam as Américas de Novo Mundo.
native_language_example: Europeans called the Americas the New World.

meaning: in the blink of an eye; very quickly.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens extremely fast or suddenly. Common in both Brazilian and European Portuguese. Often follows verbs like "acontecer" (to happen), "passar" (to pass), or "resolver" (to solve). Variant: "em um piscar de olhos".
target_language_example: A tempestade começou num piscar de olhos.
native_language_example: The storm started in the blink of an eye.

meaning: calmly; in a good way/with good intentions (no hard feelings).
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression (from “em uma boa”). Used to signal that something is okay, that you’re relaxed about it, or to ask someone to take it easy: “Fica numa boa” = “Stay calm.” Can also mean “friendly/peacefully,” as in doing something without conflict.
target_language_example: Fica numa boa, eu não tô bravo com você.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m not mad at you.

additional_notes: A common saying used to remind someone that things can change and that you shouldn’t be too certain something will never happen. Often said after someone says “I’ll never…” or “That will never happen.”
target_language_example: Você acha que nunca vai voltar? Nunca diga nunca!
native_language_example: You think you’ll never come back? Never say never!

additional_notes: A common saying used to remind someone that things can change and you shouldn’t rule something out completely. Uses the informal "tu" form ("digas"), so it sounds more casual/personal; you may also hear the more formal/plural version "nunca diga nunca".
target_language_example: Achas que nunca vais viajar? Nunca digas nunca!
native_language_example: Do you think you’ll never travel? Never say never!

additional_notes: Used to say you shouldn’t rule something out completely, because circumstances can change. Often said after someone claims something will never happen, or to suggest staying open-minded about future possibilities.
target_language_example: Você acha que nunca vai morar fora, mas nunca dizer nunca.
native_language_example: You think you’ll never live abroad, but never say never.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen again: Nunca mais faço isso. It can also mean “not anymore/no longer” when combined with a negative verb: Não quero nunca mais falar disso (“I don’t want to talk about that anymore”). Often used for emphasis in promises, complaints, or strong decisions.
target_language_example: Eu nunca mais vou chegar atrasado.
native_language_example: I’m never going to be late again.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about the future or an outcome, often as a reason to be cautious or prepared. Literally “never (one) knows,” with the impersonal "se" (general meaning: “people/you”). Common as a standalone comment or added after a suggestion.
target_language_example: Leva um casaco — nunca se sabe.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket—you never know.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to react to surprising news, similar to “Seriously?” or “You’re kidding!” Often said with emphasis: “Não brinca!” It can also be understood literally as a negative command (“Don’t joke / don’t mess around”), depending on context and tone. You may also hear it as “Não brinca comigo” (“Don’t mess with me / Don’t kid me”).
target_language_example: —Ganhei dois ingressos VIP. —Não brinca!
native_language_example: —I won two VIP tickets. —No kidding!

meaning: “It doesn’t cost anything” / “It can’t hurt (to ask/try).”
additional_notes: Literally “it doesn’t cost anything,” used both for saying something is free and as a polite way to suggest doing something because there’s no downside (like “it can’t hurt”). Often followed by an infinitive: “Não custa nada perguntar/tentar.”
target_language_example: Não custa nada perguntar — talvez eles ajudem.
native_language_example: It can’t hurt to ask—maybe they’ll help.

additional_notes: Literally “don’t say (it)”. Common as an exclamation reacting to news, similar to “Really?” or “You’re kidding!” Depending on tone, it can be sincere surprise or mildly sarcastic. Also possible as an actual command: “Não diga isso” (“Don’t say that”).
target_language_example: —A Ana vai mudar para o Canadá. —Não diga!
native_language_example: —Ana is moving to Canada. —No way!

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or doesn’t change the situation. Often followed by an indirect question (e.g., “não importa se...”—“it doesn’t matter if...”) or by “o que/quem/onde/quando/como” (“no matter what/who/where/when/how”). It can also mean “don’t worry about it.”
target_language_example: Não importa se você chegar um pouco tarde.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter if you arrive a little late.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or not relevant. Often comes after a question or suggestion to dismiss it: "Não interessa" = "Doesn’t matter." You can also hear it with an implied object: "Não interessa quem" = "It doesn’t matter who." Tone can be neutral or slightly impatient depending on context.
target_language_example: — A que horas a gente sai? — Não interessa, a gente vê depois.
native_language_example: — What time are we leaving? — It doesn’t matter, we’ll figure it out later.

additional_notes: Literally “don’t tell me,” but commonly used as a reaction to news. Depending on tone, it can be genuine surprise or sarcastic/ironic (like English “You don’t say”). You can also say “Não me diga!” with stronger emphasis.
target_language_example: —A reunião foi cancelada. —Não me diga!
native_language_example: —The meeting was canceled. —You don’t say!

meaning: to not care; to have no interest in (something).
additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t want to hear about something or doesn’t care what happens. Often followed by "de" + noun/phrase: "não quero saber disso" (I don’t want to hear/care about that). Can sound blunt/strong depending on tone. Common in the imperative: "Não quero saber!" (I don’t care!/I don’t want to hear it!).
target_language_example: Eu não quero saber do que ele disse.
native_language_example: I don’t care what he said.

meaning: "I don’t want to know / I don’t care."
additional_notes: Literally “I don’t want to know.” Often used to show you’re not interested in details or you refuse to discuss something. Depending on tone, it can range from neutral (“don’t tell me”) to blunt/annoyed (“I don’t care”). Common variants: “não quero nem saber” (even stronger), “eu não quero saber” (more explicit).
target_language_example: Não quero saber de desculpas — quero uma solução.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hear excuses — I want a solution.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to reassure someone. Literally “don’t worry yourself” (formal/polite), using the imperative of preocupar-se. Often used as a response to an apology or thanks, similar to “it’s okay.” In Brazil you may also hear the informal equivalent “não se preocupa” or “não preocupa.”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, eu resolvo isso amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll sort that out tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common, neutral reply when you don’t have the information. Often used alone (“Não sei.”) or with the subject for emphasis (“Eu não sei.”). You can also add “desculpa” to sound more polite (“Não sei, desculpa.”).
target_language_example: Não sei onde fica o banheiro.
native_language_example: I don’t know where the bathroom is.

meaning: to really look forward to (can’t wait to).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re very excited or impatient for something to happen. It’s often followed by “de” + infinitive: “não vejo a hora de + verb”. You can conjugate it: “não vejo”, “não vê”, “não vemos”, etc. Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Não vejo a hora de viajar nas férias!
native_language_example: I can’t wait to travel on vacation!

additional_notes: Made of “não” (not) + “é” (is, from the verb *ser*). Used to negate statements with *ser*: “X não é Y” = “X isn’t Y.” Very common in everyday speech; in questions you’ll often see “não é?” meaning “isn’t it?/right?”
target_language_example: Isso não é verdade.
native_language_example: That isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something doesn’t concern them. Can sound rude/defensive, especially with a sharp tone; a softer alternative is "não é da sua conta, desculpe" or "não é assunto seu". Often used when someone is being too nosy.
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas isso não é da sua conta.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that’s none of your business.

additional_notes: Used to reinforce that a refusal is final and must be respected. Common in Brazilian Portuguese as a slogan about consent and personal boundaries, but it can also be used for any situation where someone keeps insisting after you’ve said no. Often said with a firm tone, sometimes after already saying “não”.
target_language_example: Eu já disse: não é não.
native_language_example: I already said it: no means no.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or give someone’s phone contact information. Often appears with the verb "dar" (to give) or "qual é" (what is): "Qual é o seu número de telefone?" In Brazil, people also commonly say "número de celular" (cell phone number) or just "telefone" in context.
target_language_example: Qual é o seu número de telefone?
native_language_example: What is your phone number?

additional_notes: Used to rank something as #1 or to emphasize top priority/importance. It can describe a person/thing (“o número um”) or act as a short exclamation (“Número um!”). Can also refer to “the number 1” in a literal counting context.
target_language_example: Ela é a número um da turma.
native_language_example: She is number one in the class.

additional_notes: "O" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). Use "o jogo" for a game in general (sports, video games, board games). In sports talk, it can also mean a specific match (like a soccer game). Capitalization ("Jogo") is usually only used in titles or when referring to a specific named event; normally it’s written "o jogo."
target_language_example: Vamos ver o jogo hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the game tonight.

additional_notes: Extremely rude and offensive in Brazilian and European Portuguese. Used as a strong insult or as an emphatic exclamation/intensifier (e.g., in fixed expressions like “vai pro caralho” = “go to hell/fuck off”; “pra caralho” = “a lot/as hell”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Vai pro caralho!
native_language_example: Go to hell! / Fuck off!

additional_notes: Uses masculine singular because it refers back to a masculine noun (or is used neutrally to mean “the same thing/one”). Often appears after a noun or pronoun: “o livro é o mesmo” (“the book is the same”) or “é o mesmo” (“it’s the same”). For feminine/plural agreement, you’ll hear: “a mesma”, “os mesmos”, “as mesmas”.
target_language_example: Quero o mesmo de sempre, por favor.
native_language_example: I want the same as always, please.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “the maximum” (e.g., a limit). In everyday speech, especially in Brazil, it’s also used as praise meaning “awesome,” “the best,” or “great.” Often appears after a verb like “ser”: “Você é o máximo!”
target_language_example: Você é o máximo! Obrigado pela ajuda.
native_language_example: You’re awesome! Thanks for the help.

additional_notes: Used mainly in more formal Portuguese as a relative pronoun meaning “which/that,” referring back to a masculine singular noun (feminine: a qual; plural: os quais/as quais). It often follows a preposition (e.g., em/para/de/com), like “em o qual” → usually contracted to “no qual.” In everyday speech, people often use “que” instead.
target_language_example: Este é o livro do qual eu falei.
native_language_example: This is the book (that/which) I talked about.

additional_notes: Used to ask or emphasize degree/amount, often before an adjective or adverb: "o quanto é importante" = "how important it is." It can also appear after verbs like "saber/imaginar" to mean "how much" ("Você sabe o quanto eu gosto..." = "Do you know how much I like..."). In questions about quantity, Portuguese also commonly uses just "quanto/quantos" (e.g., "Quanto custa?").
target_language_example: Você sabe o quanto isso é importante para mim?
native_language_example: Do you know how important this is to me?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something to be done with urgency. Often follows verbs like "fazer" (to do), "voltar" (to return), "responder" (to reply), or "enviar" (to send): "Faça isso o quanto antes." You can also say "o mais rápido possível" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Por favor, responda o quanto antes.
native_language_example: Please reply as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Very common in questions and indirect questions to ask about a thing/idea: "O que você quer?" (What do you want?) and "Não sei o que fazer." (I don’t know what to do.) It can also introduce a clause meaning “the thing that…” / “what…”: "Não entendi o que você disse." (I didn’t understand what you said.) Often appears in longer question patterns like "O que é isso?" (What is that?) or "O que é que você quer?" (What is it that you want?).
target_language_example: O que você quer comer?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat?

additional_notes: Used to show surprise, irritation, or confusion in a stronger way than plain “o que?” (“what?”). It can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone and context, so it’s best avoided in formal situations. Similar alternatives: “o que raios” (a bit softer), “o que infernos” (also strong).
target_language_example: O que diabos você está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or what happened, often as a response when someone calls you (“Ei!” — “O que foi?”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“What is it?”) or a bit annoyed (“What do you want?”). Literally it’s “what was (it)”, but it’s commonly used with a present meaning in conversation.
target_language_example: Você me chamou? O que foi?
native_language_example: Did you call me? What is it?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an open or indefinite choice: “whatever (it may be)”. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “seja”, “faça”, “aconteça”): “o que quer que seja” = “whatever it is”. Can also appear before a verb phrase: “o que quer que você diga” = “whatever you say”.
target_language_example: Vou apoiar você, o que quer que aconteça.
native_language_example: I’ll support you, whatever happens.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese to ask what just happened or to question something you heard/saw. "é que" adds emphasis (like “so/then”), and "foi" (past of "ser") points to something that just occurred. Often said with a surprised or annoyed tone. Also used when someone calls you and you reply: "O que é que foi?" ("What is it?").
target_language_example: —O que é que foi? Porque estás a gritar?
native_language_example: —What happened? Why are you shouting?

meaning: 'what?' (often used for emphasis or when 'what' is stressed).
additional_notes: Often written with an accent ("quê") when it’s stressed—typically at the end of a question or before a pause/punctuation: "O quê?" / "Você quer o quê?" In the middle of a sentence, it’s usually written without the accent: "O que você quer?" (same meaning: 'What do you want?').
target_language_example: Você disse o quê?
native_language_example: What did you say?

meaning: “sir”; a formal way to address an older man or a male stranger (also used as formal “you”).
additional_notes: Used in polite, formal situations (shops, customer service, speaking to elders, etc.). It often pairs with third-person verb forms: “O senhor quer…?” (“Do you want…?”). The feminine form is “a senhora” (“ma’am”). In Brazil it’s very common; in Portugal it exists but “o senhor + name/title” is often used for extra formality.
target_language_example: O senhor pode me ajudar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please, sir?

additional_notes: Used to say that the answer/outcome will only be known in the future. Often said when you can’t know yet, or when you want to be patient and wait. It can sound neutral, reassuring, or slightly skeptical depending on tone. Literally “the time will say.”
target_language_example: Não sabemos se vai dar certo — o tempo dirá.
native_language_example: We don’t know if it will work out—time will tell.

meaning: all the time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously or during the entire duration of an activity/event. Often follows the verb: "Estou trabalhando o tempo inteiro." You can also say "tempo inteiro" without "o" in some contexts (e.g., "trabalho em tempo inteiro" = full-time job).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei pensando nisso o tempo inteiro.
native_language_example: I kept thinking about it the whole time.

meaning: all the time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously or very often. It can describe an ongoing situation (“the whole time”) or a repeated habit (“all the time”). Often comes at the end of the sentence for emphasis, but can also appear near the verb.
target_language_example: Ele fica no celular o tempo todo.
native_language_example: He’s on his phone all the time.

additional_notes: Common expression meaning time seems to pass very quickly, often used when you’re busy, having fun, or noticing how fast things have changed. Literally “the time flies” (o tempo = the time; voa = flies, from voar).
target_language_example: Quando a gente está se divertindo, o tempo voa!
native_language_example: When we’re having fun, time flies!

meaning: 'a work by' / 'a work of' (used before an author/artist or a type of work).
additional_notes: Used to introduce who created something or what kind of work it is. Common patterns: "uma obra de + [autor/artista]" (a work by [author/artist]) and "uma obra de + [tipo]" (a work of + [type], e.g., "obra de arte" = work of art; "obra de ficção" = work of fiction). In Portuguese you typically use "de" where English often uses "by" for authorship.
target_language_example: Este livro é uma obra de Machado de Assis.
native_language_example: This book is a work by Machado de Assis.

additional_notes: Used for visual art or artistic creations (a painting, sculpture, installation, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to praise something as extremely well made (“Isso é uma obra de arte!”). Plural: “obras de arte”.
target_language_example: Este museu tem uma obra de arte do século XIX.
native_language_example: This museum has a work of art from the 19th century.

additional_notes: Literally “look there,” but in conversation it’s very often used as a quick warning or to get someone’s attention, similar to “Hey, watch it!” or “Careful!” Depending on tone, it can also signal mild disapproval (“Now, now…” / “Don’t do that”). Common in speech; you may also hear it as “Olha lá!” with emphasis.
target_language_example: Olha lá! Vai cair.
native_language_example: Careful! You’re going to fall.

additional_notes: Used in phrases like “a olho nu” (“with the naked eye”) to say something can be seen without glasses, a microscope, binoculars, etc. Often appears with verbs like “ver” (to see) and “ser visível” (to be visible).
target_language_example: A lua pode ser vista a olho nu em noites claras.
native_language_example: The moon can be seen with the naked eye on clear nights.

additional_notes: Used for the injury/bruise around the eye, often after being hit or bumping into something. Literally “purple eye,” since roxo can describe the purplish color of bruises. Common with ter/ficar: “Estou com/tenho um olho roxo” (I have a black eye); “Fiquei com o olho roxo” (I ended up with a black eye).
target_language_example: Ele apareceu no trabalho com um olho roxo.
native_language_example: He showed up at work with a black eye.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening via the internet or that a service/content is available on the web. In modern Portuguese, the most common spelling is "online" (without a hyphen); "on-line" is also understood and may appear in older texts or formal writing.
target_language_example: Posso fazer a inscrição on-line?
native_language_example: Can I register online?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “no matter where.” It’s typically followed by a verb: “onde quer que você esteja” (“wherever you are”). It can also appear as “aonde quer que” when emphasizing movement/destination (“wherever (to)”).
target_language_example: Onde quer que você esteja, me ligue.
native_language_example: Wherever you are, call me.

additional_notes: Plural masculine definite form: "os" = "the" (plural), "lobos" = "wolves". Often written lowercase ("os lobos") when referring to actual wolves; capitalized ("os Lobos") when it’s a name/title (e.g., a sports team, a group, a book/film title).
target_language_example: Os lobos vivem em matilhas.
native_language_example: Wolves live in packs.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as a respectful, formal way to address more than one person (“you”), especially in customer service, meetings, or when speaking to older people. It’s the plural of “o senhor.” In sentences it typically takes 3rd-person plural verb forms (like “vocês”): “Os senhores querem…?” It can also literally mean “the gentlemen” depending on context.
target_language_example: Os senhores precisam de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you (gentlemen/sirs) need help?

additional_notes: Used to clarify, rephrase, or give a more precise explanation of what you just said. Common in both speech and writing; in writing it’s often set off by commas. Similar function to English “i.e.” (not “e.g.”).
target_language_example: Ele mora em Lisboa, ou seja, não vai chegar hoje.
native_language_example: He lives in Lisbon, so (that is to say) he won’t arrive today.

meaning: “another story” (i.e., a different matter; that’s a different story).
additional_notes: Used to say that a topic/situation is different from what was just mentioned, often implying it would require a separate explanation or has different conditions. Common in the phrase “Isso é outra história.”
target_language_example: Eu posso ajudar hoje, mas amanhã é outra história.
native_language_example: I can help today, but tomorrow is a different story.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or should happen another time. Very common in everyday speech for repeating an action, question, or request. Often used with verbs like “fazer” (do), “dizer” (say), “tentar” (try), “vir” (come). Similar to “de novo”; in many contexts they’re interchangeable.
target_language_example: Pode repetir outra vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat it again, please?

meaning: “another world” (a different place/reality; sometimes figuratively “out of this world”).
additional_notes: Used literally to mean a different world/planet, and very commonly in a figurative sense to say something feels totally different from what you’re used to (e.g., a new city, a new job, a different lifestyle). In some contexts it can praise something as extraordinary (“é de outro mundo”).
target_language_example: Depois que me mudei, minha vida virou outro mundo.
native_language_example: After I moved, my life became a whole different world.

meaning: to have heard of; to hear people talk about (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you know about something because you’ve heard people mention it, not necessarily because you’ve experienced it yourself. Common patterns: "Já ouvi falar de..." (I’ve heard of...), "Nunca ouvi falar de..." (I’ve never heard of...), "Você já ouviu falar em...?" (Have you ever heard of...?). Often followed by "de" or "em" + noun/topic.
target_language_example: Já ouvi falar desse restaurante, mas nunca fui lá.
native_language_example: I’ve heard of that restaurant, but I’ve never been there.

additional_notes: Common written abbreviation for "por exemplo" in Portuguese. Used in texts, emails, and notes to introduce an example; in speech you normally say "por exemplo" (or "por ex."). Often written in parentheses: "(p. ex., ...)".
target_language_example: Você pode trazer uma bebida (p. ex., água ou suco).
native_language_example: You can bring a drink (e.g., water or juice).

additional_notes: Used for paying household or personal bills (rent, electricity, phone, etc.). In Portuguese, you can also say "pagar as contas" to mean settling what you owe in general. Often used with time expressions like "no fim do mês" (at the end of the month).
target_language_example: Preciso pagar as contas até sexta-feira.
native_language_example: I need to pay the bills by Friday.

additional_notes: A Christian religious phrase referring to the prayer that begins with “Pai nosso que estais no céu…”. Often said or written with capitals as the title of the prayer (“Pai-Nosso” is also common). In running text, “pai nosso” can also literally mean “our father,” but most commonly it refers to the prayer.
target_language_example: Vamos rezar o Pai Nosso antes de dormir.
native_language_example: Let’s say the Our Father before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used for devices that capture sunlight to produce electricity or heat water. Plural: "painéis solares".
target_language_example: Vamos instalar um painel solar no telhado.
native_language_example: We’re going to install a solar panel on the roof.

meaning: "word for word"; literally, exactly as written/said.
additional_notes: Used when translating or repeating something very literally (often implying a strict, exact translation). Similar to English "word for word" and can also be used to emphasize that something was quoted exactly.
target_language_example: Consegue traduzir este texto palavra por palavra?
native_language_example: Can you translate this text word for word?

additional_notes: Common everyday noun phrase. Often used with verbs like "comprar" (to buy) and "precisar de" (to need). In Brazil, you may also see "papel higiênico" shortened to "papel" in context (e.g., in a bathroom), but "papel" alone can also mean paper in general, so the full phrase is clearer.
target_language_example: Você sabe onde tem papel higiênico?
native_language_example: Do you know where there is toilet paper?

additional_notes: Informal. Used to dismiss something as not credible or not serious (like “that’s nonsense” / “that’s BS”). Can describe an excuse, rumor, sales pitch, or conversation that goes nowhere. Often used with verbs like "ser" ("Isso é papo furado") or "conversa" as a synonym ("conversa fiada").
target_language_example: Não acredita nele, isso é papo furado.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him, that’s nonsense.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward a lower position (the opposite of “para cima”). Common in instructions and everyday speech: “olhe para baixo” (look down), “desça para baixo” (go down). It can also be used more figuratively to mean feeling low/sad in some contexts (“estar para baixo”).
target_language_example: Olha para baixo, por favor.
native_language_example: Look down, please.

additional_notes: Strong, vulgar slang used to intensify adjectives/adverbs, similar to “as hell” but cruder. Common in European Portuguese; in Brazil you may hear it too, but it’s still very offensive. Typically used in casual speech among close friends; avoid in polite conversation, at work, or with strangers. Often follows an adjective/adverb: "fixe para caralho" (really cool), "longe para caralho" (really far).
target_language_example: Estou cansado para caralho.
native_language_example: I’m tired as hell / really damn tired.

additional_notes: Informal intensifier used to emphasize degree or quantity, similar to "a ton" or "so much" in English. It often comes after the word it modifies (e.g., "gosto para caramba"). Can sound a bit strong; a milder alternative is "pra caramba" (same meaning) or "muito" (neutral).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de pizza para caramba!
native_language_example: I like pizza a lot!

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement to indicate direction/destination: **ir/voltar para casa** = “go/come back home.” For location (being at home), Portuguese usually uses **em casa** (“at home”), not *para casa*. It can also mean “to take home/for home” depending on context (e.g., something you’ll do at home).
target_language_example: Vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction upward (e.g., going upstairs, looking up). It can also mean “on/over” in the sense of being placed on top of something (“em cima de” is often used similarly and is very common). In some contexts it can imply an increase (“de… para cima” = “and up,” “from… upward”).
target_language_example: Olha para cima! O elevador vai para cima agora.
native_language_example: Look up! The elevator is going up now.

additional_notes: Used for position/movement upward or above something: "O livro está para cima da mesa" (common in some regions, though "em cima" is often more natural). Also used with numbers to mean "more than" or "over": "para cima de 100" = over 100. Can also introduce an approximate higher estimate: "para cima de duas horas" = more than/over about two hours.
target_language_example: O conserto vai custar para cima de 200 euros.
native_language_example: The repair is going to cost over 200 euros.

meaning: toward; toward (someone) / in relation to (someone), usually about an attitude, feeling, or duty.
additional_notes: Used with people or groups to express an attitude, feeling, responsibility, or behavior directed at them (often in more formal Portuguese). Common with nouns like "respeito" (respect), "obrigação" (obligation), "dever" (duty), "responsabilidade" (responsibility), "atitude" (attitude), or "comportamento" (behavior). Similar idea to "em relação a"; not the same as "para" alone (destination/purpose) or "com" alone (with).
target_language_example: Ele tem uma grande responsabilidade para com a família.
native_language_example: He has a great responsibility toward his family.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something goes past a limit or expectation (“beyond”), or that there is something extra in addition to what was already mentioned (“besides/plus”). Common in phrases like “para lá de X” = “more than X / beyond X”.
target_language_example: Isto é para lá de caro.
native_language_example: This is beyond expensive (way too expensive).

additional_notes: Used (1) to express purpose: "para que" + verb, very often followed by the subjunctive (especially when there are two different subjects): "Feche a porta para que o gato não saia." (2) as a question meaning "for what purpose?" / "why?": "Para que isso?" In Brazil you may also hear "pra que" (more informal pronunciation/spelling).
target_language_example: Estou estudando para que eu possa passar no exame.
native_language_example: I’m studying so that I can pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will last indefinitely, often in emotional or formal contexts (love, promises, memories). Common collocations include “para sempre” after verbs like “amar” (to love) or “lembrar” (to remember).
target_language_example: Vou te amar para sempre.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction backward: "voltar para trás" (to go back), "dar um passo para trás" (to take a step back). It can also mean leaving something behind or being behind in progress: "ficar para trás" (to fall behind / be left behind). Often contrasts with "para a frente" (forward).
target_language_example: Dá um passo para trás, por favor.
native_language_example: Take a step back, please.

additional_notes: Literally “to vary/for varying,” but commonly used as a set phrase. It can be sincere (“for a change”) or sarcastic/ironic to mean “as usual” when something predictable happens again. Often used as a short comment: “Para variar…”.
target_language_example: Ele chegou atrasado, para variar.
native_language_example: He arrived late, as usual (surprise, surprise).

additional_notes: Used especially in Brazil for the front glass of a car. In European Portuguese you’ll often see “pára-brisas” (usually in the plural) for the same thing. Common related phrase: “limpador de para-brisa” = windshield wiper.
target_language_example: O para-brisa do meu carro quebrou.
native_language_example: My car’s windshield broke.

additional_notes: A place with rides and attractions (roller coasters, ferris wheel, games). Also commonly said as “parque de diversão” (singular) in some regions. Typically used with verbs like “ir a(o)”, “visitar”, and “ficar em”.
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos ao parque de diversões com as crianças.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we’re going to the amusement park with the kids.

additional_notes: A protected natural area managed by the government, often with rules about conservation, camping, wildlife, and access. Common on signs and in travel contexts (e.g., “entrada do parque nacional”, “trilhas do parque nacional”).
target_language_example: Vamos visitar o parque nacional no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit the national park this weekend.

meaning: a pastime; something you do to pass the time.
additional_notes: Often written as one word in Portuguese: "passatempo" (noun). "Passar o tempo" means "to pass the time" (verb phrase). You can use it for hobbies or any activity done for fun or to kill time (games, reading, etc.).
target_language_example: Ler é um ótimo passatempo para passar o tempo.
native_language_example: Reading is a great pastime to pass the time.

meaning: to trick someone; to cheat someone.
additional_notes: Common idiom (especially in Brazil) meaning to deceive someone for personal advantage (e.g., in business, a deal, or a game). Often used as "passar a perna em alguém" (to trick someone).
target_language_example: Ele tentou me passar a perna na negociação.
native_language_example: He tried to trick me in the negotiation.

meaning: to be well / to be doing well; (as a goodbye) “take care.”
additional_notes: Often used in Brazil. Literally “to pass well,” but it means “to be well” (how someone is doing) or is used as a closing in messages, similar to “take care” / “be well.” Common in more neutral-to-formal contexts (emails, messages, phone calls).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela ajuda. Até logo e passe bem!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help. See you soon, and take care!

meaning: to cross the line; to go too far.
additional_notes: Used when someone’s behavior, words, or actions become unacceptable or excessive (morally, socially, or emotionally). Often said as a criticism or warning. Common variations: “passar do limite” (singular) and “isso já passou dos limites” (“this has gone too far”).
target_language_example: Você passou dos limites com o que disse ontem.
native_language_example: You crossed the line with what you said yesterday.

meaning: to feel sick; to be unwell (often suddenly).
additional_notes: Common with physical symptoms like nausea, dizziness, faintness, or low blood pressure. Often used in the past: "Passei mal" (I felt sick). You can specify the moment: "passar mal no ônibus" (feel sick on the bus). Related: "passar bem" = to be doing well.
target_language_example: Passei mal depois do almoço e tive que ir embora.
native_language_example: I felt sick after lunch and had to leave.

meaning: to pass by; to go through; to stop by (briefly).
additional_notes: Often used with a place or person: "passar por aqui/aí/lá" = to pass by / stop by. It can also mean "to go through" an experience ("passar por dificuldades" = to go through difficulties). In some contexts it can mean "to be mistaken for" or "to pretend to be" ("passar por médico" = to pass as a doctor).
target_language_example: Vou passar por aí amanhã à tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll stop by there tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something one stage at a time, often in instructions or explanations. You’ll also see it as a noun meaning a guide/tutorial: "um passo a passo" = "a step-by-step guide."
target_language_example: Vou te explicar passo a passo como preencher o formulário.
native_language_example: I’ll explain to you step by step how to fill out the form.

additional_notes: Common everyday item. Literally “paste of tooth/teeth,” and it’s the standard term in Brazil and Portugal. You may also hear the more technical term “creme dental,” but “pasta de dente” is the most common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Esqueci de comprar pasta de dente.
native_language_example: I forgot to buy toothpaste.

meaning: a cardinal sin; a very serious sin or wrongdoing.
additional_notes: Common in religious contexts (especially Catholicism) to refer to one of the seven deadly sins (e.g., pride, greed, lust). In everyday speech it can be used more loosely/hyperbolically to mean a “big mistake” or “major no-no.” Plural: "pecados capitais."
target_language_example: Para ele, mentir é um pecado capital.
native_language_example: For him, lying is a cardinal sin.

additional_notes: Used when something starts burning (often accidentally): "A casa pegou fogo" = "The house caught fire." It can also be used figuratively to mean a situation “heated up” or got intense: "A discussão pegou fogo" = "The argument heated up." In Brazil, "pegar" is very common for “to catch/get,” which helps make the meaning feel natural.
target_language_example: Cuidado: essa panela pode pegar fogo se você deixar o óleo esquentar demais.
native_language_example: Careful: that pan can catch fire if you let the oil get too hot.

meaning: to take it easy; to go easy (on someone/something).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese. Used as advice or a request to relax, slow down, not overdo something, or not be too strict/harsh. Often appears as an imperative: “Pega leve!” You can also add “com” to specify the target: “Pega leve comigo” (go easy on me) / “pegar leve na bebida” (take it easy on the drinking).
target_language_example: Pega leve, você está trabalhando demais.
native_language_example: Take it easy—you’re working too much.

additional_notes: A common name for the small orange aquarium fish. Literally “golden fish” (peixe = fish, dourado = golden). Often used with an article: “um peixe-dourado” (a goldfish), “o peixe-dourado” (the goldfish). Plural: “peixes-dourados”.
target_language_example: Minha irmã tem um peixe-dourado no aquário.
native_language_example: My sister has a goldfish in the aquarium.

additional_notes: A common, everyday noun for the small orange/gold aquarium fish. Diminutive: "peixinho" (little fish) + "dourado" (golden). You may also see "peixe dourado" without the diminutive.
target_language_example: Meu irmão ganhou um peixinho dourado e colocou no aquário.
native_language_example: My brother got a goldfish and put it in the aquarium.

meaning: "by the hands of" / "by" (done by someone; often who made/created it).
additional_notes: Used to say that something was done, made, written, or delivered by a particular person (the agent). Common in more formal or literary contexts, especially with art or authorship: "uma obra pelas mãos de...". It can also imply direct involvement or responsibility (sometimes even blame) depending on context.
target_language_example: O livro foi escrito pelas mãos de uma autora angolana.
native_language_example: The book was written by an Angolan author.

meaning: “For the love of God” / “Please!” (an emphatic plea).
additional_notes: Used to beg, insist, or show frustration/exasperation. Common in everyday speech; intensity depends on tone. Also appears as a stronger request like “Come on!” or “Give me a break!” In writing you may see it with punctuation for emphasis: “Pelo amor de Deus!” Literally “for the love of God.”
target_language_example: Pelo amor de Deus, fala mais devagar!
native_language_example: For the love of God, speak more slowly!

meaning: “for the love of God!” / “please!” (an emphatic plea).
additional_notes: Used to beg, urge, or show strong frustration or disbelief. Common in speech and texting; intensity depends on tone and context. Often written without accents ("deus"), but the standard is "Deus" (God). It can sound dramatic or rude if said sharply.
target_language_example: Pelo amor de Deus, fala mais baixo!
native_language_example: For the love of God, speak more quietly!

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something to benefit someone/something, or to justify an action (often a request) as being in someone’s best interest. It’s common in both spoken and written Portuguese. You can also hear it with articles/pronouns: “pelo bem do país” (for the good of the country), “pelo bem dela” (for her sake).
target_language_example: Pelo bem de todos, vamos manter a calma.
native_language_example: For everyone’s sake, let’s stay calm.

additional_notes: Used to contradict what was just said or to emphasize the opposite idea. Very common in conversation and writing. Often appears after a negative statement (e.g., “Não..., pelo contrário, ...”).
target_language_example: Eu não estou cansado; pelo contrário, estou cheio de energia.
native_language_example: I’m not tired; on the contrary, I’m full of energy.

additional_notes: Used to express a minimum quantity/number/time ("at least 3", "at least today"), or to soften a statement by focusing on a minimum positive point ("at least it’s not raining"). Very common in everyday speech. Often followed by a number or amount ("pelo menos dois"), or used as a sentence starter ("Pelo menos..." = "At least...").
target_language_example: Preciso de pelo menos três dias para terminar.
native_language_example: I need at least three days to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears to be true based on what you’ve seen/heard, often when you didn’t know it before. Common in European Portuguese and usually placed at the start (or mid-sentence): "Pelos vistos, ...".
target_language_example: Pelos vistos, o João já chegou.
native_language_example: Apparently, João has already arrived.

meaning: to think about; to consider; to plan to (do something).
additional_notes: Common verb + preposition combo. Use "pensar em" + noun/pronoun/infinitive: "pensar em você" (think about you), "pensar nisso" (think about that), "pensar em viajar" (think about traveling / plan to travel). For opinions, Portuguese often uses "achar" (e.g., "O que você acha?") rather than "pensar em". In the past, "pensei em" can mean "I considered" or "I was thinking of".
target_language_example: Estou pensando em viajar no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I'm thinking about traveling this weekend.

additional_notes: Common in Portugal; in Brazil people usually say "café da manhã". Literally "small lunch" (pequeno + almoço), but it simply means the morning meal. Often used with the verbs "tomar" or "comer": "tomar o pequeno-almoço" / "comer o pequeno-almoço".
target_language_example: Costumo tomar o pequeno-almoço às sete da manhã.
native_language_example: I usually have breakfast at seven in the morning.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese to ask someone to pause briefly (e.g., you need time to think, check something, or stop the conversation for a moment). It’s an informal contraction of “espera aí” (“wait there”). Often said as “peraí” in fast speech. Can also be used to interrupt or correct: “Pera aí! Não é bem assim.”
target_language_example: Pera aí, vou pegar meu celular.
native_language_example: Hold on a second, I’m going to get my phone.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not worth doing because it won’t bring a good result. You can use it with verbs like "ser" (É uma perda de tempo.) or "achar" (Acho que é perda de tempo.). Often comes with "uma" (uma perda de tempo), but it can also appear without an article in general statements.
target_language_example: Discutir com ele é uma perda de tempo.
native_language_example: Arguing with him is a waste of time.

meaning: to lose your temper; to panic.
additional_notes: Used when someone stops thinking calmly and reacts emotionally (anger, stress, or fear). In the anger sense, it’s like “to lose it.” Often used with "com" (with) to say who you lost your temper with: "perder a cabeça com alguém".
target_language_example: Ele perdeu a cabeça e começou a gritar comigo.
native_language_example: He lost his temper and started yelling at me.

meaning: to lose sight of; to lose track of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used when you can no longer see something/someone, or when you stop knowing where they are (physically or figuratively). Often appears with pronoun objects: “perdi-o de vista” (I lost sight of him), “perdi-a de vista” (…of her).
target_language_example: Eu me distraí por um segundo e perdi a criança de vista.
native_language_example: I got distracted for a second and lost sight of the child.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "não quero" (I don’t want to), "parar de" (stop), or "ficar" (to end up): "Não quero perder tempo" / "Pare de perder tempo". It can also mean spending time on something that won’t bring results (e.g., waiting, doing something unnecessary).
target_language_example: Não quero perder tempo esperando; vamos embora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time waiting; let’s go.

additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity or approximate time/quantity. It is usually followed by a noun, pronoun, or place name (e.g., perto de casa, perto de mim). Common with verbs like ficar/morar/estar (ficar perto de…, morar perto de…).
target_language_example: O hotel fica perto da estação.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the station.

additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with paddles and a small ball. Often used with the verb "jogar" (to play): "jogar pingue-pongue". You may also see "tênis de mesa" as a more formal/official term for the same sport.
target_language_example: A gente joga pingue-pongue no clube aos sábados.
native_language_example: We play ping-pong at the club on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: “X é pior que Y” = “X is worse than Y.” In conversation, it can introduce something even more negative: “Pior que…” ≈ “Worse yet / The worst part is…”. Often followed by a clause: “Pior que eu nem sabia.”
target_language_example: Eu estava cansado e, pior que, ainda tinha que trabalhar.
native_language_example: I was tired and, worse yet, I still had to work.

meaning: to mess up; to screw up (often: to let someone down).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used when someone makes a mistake, behaves badly, or disappoints someone. It’s often said directly to the person who did it ("Você pisou na bola") or about them ("Ele pisou na bola").
target_language_example: Você pisou na bola comigo ontem.
native_language_example: You really let me down yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when the first option (plano A) doesn’t work or might not work. Very common in everyday speech, including work and travel contexts. Often appears with verbs like “ter” (to have) or “precisar de” (to need): “Temos um plano B.”
target_language_example: Se chover, a gente tem um plano B.
native_language_example: If it rains, we have a plan B.

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese to strongly confirm something or show confidence. It can answer a yes/no question (“Pode apostar!” = “Absolutely!”) or reassure someone (“Pode apostar que eu vou.” = “You can bet I’m going.”). Often followed by “que” + a clause. Slightly informal in tone.
target_language_example: —Você vem amanhã? —Pode apostar!
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —You bet!

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese as an informal way to agree, confirm, or reassure someone (similar to “yeah, definitely” / “you got it”). Often used as a short stand-alone reply. Literally it’s like “you can believe (it)”, but the natural meaning is closer to strong agreement/confirmation.
target_language_example: —Você vem amanhã? —Pode crer!
native_language_example: —Are you coming tomorrow? —For sure!

additional_notes: Very common in Brazil, especially in customer service and polite conversation. Often said when you call someone (like a waiter or a clerk) to show they’re ready to help: similar to “Yes?” or “Sure, go ahead.” It can also be used to agree politely to a request. Despite containing “não” (“no”), it usually does not mean “no.”
target_language_example: —Com licença! —Pois não, em que posso ajudar?
native_language_example: —Excuse me! —Yes? How can I help?

additional_notes: Very common conversational filler. Often reacts to something the other person said, meaning “that’s true,” “I know,” or “it is what it is,” depending on tone. Can also be used to show mild disappointment or acceptance of an unfortunate situation. Usually informal and spoken.
target_language_example: —O ônibus já saiu. —Pois é, vamos ter que esperar o próximo.
native_language_example: —The bus already left. —Yeah… we’ll have to wait for the next one.

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or perspective about something. Very common with verbs like "ter" (to have), "ver" (to see), and phrases like "do meu/seu ponto de vista" (from my/your point of view).
target_language_example: Do meu ponto de vista, essa é a melhor opção.
native_language_example: From my point of view, that’s the best option.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you wait for and catch a city bus. Common in Brazil; in Portugal you’ll also hear "paragem de autocarro". Often used with the verb "esperar" (to wait) or "pegar" (to take/catch) in Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: O ponto de ônibus fica na esquina, em frente ao mercado.
native_language_example: The bus stop is on the corner, in front of the market.

meaning: a period/full stop; (figuratively) the end of something.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the punctuation mark “.” at the end of a sentence. It can also be used figuratively to mean “that’s final” or “the end,” often to emphasize that a discussion or situation is finished.
target_language_example: Coloque um ponto final no fim da frase.
native_language_example: Put a period at the end of the sentence.

meaning: a pop-up (usually a small window/message on a screen; sometimes a temporary store/event).
additional_notes: Common loanword in Portuguese, especially in tech: "janela pop-up" (pop-up window) and "anúncio pop-up" (pop-up ad). In retail/events, you may also hear "loja pop-up" for a temporary shop. Often written with a hyphen and pronounced roughly like English.
target_language_example: Cuidado ao clicar nesses links: pode abrir um pop-up com propaganda.
native_language_example: Be careful when clicking those links: it might open a pop-up with ads.

meaning: by chance; accidentally; (in questions) “by any chance…?”
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian and European Portuguese. Often used to talk about coincidence or something not planned: “Encontrei-o por acaso” (I ran into him by chance). Very frequently used in polite questions to soften a request or check availability: “Você por acaso tem…?” ≈ “Do you happen to have…?” It can also appear with “ser” to mean “to be a coincidence”: “Foi por acaso?” (Was it by chance?).
target_language_example: Por acaso, você tem um carregador de celular?
native_language_example: Do you happen to have a phone charger?

additional_notes: Used to say something is temporary or limited to the present situation. Common in phrases like “isso é tudo por agora” (that’s all for now) or to soften decisions: “vamos deixar assim por agora” (let’s leave it like this for now).
target_language_example: Vamos deixar isso por agora e falar amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s leave that for now and talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify what you’re saying, often when using a metaphor, an unusual expression, or when you want to make a statement sound less absolute. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese. Often set off by commas: "..., por assim dizer,".
target_language_example: Ele é o braço direito do chefe, por assim dizer.
native_language_example: He’s the boss’s right-hand man, so to speak.

meaning: 'around there/thereabouts'; also 'and so on' or 'just hanging around'.
additional_notes: Common, very flexible expression. (1) Place: means 'around there/over there/in that general area' (often vague). (2) Continuation/list: after examples, it means 'and so on/and stuff like that' (e.g., "comida, bebida e por aí"). (3) Status/whereabouts: with verbs like "andar/estar/ficar", it means 'to be around/to be out and about' ("Ele anda por aí" = he's around/out there).
target_language_example: Estou por aí depois do trabalho; se quiser, me liga.
native_language_example: I’ll be around after work; if you want, call me.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason/cause and is followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive (often with a verb in the infinitive): "por causa do trânsito" (because of traffic), "por causa dele" (because of him), "por causa de chover" (because it’s raining). Very common in everyday speech. Variants: "por causa do/da/dos/das" (with definite articles) and informal "por causa que" (because), which many speakers use but is less formal.
target_language_example: Cheguei atrasado por causa do trânsito.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used after a number to express a percentage. In Portuguese it literally means “per hundred” (por = per/for, cento = hundred). In writing you’ll also see the symbol “%”.
target_language_example: A taxa de desconto é de 20 por cento.
native_language_example: The discount rate is 20 percent.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason/cause for something (similar to "por causa de"). It’s followed by a noun or noun phrase: "por conta do trânsito" (because of traffic), "por conta da chuva" (due to the rain). Very common in speech; can also imply something happens as a consequence of a situation.
target_language_example: Cheguei atrasado por conta do trânsito.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without help, without being told, or without depending on others. Common with verbs like fazer (to do), ir (to go), aprender (to learn), and trabalhar (to work). Similar idea to “sozinho(a)”, but “por conta própria” emphasizes independence/initiative (sometimes also “on your own initiative”).
target_language_example: Aprendi português por conta própria.
native_language_example: I learned Portuguese on my own.

additional_notes: Literal sense: refers to the interior of something (often with verbs like "estar", "ficar", "ver": "por dentro" = on the inside). Figurative sense: "estar por dentro (de algo)" means to be up to date / in the know about a topic or situation. Often used with "de": "Você está por dentro do assunto?"
target_language_example: Você está por dentro das novidades do trabalho?
native_language_example: Are you up to date on the news at work?

meaning: for now; for the time being.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true only temporarily, and may change later. Common in everyday conversation to set a temporary plan or situation. Can also appear alone as a short answer meaning “for now.”
target_language_example: Por enquanto, vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: For now, I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce one or more examples of what you just mentioned. Often appears mid-sentence or after a pause. Common in both speaking and writing; can be followed by a comma in writing.
target_language_example: Gosto de frutas, por exemplo, maçã e banana.
native_language_example: I like fruit, for example, apples and bananas.

additional_notes: Most commonly used to make a request more polite (before or after what you’re asking for). It can also be used alone to mean “please?” (as in “come on” / “I’m asking you”), especially in spoken Portuguese. In Brazil you may also hear it as a reply to “obrigado/obrigada” meaning “you’re welcome,” though “de nada” is also very common.
target_language_example: Pode me ajudar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

meaning: “pretty please”; a very polite/cute way to say “please.”
additional_notes: Diminutive of “por favor” (please). Used to soften a request, sound extra polite, pleading, or affectionate. Common in casual speech with friends/family; can sound childish or overly cute in formal/professional situations.
target_language_example: Você pode fechar a janela, por favorzinho?
native_language_example: Could you close the window, pretty please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the last point in a sequence (like “finally,” “lastly,”). It can also mean “in the end/ultimately” when talking about a final outcome. Common in writing and speech; slightly more formal than “finalmente” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Por fim, vamos assinar o contrato.
native_language_example: Finally, we’re going to sign the contract.

meaning: from the outside; outwardly; not included (separately).
additional_notes: Used for (1) physical position/appearance: "por fora" = on the outside / externally; (2) how someone seems vs. how they feel: "por fora" = outwardly; (3) extra items not included in a price or package, often with money: "por fora" = separately / on top (not included). In (3) it can imply something unofficial depending on context.
target_language_example: O almoço é R$ 25, e a bebida é por fora.
native_language_example: Lunch is R$25, and the drink is separate (not included).

additional_notes: A polite, slightly formal way to say “please,” common in customer service and requests. Often placed before or after the request: “Por gentileza, ...” / “..., por gentileza.” Similar in tone to “por favor,” but a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Por gentileza, pode me dizer onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Please, can you tell me where the bathroom is?

meaning: for now; for the time being.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true/valid only temporarily, and it may change later. Common in everyday speech and writing. It can also mean “per hour” in some contexts (especially with prices or rates), but in that case “por hora” usually comes right after a number (e.g., “20 euros por hora”).
target_language_example: Por hora, vamos ficar em casa e ver o que acontece.
native_language_example: For now, we’re going to stay at home and see what happens.

additional_notes: Used to link a reason to a result or conclusion. Often comes after a statement of the reason (or at the start of the next sentence) and can be followed by a comma: "…, por isso, …". Very common in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Estou cansado, por isso vou para casa.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so/that’s why I’m going home.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something just mentioned, giving a reason or explanation. Often appears as "Por isto," at the start of a sentence meaning "For this reason". In everyday Portuguese, it’s very common to use the more contracted form "por isso" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Por isto, decidi ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Because of this, I decided to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to express the method or channel used to do something (often in formal or written contexts). Common with nouns like "internet", "e-mail", "telefone", "aplicativo". Similar in meaning to "através de" (through/via), but "por meio de" is usually the safer choice when you mean "by using" (method).
target_language_example: Conseguimos resolver o problema por meio de uma atualização do sistema.
native_language_example: We managed to solve the problem by means of a system update.

additional_notes: Common reply after someone says "obrigado/obrigada". Often implies “it was nothing” or “don’t mention it.” You may also hear the variant "não foi nada" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: —Obrigado pela ajuda! —Por nada!
native_language_example: —Thanks for the help! —No problem!

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only temporarily, and may change later. Very common in conversation and writing. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Por ora, tudo bem." / "Tudo bem, por ora."
target_language_example: Por ora, vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: For now, I’m going to stay at home.

meaning: on the other hand; however (introducing a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to contrast with a previous idea or to present a different perspective. Common in both speech and writing. Often pairs with an earlier point (sometimes introduced with "por um lado" = "on the one hand").
target_language_example: Gosto de morar no centro; por outro lado, é muito barulhento.
native_language_example: I like living downtown; on the other hand, it’s very noisy.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is close or in the area (not far away), often with verbs like estar/ficar/haver: "Estou por perto" (I’m nearby), "Tem um banco por perto?" (Is there a bank nearby?). It’s also common in the sense of "around" meaning not gone: "Ele ainda está por perto" (He’s still around).
target_language_example: Tem algum supermercado por perto?
native_language_example: Is there a supermarket nearby?

additional_notes: Used to say something nearly happened but didn’t, or that you succeeded/fell short by a very small amount. Often followed by a verb phrase: "Por pouco eu..." (I almost...). Also common with "foi por pouco" = "it was a close call."
target_language_example: Por pouco eu perdi o ônibus.
native_language_example: I almost missed the bus.

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions (direct or indirect): "Por que...?" = "Why...?" It’s written as two words when "por" (for) + "que" (what/which) function separately. Common spelling contrast: "porque" (one word) usually means "because" in answers; "por quê" is often used at the end of a question (with stress); "porquê" (one word, with accent) is the noun "the reason".
target_language_example: Por que você não veio ontem?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you come yesterday?

additional_notes: Used in questions to express irritation, disbelief, or strong curiosity. "Diabos" literally means "devils," but in this expression it’s just an intensifier. Common in spoken Portuguese; can sound rude depending on tone and situation—use with friends, not in formal settings. Often followed by a verb: "Por que diabos você fez isso?"
target_language_example: Por que diabos você não me avisou antes?
native_language_example: Why on earth didn’t you tell me earlier?

meaning: 'why not?' (suggesting an idea or agreeing to try something).
additional_notes: Used as a casual, positive response to a suggestion (“Sure, why not?”) or to propose something (“Why not do X?”). In questions, it’s written with a space: “por que”.
target_language_example: Vamos ao cinema hoje? — Por que não?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the movies today? — Why not?

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or speculation about a reason, often in a rhetorical way. It’s common in conversation when you’re thinking out loud: "Por que será que..." can also be followed by a clause ("I wonder why it is that..."). The verb "será" is the future tense of "ser" (to be), but here it usually implies uncertainty (“could it be?”) rather than a real future meaning.
target_language_example: Ela não respondeu às mensagens... por que será?
native_language_example: She didn’t reply to the messages... I wonder why.

meaning: “why?” (used at the end of a question).
additional_notes: Used as an interrogative meaning “why,” typically placed at the end of a sentence (often after a pause): “... por quê?”. It’s written with an accent (quê) because it’s stressed at the end. Contrast: “por que” is usually used at the beginning or in the middle of a question (“Por que você fez isso?”).
target_language_example: Você fez isso por quê?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

meaning: by the way; actually (as it happens).
additional_notes: Used to add extra information, often like English “by the way.” It can also introduce a confirming detail (“actually / as it happens”), especially in conversation. Common placement is at the start or middle of a sentence: “Por sinal, …” / “…, por sinal.”
target_language_example: Por sinal, você viu minhas chaves?
native_language_example: By the way, have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Used to say something good happened by chance or thanks to luck. It’s similar to (and often interchangeable with) “felizmente”. You may also hear “por sorte” in European Portuguese; in Brazil, “por sorte” exists but “por sorte/por sorte que” and “ainda bem” are often more common depending on the context.
target_language_example: Por sorte, chegámos a tempo.
native_language_example: Luckily, we arrived on time.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to say something is in many places or scattered. Often appears as "por todo lado" or "por todo lado(s)" (you may also hear "por toda parte"). Used with verbs like "ter", "estar", "haver" and "ver": "Tem gente por todo lado" (There are people everywhere).
target_language_example: Tem gente por todo lado hoje.
native_language_example: There are people everywhere today.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position (behind something/someone) or movement to the back area. Common with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay) and ir/passar (to go/pass): "por trás da casa" (behind the house), "por trás de mim" (behind me). Also used figuratively to mean "behind" in the sense of "responsible for" or "the reason for": "por trás do projeto" (behind the project). Often appears in the fixed phrase "por trás de" (behind/of).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica por trás da cozinha.
native_language_example: The bathroom is behind the kitchen.

meaning: each time; at a time (per turn).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens one occurrence at a time or per person/turn. Common in instructions and scheduling (e.g., one customer at a time). Often appears as “uma vez por vez” (one at a time) or “um(a) … por vez” (one … at a time).
target_language_example: Por favor, entre um de cada vez — só uma pessoa por vez.
native_language_example: Please come in one at a time — only one person at a time.

additional_notes: A noun for the animal “porcupine.” It’s a compound word: porco (“pig”) + espinho (“thorn/spine”), referring to its quills. Usually used with an article (o/a) and the plural is porcos-espinhos.
target_language_example: Vi um porco-espinho no zoológico.
native_language_example: I saw a porcupine at the zoo.

meaning: a vulgar way to say “damn/____ing” (to show anger or annoyance).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive/vulgar. Used before a noun to insult it or emphasize frustration: “essa porra de ___” = “this damn ____.” Common in Brazilian Portuguese; avoid in polite conversation, with strangers, at work, or in formal settings.
target_language_example: Não aguento mais essa porra de trânsito.
native_language_example: I can’t stand this damn traffic anymore.

additional_notes: Very informal and offensive intensifier meaning “nothing at all.” Common in Brazilian Portuguese in complaints or strong emphasis. Avoid in polite situations; use “nada” or “nada mesmo” for a neutral option.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi porra nenhuma do que ele falou.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a damn thing he said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the door/entrance at the back of a building or house. Often appears with prepositions like "pela/na porta dos fundos" (through/at the back door). It’s also used figuratively to mean doing something “through the back door,” i.e., by an indirect or unofficial way, though the literal meaning is most common for beginners.
target_language_example: A entrega é pela porta dos fundos.
native_language_example: The delivery is through the back door.

additional_notes: Refers to the storage compartment on the passenger side of a car’s dashboard. Literally “glove-holder.” In Brazil, plural is common: “o porta-luvas”; plural: “os porta-luvas.”
target_language_example: Os documentos do carro estão no porta-luvas.
native_language_example: The car documents are in the glove compartment.

additional_notes: Used for the trunk/boot of a car (the storage compartment, usually in the back). In Brazil, the plural is usually "porta-malas" as well; you may also see "porta-mala". In European Portuguese, "bagageira" is more common.
target_language_example: Coloque as malas no porta-malas, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the suitcases in the trunk, please.

additional_notes: Used in Brazil for a place where you buy fuel for a car (and often find services like a convenience store, car wash, air for tires). In Portugal, you’ll also hear "bomba de gasolina" or "posto de combustível". You can say "parar no posto" (to stop at the gas station) and "abastecer" (to fill up).
target_language_example: Vou parar no posto de gasolina para abastecer.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop at the gas station to fill up.

additional_notes: Used to describe something happening slowly, step by step, over time. Common in everyday speech and writing. Often interchangeable with “aos poucos” (“gradually”).
target_language_example: Pouco a pouco, estou aprendendo português.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar Brazilian Portuguese intensifier (literally refers to male genitalia). Used after adjectives/adverbs to mean “very/really,” or after verbs to mean “a lot.” Not appropriate in polite company, with strangers, at work, or in formal situations. Milder alternatives: "pra caramba", "pra cacete", "muito".
target_language_example: Eu gosto pra caralho dessa música.
native_language_example: I really like this song (a lot).

additional_notes: Very common informal intensifier in Brazilian Portuguese. Used after adjectives/adverbs ("bom pra caramba" = "really good") or after a verb phrase to mean “a lot” ("trabalhei pra caramba" = "I worked a lot"). "Pra" is a casual form of "para". Mild slang; in more formal situations you might use "muito" or "pra valer" instead.
target_language_example: Esse filme é bom pra caramba!
native_language_example: This movie is really good!

additional_notes: Informal contraction of “para lá de”. Used to intensify an adjective or judgment, meaning “extremely/very” or “beyond what’s normal.” It often appears as “pra lá de + adjective” (e.g., pra lá de difícil = extremely difficult).
target_language_example: Esse trabalho é pra lá de complicado.
native_language_example: This work is way beyond complicated / extremely complicated.

meaning: for real; seriously; for good (not just as a joke or practice).
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of "para valer". Used to emphasize that something is genuine, serious, or official—often contrasting with "de brincadeira" (as a joke) or "de mentirinha" (pretend). Common in phrases like "agora é pra valer" (now it’s for real) or "pra valer mesmo" (really, truly).
target_language_example: Agora é pra valer: amanhã eu começo a estudar todos os dias.
native_language_example: Now it’s for real: tomorrow I start studying every day.

additional_notes: Used for intentionally not breathing for a short time (e.g., underwater, during a test, or when waiting anxiously). Also used figuratively in expressions like "ficar/estar com a respiração presa" (“to be holding your breath,” i.e., in suspense).
target_language_example: Prenda a respiração e mergulhe devagar.
native_language_example: Hold your breath and dive in slowly.

additional_notes: A common medical term used in clinics, pharmacies, and health contexts. Often appears with the verb "medir" (to measure) or "verificar" (to check): "medir/verificar a pressão sanguínea". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also commonly say just "pressão" to mean blood pressure when the context is clear.
target_language_example: O médico vai medir a minha pressão sanguínea.
native_language_example: The doctor is going to measure my blood pressure.

meaning: to pay attention; to pay close attention to.
additional_notes: Common way to tell someone to focus or notice something. Usually used with "a/em" + thing/person: "Presta atenção ao professor" (Pay attention to the teacher). In the imperative you’ll often hear: "Presta atenção!" (Portugal also: "Preste atenção!" as a more formal/neutral command).
target_language_example: Presta atenção no que eu estou dizendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I’m saying.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is imminent: "estar/ficar + prestes a + infinitive". It often suggests something will happen soon (but it may or may not actually happen). Agreement: "prestes" is used for plural; for singular you usually see "presto/presta a" (e.g., "Estou prestes a..." / "Ela está presta a...").
target_language_example: Estou prestes a sair.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave.

meaning: black and white; (figuratively) overly simplistic, with no nuances.
additional_notes: Used literally for photos, movies, printing, clothing, etc. It can also be used figuratively to describe thinking that treats things as only one of two extremes (right/wrong, good/bad) without considering gray areas. Often appears with verbs like “ser/estar” (É tudo muito preto e branco.) or as an adjective phrase after a noun (uma foto preto e branco).
target_language_example: Gosto de fotografias em preto e branco, mas a vida não é tão preto e branco assim.
native_language_example: I like black-and-white photos, but life isn’t that black and white.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the forecast for the next hours/days (TV, apps, websites). Often appears with verbs like "ver" (to check) and "dizer" (to say), and with days like "para amanhã" (for tomorrow). You may also hear "a previsão" alone when the context is clear.
