target_language_example: Vou ver a previsão do tempo para amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to check the weather forecast for tomorrow.

meaning: first class (top category; premium travel seating/service).
additional_notes: Used for travel (plane/train/bus) and sometimes for quality ranking (e.g., a product or service of the highest quality). In travel, it often contrasts with "classe econômica" (economy class) or "segunda classe" (second class). Often appears with the verb "viajar" (to travel) or "ir" (to go).
target_language_example: A gente vai viajar de primeira classe.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel first class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your initial opinion or feeling about someone/something when you first meet/see it. Common with the verb "causar" (to make/leave): "causar uma boa/má primeira impressão". Can also be used with "ter": "Tive uma boa primeira impressão".
target_language_example: Ele causou uma boa primeira impressão na entrevista.
native_language_example: He made a good first impression in the interview.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing/experiencing something for the first time. Often appears in phrases like "É a minha primeira vez" (It’s my first time) or "pela primeira vez" (for the first time). Literally "first" + "time/occasion".
target_language_example: É a minha primeira vez em Portugal.
native_language_example: It’s my first time in Portugal.

additional_notes: Used for a woman who is the head of government. Often written without a hyphen in modern usage ("primeira ministra"), but both forms are seen. The masculine form is "primeiro-ministro" (or "primeiro ministro").
target_language_example: A primeira-ministra falou na televisão ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The prime minister spoke on TV last night.

additional_notes: Used when filling out forms or identifying someone. In Portuguese, the “primeiro nome” is your given name (e.g., “Ana”, “João”), not your family name (“sobrenome” / “apelido” in Portugal). You may also see “nome próprio” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Qual é o seu primeiro nome?
native_language_example: What is your first name?

additional_notes: Title for the head of government in many countries. In Portuguese it’s usually written with a hyphen: "primeiro-ministro" (feminine: "primeira-ministra"). Often used with the definite article: "o primeiro-ministro" / "a primeira-ministra".
target_language_example: O primeiro-ministro anunciou novas medidas econômicas.
native_language_example: The prime minister announced new economic measures.

additional_notes: Used to talk about immediate basic medical care given in an emergency before professional help arrives. Common in signs and labels (e.g., a first-aid kit) and in workplace/school contexts (training courses, stations). Often appears with verbs like "prestar" (to give) or "fazer" (to do): "prestar primeiros socorros".
target_language_example: Você sabe prestar primeiros socorros?
native_language_example: Do you know first aid?

additional_notes: A legal term meaning that someone is sentenced to stay in prison for the rest of their life. Common in news and legal contexts. Often used with verbs like “ser condenado a” (to be sentenced to) and “pegar” (to get/receive a sentence), e.g., “condenado a prisão perpétua”.
target_language_example: Ele foi condenado a prisão perpétua.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to life imprisonment.

additional_notes: Used for chemicals in general (e.g., cleaning products, lab chemicals, industrial chemicals). In everyday contexts you’ll often see it on labels or warnings ("Cuidado: produto químico"). Plural: "produtos químicos".
target_language_example: Não misture este produto químico com outros produtos de limpeza.
native_language_example: Don’t mix this chemical product with other cleaning products.

additional_notes: Common everyday term in Brazil and Portugal for lotion/spray that protects your skin from the sun. Also said as "filtro solar". Often used with an SPF number: "protetor solar FPS 30" (FPS = SPF).
target_language_example: Não esqueça de passar protetor solar antes de sair.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to put on sunscreen before you go out.

meaning: jump rope (the game/activity); also used as “jump rope!” (an instruction).
additional_notes: Often seen in Brazilian Portuguese as a noun for the activity/game (sometimes hyphenated as "pula-corda"). Related verb phrase: "pular corda" = "to jump rope". As an instruction, it can be the imperative of "pular": "Pula corda!" = "Jump rope!"
target_language_example: As crianças gostam de brincar de pula corda no recreio.
native_language_example: The kids like to play jump rope at recess.

additional_notes: A common side dish. In Portugal you’ll also see the spelling "puré" (and sometimes "purê" in Brazil). You can order it or talk about it as food: "com puré" = "with mashed potatoes."
target_language_example: Queria frango grelhado com puré de batata, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like grilled chicken with mashed potatoes, please.

additional_notes: Very vulgar exclamation used to show anger, frustration, shock, or annoyance. Not appropriate in polite situations, at work, or around strangers. Often said on its own, or followed by "!". Similar in force to English strong swearing.
target_language_example: Puta merda! Eu esqueci minhas chaves em casa.
native_language_example: Holy shit! I forgot my keys at home.

meaning: a very strong, vulgar exclamation like “for fuck’s sake!” / “holy shit!”
additional_notes: Extremely offensive profanity (common in Brazil). Used to show strong anger, frustration, shock, or to insult someone. Avoid in polite conversation; use only if you understand the tone and context well.
target_language_example: Puta que o pariu, perdi o ônibus!
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake, I missed the bus!

meaning: A very vulgar exclamation: “fuck!” / “holy shit!” (anger, frustration, shock).
additional_notes: Strong profanity in Brazilian Portuguese. Used as an emotional outburst (similar to shouting “fuck!”). Avoid in formal situations or with people you don’t know well. Often abbreviated as “PQP” in texting. Not used literally; it’s just an idiomatic curse.
target_language_example: Puta que pariu, eu perdi o ônibus!
native_language_example: Fuck, I missed the bus!

additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression used to complain that someone or something is bothering you a lot (similar to “a pain in the neck” / “a hassle”). Often used with the verb “ser”: “Ele é um pé no saco.” You can also say “Que pé no saco!” to mean “How annoying!”
target_language_example: Esse barulho é um pé no saco.
native_language_example: This noise is a pain.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to the time of day when the sun goes down or the sunset itself. Often used with verbs like "ver" (to watch) or "assistir a" (to watch), and in phrases like "ao pôr do sol" (at sunset). Note: "pôr" is an irregular verb meaning "to put/set"; in this expression it refers to the sun setting.
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr do sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: A common noun for the time of day when the sun goes down. Often used with verbs like ver (to see/watch) and with time expressions (ao pôr-do-sol = at sunset). Hyphenation is common in Portuguese (pôr do sol / pôr-do-sol).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr-do-sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Used for the board in a classroom that you write on with chalk. In modern contexts you may also hear "quadro" (board) or "lousa" for both chalkboards and whiteboards.
target_language_example: A professora escreveu a data no quadro-negro.
native_language_example: The teacher wrote the date on the blackboard.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of something or to choose between options. Often followed by a noun: "Qual é o endereço?" (What’s the address?). For plural, it changes to "quais são" (e.g., "Quais são as opções?" = What are the options?).
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used when the exact thing doesn’t matter or isn’t specified. It can mean “anything” in offers/requests (e.g., “Do you want anything?”) or “something” in vague statements (“I need something”). In some contexts it can sound dismissive (“whatever/anything”) depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você quer qualquer coisa para comer?
native_language_example: Do you want anything to eat?

additional_notes: Used to say it doesn’t matter which person, or to mean people in general. It agrees with gender/number: "qualquer uma" (any one woman/thing), "quaisquer" (plural, less common in everyday speech). Often used with "pode" to express permission/possibility: "Qualquer um pode..."
target_language_example: Qualquer um pode aprender português com prática.
native_language_example: Anyone can learn Portuguese with practice.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic or shift focus to a particular person/thing. It’s common in both speech and writing. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: “Quanto a mim…” (As for me…), “Quanto ao trabalho…” (Regarding work…). It can also appear as “quanto ao / quanto à / quanto aos / quanto às” to agree with the following noun (ao = a + o; à = a + a).
target_language_example: Quanto ao jantar, podemos pedir comida em vez de cozinhar.
native_language_example: As for dinner, we can order food instead of cooking.

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of an item or service. You can add the thing you’re asking about: “Quanto custa isto?” (this) / “Quanto custa o café?” (the coffee). In Brazil, you’ll also commonly hear “Quanto é?” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Quanto custa este livro?
native_language_example: How much does this book cost?

meaning: "the more" (used in comparisons: the more..., the more...).
additional_notes: Used to build correlative comparisons, often in the pattern “Quanto mais X, (tanto) mais Y” (“The more X, the more Y”). “Tanto” is optional and adds emphasis. You can also use “quanto menos” (“the less”).
target_language_example: Quanto mais eu estudo, mais eu aprendo.
native_language_example: The more I study, the more I learn.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 45 (age, quantity, price, time, etc.). In Brazil, it can also mean “a 45-minute period” (e.g., a half of a soccer match or a class period), depending on context.
target_language_example: Tenho quarenta e cinco anos.
native_language_example: I am forty-five years old.

additional_notes: Day of the week. In Portuguese, weekdays are often said with the definite article (e.g., "na quarta-feira" = "on Wednesday"). You can also use it without the article, especially in schedules and headings ("Quarta-feira: reunião").
target_language_example: Tenho uma consulta na quarta-feira.
native_language_example: I have an appointment on Wednesday.

meaning: “what a thing!” / “what the heck!” (an exclamation of surprise, annoyance, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Often used as an exclamation, sometimes by itself (“Que coisa!”) or followed by an adjective (“Que coisa estranha!”). Depending on tone, it can sound mildly informal and express frustration or disbelief. Literally it’s “what thing,” but in English you usually translate it more naturally as “what a thing” or “what the heck.”
target_language_example: Que coisa! Eu acabei de perder minhas chaves de novo.
native_language_example: What the heck! I just lost my keys again.

meaning: “what the hell…?” / “what on earth…?” (strong surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis to a question, often showing shock, confusion, irritation, or disbelief. It’s informal and can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone and context. Commonly appears in questions like “Que diabos é isso?” (“What the hell is that?”).
target_language_example: Que diabos você está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

additional_notes: Usually used as a short question, often as a reduced form of “O que foi?”. Even though “foi” is past tense (“was/went”), in everyday speech “Que foi?” is commonly used to mean “What is it?” when someone calls you or something seems wrong. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, concerned, or slightly annoyed.
target_language_example: —Maria! —Que foi?
native_language_example: —Maria! —What is it?

additional_notes: Used after "que" to introduce a clause in the imperfect subjunctive, common after expressions of desire, preference, doubt, or evaluation (e.g., "querer que...", "preferir que...", "duvidar que..."). Often corresponds to English "that ... were" / "I wish it were..." in hypothetical or unreal situations.
target_language_example: Eu queria que fosse mais barato.
native_language_example: I wish it were cheaper.

additional_notes: Common way to ask for the current time. Often used as “Que horas são?” or more politely “Que horas são, por favor?”. In Brazil you may also hear “Que horas é?” (less standard) and “Que horas são agora?” (“What time is it now?”).
target_language_example: Com licença, que horas são?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to react to something surprising, wrong, or unacceptable. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese in the form “Que isso?” or “Que isso, cara!” It can express shock, disapproval, or telling someone to stop. Literal word-by-word is “what (is) that?”, but the tone often matters more than the literal meaning.
target_language_example: Que isso? Você não pode falar assim comigo.
native_language_example: What is that? You can’t talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Common in casual speech, often said as an exclamation: “Que nada!” It can reject what someone just said (“No way!”) or downplay credit/praise (“Not at all / don’t mention it”). Sometimes it’s used like “Yeah, right!” in a skeptical tone.
target_language_example: —Você vai desistir? —Que nada! Vou até o fim.
native_language_example: —Are you going to quit? —No way! I’m going to the end.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese, often used to make comparisons, similar to "como" or "igual" (e.g., "que nem você" = "like you"). Can also appear in the structure "que nem..." meaning "as if..." in informal speech. Generally avoided in more formal writing.
target_language_example: Ele corre que nem um louco.
native_language_example: He runs like a madman.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to show anger, frustration, or that you don’t care (about a situation or a person). Literally relates to “to fuck,” but it’s used as a fixed curse; avoid in polite contexts. Variants include “que se foda isso” (“fuck this”) and “que se foda ele/ela” (“fuck him/her”).
target_language_example: Perdi o ônibus — que se foda, vou a pé.
native_language_example: I missed the bus—fuck it, I’ll walk.

meaning: “that is/that would be” or “at least” (after a number/amount).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" in the present subjunctive ("seja") to express a desired/possible option or minimum requirement. Common in set phrases like "seja como for" (“be that as it may / anyway”) and in requests: "Qualquer um que seja" (“whichever it is”). After quantities, it often means “at least”: "10 euros, que seja".
target_language_example: Traga um casaco, que seja leve.
native_language_example: Bring a jacket, even if it’s a light one.

meaning: (informal) “as can be”; “really/very” (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective to emphasize it, similar to “___ as can be” or “really/very ___” in English: “bonito que só” = “beautiful as can be.” Very common in Brazilian Portuguese and mostly conversational. You’ll also see variations like “que só!” used alone for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ela ficou feliz que só quando recebeu a notícia.
native_language_example: She was really happy when she got the news.

meaning: 'how about…?' / 'what’s it like?' / 'how are…?' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Very common and informal-friendly. Used to: (1) make a suggestion: "Que tal irmos ao cinema?" = "How about we go to the movies?" (2) ask for an opinion/condition: "Que tal o filme?" = "How was the movie?" (3) greet/ask how someone is: "Que tal?" = "How’s it going?" Often followed by a noun/pronoun ("Que tal o trabalho?") or by an infinitive ("Que tal fazer…?").
target_language_example: Que tal irmos tomar um café depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: How about we go have a coffee after work?

meaning: “that/which comes”; often used to mean “next” (the one coming).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to talk about the next occurrence of something (usually time-related): "semana que vem" = next week, "mês que vem" = next month, "ano que vem" = next year. Also used in relative clauses meaning “that comes/that is coming,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu vou viajar na semana que vem.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel next week.

meaning: "what happened to…?" / "where is…?" (asking about someone/something’s whereabouts or situation).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the expression "O que é de + noun/pronoun?" to ask what became of someone/something, often when you haven’t seen them/it in a while. It can sound a bit literary/old-fashioned in some contexts; in everyday speech people also say "Onde está…?" (Where is…?) or "O que aconteceu com…?" (What happened to…?). Example with a pronoun: "O que é de você?" = "What’s become of you?"
target_language_example: O que é do Paulo? Faz tempo que não o vejo.
native_language_example: What happened to Paulo? I haven’t seen him in a long time.

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese to emphasize that something works very well, tastes great, looks great, or happens intensely/quickly. It often follows a verb: “dormir que é uma beleza” (sleep really well), “funcionar que é uma beleza” (work perfectly), “chover que é uma beleza” (rain a lot). Informal and idiomatic; it doesn’t translate word-for-word as natural English.
target_language_example: Esse carro tá funcionando que é uma beleza.
native_language_example: This car is running really well.

additional_notes: Commonly used for a jigsaw puzzle (a puzzle you assemble from pieces) or for a difficult problem that requires thinking. The plural is usually “quebra-cabeças.” Often used with “fazer/montar um quebra-cabeça” (do/put together a puzzle).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vou montar um quebra-cabeça de 1.000 peças.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I’m going to put together a 1,000-piece puzzle.

meaning: to be proven wrong; to be disappointed (after being sure about something).
additional_notes: Informal idiom in Brazilian Portuguese. Used when someone is confident about an outcome or opinion and then reality shows they were wrong (or they get let down). Often appears as "quebrei a cara" (I was wrong) or "vai quebrar a cara" (you’ll be proven wrong).
target_language_example: Eu achei que ia ser fácil, mas quebrei a cara.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to be easy, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to express desire for something that is unlikely or not currently true. Often followed by a clause with the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "Quem dera eu tivesse...") or used alone as an exclamation ("Quem dera!"). It’s a set expression and doesn’t literally mean "who gives" in modern Portuguese.
target_language_example: Quem dera eu tivesse mais tempo para viajar.
native_language_example: If only I had more time to travel.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to show surprise about something that happened or turned out to be true. Literally "who would say," but it’s used idiomatically like English "who would’ve thought." Often followed by a clause with "que" (e.g., "Quem diria que...").
target_language_example: Quem diria que ele ia chegar tão cedo!
native_language_example: Who would have thought he would arrive so early!

additional_notes: Used to express a desire for something that is unlikely or not currently true. Very common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear it, but “quem dera” (without “me”) is more common. Often followed by a clause introduced by “que” (e.g., “Quem me dera que…”), or by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Quem me dera ter mais tempo para viajar.
native_language_example: If only I had more time to travel.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unknown or irrelevant person: it emphasizes that the identity doesn’t matter. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive), similar to English “whoever + verb.” Common in formal or neutral speech/writing. Related forms: “o que quer que” (“whatever”), “onde quer que” (“wherever”).
target_language_example: Quem quer que seja o responsável, precisa falar comigo.
native_language_example: Whoever is responsible needs to talk to me.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or possibility. Often means “maybe” in answers (similar to “perhaps”), and can also be used as a rhetorical “who knows?” In Portuguese it’s common to say it on its own as a short reply: “—Você vai? —Quem sabe.”
target_language_example: Quem sabe a gente se vê amanhã?
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll see each other tomorrow?

meaning: “if only you… / I wish you would…” (expresses a strong wish).
additional_notes: Used to express longing or regret about something you want to happen or be true. It often introduces a clause with the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "Quem te dera que fosses..."), or can be used on its own as an exclamation. Commonly heard as "Quem me dera" (“If only I…”).
target_language_example: Quem te dera que pudesses vir comigo!
native_language_example: If only you could come with me!

meaning: means; I mean (used to clarify or correct).
additional_notes: Literally “(it) wants to say,” but it’s used like English “to mean” and “I mean.” Common in conversation to explain something (“Quer dizer que…”) or to rephrase/soften what you just said (“Quer dizer, não exatamente…”). In questions, it can ask for clarification: “O que quer dizer …?” (= “What does … mean?”).
target_language_example: O que quer dizer essa palavra?
native_language_example: What does that word mean?

meaning: "you want to know"; often used as "you know what?" / "wanna know?"
additional_notes: Literally "(you) want to know" (from querer + saber). In conversation it’s commonly used to introduce a decision or emphasize what comes next: "Quer saber? Vou embora." (“You know what? I’m leaving.”). It can also be a direct question inviting someone to hear information: "Quer saber uma coisa?" (“Want to know something?”).
target_language_example: Quer saber? Acho melhor a gente ir embora.
native_language_example: You know what? I think it’s better for us to leave.

additional_notes: Commonly used to clarify meaning or intentions. Often appears as “O que você quer dizer (com isso)?” (“What do you mean (by that)?”) and “Quero dizer que…” (“I mean that…”). In Portuguese, it’s also used to correct or refine what you just said, similar to English “I mean…”.
target_language_example: O que você quer dizer com isso?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: “I want to see,” often used as “we’ll see / let’s see.”
additional_notes: Literally “I want to see” (querer + ver), but very commonly used to express doubt, challenge, or suspense about what will happen (similar to “we’ll see,” “let’s see,” or “I’ll believe it when I see it,” depending on tone). Often followed by “se...” (“quero ver se...”).
target_language_example: Você diz que vai terminar hoje? Quero ver!
native_language_example: You say you’ll finish today? We’ll see!

additional_notes: Name of the day of the week. Often used with prepositions like "na quinta-feira" (on Thursday) or "toda quinta-feira" (every Thursday). In Brazil, it’s common to shorten it to "quinta" in conversation; in Portugal you may also hear "quinta" informally.
target_language_example: Tenho uma reunião na quinta-feira.
native_language_example: I have a meeting on Thursday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about materials and sources found in nature that people use (e.g., water, forests, oil, minerals). Often appears in environmental, economic, and political contexts. Plural: "recursos naturais".
target_language_example: A água é um recurso natural essencial.
native_language_example: Water is an essential natural resource.

additional_notes: Used to talk about platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, etc. Usually refers to the online service/platform (often countable: "uma rede social"), while "redes sociais" is common when speaking about social media in general.
target_language_example: Eu quase não uso redes sociais.
native_language_example: I hardly use social media.

additional_notes: Common in Christian/religious contexts (especially the Bible). Usually used with the definite article: “o reino dos Céus”. In Portuguese, “Céus” (plural) is the standard form in this expression, even though English often says “Heaven” (singular). More formal/solemn than everyday speech.
target_language_example: Bem-aventurados os pobres em espírito, porque deles é o reino dos Céus.
native_language_example: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.

meaning: to be responsible for; to answer for.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is accountable for a person, task, area, or consequences. Common in formal contexts (work, legal, administration): "responder por uma equipe" (be in charge of a team), "responder por danos" (be liable for damages). It can also mean to cover/pay for something in some contexts (e.g., expenses), but the core idea is responsibility/accountability.
target_language_example: Eu respondo por este projeto na empresa.
native_language_example: I’m responsible for this project at the company.

additional_notes: Used for the big rotating wheel ride at fairs, amusement parks, or on the waterfront. It’s a compound noun: roda (“wheel”) + gigante (“giant”), and it’s commonly written with a hyphen. Plural: rodas-gigantes.
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma volta na roda-gigante?
native_language_example: Shall we take a ride on the Ferris wheel?

additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to show uncertainty or that you don’t know (often with a shrugging tone). It can sound a bit dismissive depending on context. Often appears as “Sei lá” (“I don’t know”) or “Quem sabe?” (“Who knows?”).
target_language_example: — Quando ele vai chegar? — Sei lá.
native_language_example: — When is he going to arrive? — Who knows / I have no idea.

additional_notes: Used for camping or sleeping away from home. Common with the verb "usar" (to use), "levar" (to take/bring), or "precisar de" (to need). Plural: "sacos de dormir".
target_language_example: Vou levar um saco de dormir para o acampamento.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a sleeping bag to the campsite.

additional_notes: Informal imperative of **sair** (“to leave/go out”), used to tell someone to leave or to dismiss them. It can sound rude/angry depending on tone, but it can also be used playfully among friends (similar to “Get outta here!” meaning “No way!”). Often appears as **Sai fora daqui!** (“Get out of here!”).
target_language_example: Sai fora daqui!
native_language_example: Get out of here!

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese and fairly informal. It emphasizes leaving a place (often to go elsewhere), similar to “go out” or “head out.” You’ll also hear the shorter version “sair” with the same meaning, and the very common phrase “sair fora de” (to leave/get out of a place).
target_language_example: Vou sair fora um pouco e já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to head out for a bit and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Literally “lesson/class room.” Used for the physical room where classes take place (at a school, university, or course). Common with the verb “estar” (to be) and prepositions like “na” (in the) and “para a” (to the): “Estou na sala de aula.” / “Vou para a sala de aula.”
target_language_example: Os alunos estão na sala de aula.
native_language_example: The students are in the classroom.

additional_notes: Used for the place where people wait before an appointment or service (e.g., at a doctor’s office, hospital, dentist, clinic, or airport). Also commonly appears on signs. Often used with verbs like “ficar” (to stay) and “esperar” (to wait): “Fique na sala de espera.”
target_language_example: Por favor, aguarde na sala de espera.
native_language_example: Please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for the main room in a home where people sit, relax, and receive visitors. Literally “room of being/staying,” so it’s fairly transparent from the parts (sala + de + estar). Often used with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay) and assistir (to watch): “ficar na sala de estar,” “assistir TV na sala de estar.”
target_language_example: A gente vai ficar na sala de estar para conversar.
native_language_example: We’re going to stay in the living room to chat.

additional_notes: Used for the room where people eat meals at home (often with a dining table). It’s a straightforward, literal phrase: "sala" (room) + "de" (of/for) + "jantar" (dinner/to dine). You may also hear "sala de refeições" (dining room, more general) or "sala de jantar" even if it’s mainly used for lunch.
target_language_example: A sala de jantar fica ao lado da cozinha.
native_language_example: The dining room is next to the kitchen.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a lifeguard (the person who watches swimmers and rescues people) at a beach or pool: "o salva-vidas". In some contexts it can also refer to a life preserver/life buoy (a floating rescue device), but that object is often called "boia salva-vidas" or "colete salva-vidas" (life jacket).
target_language_example: O salva-vidas viu a criança em perigo e pulou na água.
native_language_example: The lifeguard saw the child in danger and jumped into the water.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term used in everyday speech and in healthcare contexts. Often appears in phrases like “cuidar da saúde mental” (to take care of your mental health), “problemas de saúde mental” (mental health problems), and “saúde mental e bem-estar” (mental health and well-being).
target_language_example: É importante cuidar da saúde mental.
native_language_example: It’s important to take care of your mental health.

additional_notes: Used to express hope that something will happen, acknowledging that it depends on circumstances (or God’s will). Very common in everyday Portuguese, including among people who aren’t particularly religious. Often follows a future plan: "Amanhã eu vou, se Deus quiser."
target_language_example: Chego lá às oito, se Deus quiser.
native_language_example: I’ll get there at eight, God willing / hopefully.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or exception to what was just said. Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Often followed by the subjunctive when talking about something uncertain or hypothetical (e.g., “Se bem que eu ache…”), but it can also be used with the indicative when stating a fact.
target_language_example: Eu posso ir, se bem que esteja um pouco cansado.
native_language_example: I can go, although I’m a bit tired.

additional_notes: Very common in European Portuguese to express uncertainty or a possibility (similar to “maybe”/“possibly”). Often used at the start of a sentence (“Se calhar, ...”) or before a verb (“Se calhar vou...”). In Brazilian Portuguese it exists but sounds more European/less common; Brazilians often use “talvez” instead.
target_language_example: Se calhar vou chegar um pouco tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe I’ll arrive a bit late.

additional_notes: Common farewell in Brazilian Portuguese, usually said to one person (equivalent to “cuide-se” in a more formal/standard imperative). In context it means “take care” rather than literally “(he/she) takes care.” Often used with closings like “Tá bom, se cuida!”
target_language_example: Então tá, a gente se fala. Se cuida!
native_language_example: Alright then, we’ll talk soon. Take care!

meaning: “If I were you …” (used to give advice).
additional_notes: Used before giving a suggestion or warning. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of the verb "ser" ("fosse") and is often followed by something like "eu faria..." (I would do...). Common in both Brazil and Portugal and generally neutral/polite depending on tone.
target_language_example: Se eu fosse você, eu falaria com ele hoje.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would talk to him today.

meaning: (very informal/vulgar) “gets screwed / gets fucked over”; also as an insult: “fuck you / go to hell.”
additional_notes: From the verb “foder” (vulgar: to fuck; figuratively: to mess up/screw someone). Often used in Brazilian Portuguese as “se fodeu” (past: “got screwed”) or as an imperative “Se fode!” to tell someone off. Strong and rude—avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Se você mentir de novo, você se fode.
native_language_example: If you lie again, you’re screwed.

additional_notes: The days of the week in Portuguese are usually lowercase (segunda-feira, terça-feira, etc.). In Brazil, it’s common to shorten it to “segunda” in speech. Used with the preposition “na” (em + a) to mean “on Monday”: “na segunda-feira” or “na segunda”.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho na segunda-feira.
native_language_example: I work on Monday.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used for an insurance policy that pays out when someone dies. Often used with verbs like "ter" (to have), "fazer" (to take out/buy), or "contratar" (to purchase/sign up for). Example: "Eu tenho seguro de vida."
target_language_example: Ela fez um seguro de vida para proteger a família.
native_language_example: She took out a life insurance policy to protect the family.

additional_notes: Very common, informal filler used when you’re unsure, don’t want to commit to an answer, or feel indifferent. Tone depends on context: it can sound casual, dismissive, or slightly annoyed. Literally “(I) know there,” but that’s not the real meaning. Often appears as “Ah, sei lá…” or at the end of a sentence for a shrugging effect.
target_language_example: — Vamos sair hoje? — Sei lá, talvez.
native_language_example: — Are we going out today? — I don’t know, maybe.

meaning: "be that as it may" / "anyway" (no matter what).
additional_notes: Used to move past a detail or disagreement and continue with the main point. Often comes at the start of a sentence, similar to "Anyway," or "In any case,". Literally from the verb "ser" (to be): "however it may be".
target_language_example: Seja como for, precisamos tomar uma decisão hoje.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, we need to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something. Common in conversation and writing. Often followed by a comma when used as a standalone response ("Sem dúvida,") or placed at the end for emphasis ("..., sem dúvida.").
target_language_example: Sem dúvida, esse é o melhor restaurante do bairro.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, that’s the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Literally “without grace.” Used to describe (1) a situation that feels awkward or embarrassing (“Que sem graça!”), (2) a joke/comment that isn’t funny, or (3) a person who seems shy or not very outgoing. Often used as an adjective after the noun (“uma situação sem graça”) or as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Fiquei sem graça quando esqueci o nome dela.
native_language_example: I felt embarrassed when I forgot her name.

meaning: awkward; clumsy; embarrassing (not knowing what to do).
additional_notes: Literally “without a way.” Used to describe someone who is unskilled/clumsy (often physically or socially), or a situation that feels awkward/embarrassing. Can also mean “with no solution” in some contexts (“isso não tem jeito”), but “sem jeito” most commonly describes a person or moment.
target_language_example: Fiquei sem jeito quando ele perguntou a minha idade.
native_language_example: I felt awkward/embarrassed when he asked my age.

additional_notes: Used to wrap up what you’re saying and move on, often right before starting something or ending a message (like “that’s it” / “so…”). Common in speech and writing: “Sem mais, obrigado.” = “That’s all, thank you.” It can sound a bit formal or businesslike in emails.
target_language_example: Sem mais, desejo-lhe um bom dia.
native_language_example: Without further ado, I wish you a good day.

additional_notes: Used when you’re so surprised, shocked, moved, or impressed that you can’t think of what to say. Often appears as a short reaction by itself ("Sem palavras!") or after "Estou"/"Fico" ("Estou/Fico sem palavras"). Tone depends on context: it can be positive (very impressed) or negative (disbelief/indignation).
target_language_example: Quando vi a surpresa, fiquei sem palavras.
native_language_example: When I saw the surprise, I was speechless.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously, without a break. Often placed after a verb: “trabalhar sem parar” (work nonstop), “chover sem parar” (rain nonstop), “falar sem parar” (talk nonstop).
target_language_example: Ele trabalhou sem parar o dia todo.
native_language_example: He worked nonstop all day.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to accept a request politely (similar to “sure” or “that’s fine”). Common in everyday conversation. Often said as a short reply on its own: “—Obrigado!” “—Sem problemas.”
target_language_example: Pode me enviar a foto depois? — Sem problemas.
native_language_example: Can you send me the photo later? — No problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t mean to do something. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Literally “without wanting (to),” so it’s fairly transparent. Common in apologies/explanations: “Desculpa, foi sem querer.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu te empurrei sem querer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I pushed you by accident.

additional_notes: Used to describe food prepared without adding salt (often for health reasons), or to request that something be made without salt. It can also be used figuratively to mean something is bland or not interesting (e.g., a joke/story).
target_language_example: Para mim, a sopa pode ser sem sal, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, the soup can be without salt, please.

meaning: shameless; (also) a shameless person / someone with no shame.
additional_notes: Literally “without shame.” Used to criticize someone’s behavior (rude, inappropriate, dishonest) or as a mild insult (“You’re shameless!”). Can describe a person (Ele é sem vergonha.) or be used as a noun (Seu sem vergonha!).
target_language_example: Ele pegou o dinheiro e ainda mentiu — que sem vergonha!
native_language_example: He took the money and still lied — what a shameless guy!

additional_notes: Used as an adjective ("ele é sem-vergonha") or as a noun to insult someone ("seu sem-vergonha!"). Often implies the person has no respect, acts rudely, or does something they should be ashamed of. Spelling varies: you may also see “sem vergonha” (two words).
target_language_example: Ele é um sem-vergonha: prometeu ajudar e não apareceu.
native_language_example: He’s shameless: he promised to help and didn’t show up.

meaning: whenever; every time that; as soon as (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time/condition clause meaning “every time that” or “whenever.” It’s often followed by the subjunctive when referring to an indefinite or future situation (e.g., “Sempre que eu puder…” = “Whenever I can…”). In more general/present habitual situations, the indicative is also common (e.g., “Sempre que chove, eu fico em casa.”).
target_language_example: Sempre que eu puder, eu te ligo.
native_language_example: Whenever I can, I’ll call you.

meaning: 'whereas' / 'given that' (adding a clarifying or contrasting detail).
additional_notes: Used to introduce extra information that clarifies, explains, or contrasts with what was just said. Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Often similar to English “whereas” (contrast) or “given that / considering that” (explanation).
target_language_example: Ele disse que ia chegar cedo, sendo que apareceu só à noite.
native_language_example: He said he would arrive early, but (in fact) he only showed up at night.

additional_notes: A formal, polite way to address an audience (e.g., at speeches, presentations, announcements). Often used at the beginning of a talk. Similar to “senhora” (lady/Ms.) and “senhor” (sir/Mr.).
target_language_example: Senhoras e senhores, sejam bem-vindos ao evento.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the event.

additional_notes: Used to refer to practical, everyday judgment (“use your common sense”) or to a widely held, generally accepted belief/opinion (“conventional wisdom”). Often appears in expressions like “pelo senso comum” (according to conventional wisdom) and “bom senso” is a related phrase meaning “good sense/sound judgment.”
target_language_example: Pelo senso comum, é melhor evitar dirigir cansado.
native_language_example: According to conventional wisdom, it’s better to avoid driving when you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability to understand, enjoy, or make jokes. Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "não ter" (not to have): "Ele tem senso de humor" / "Ela não tem senso de humor". You can add adjectives like "bom" or "ótimo" (good/great).
target_language_example: Ela tem um ótimo senso de humor.
native_language_example: She has a great sense of humor.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or rotation in the same direction as the hands of an analog clock. Often appears after verbs like “girar/rodar” (to turn/spin) or in instructions (maps, manuals, cooking, etc.). Common opposite: “sentido anti-horário” (counterclockwise).
target_language_example: Gire a tampa no sentido horário para fechar.
native_language_example: Turn the lid clockwise to close.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person in a general, neutral, or sometimes philosophical/scientific way (more formal than just "pessoa"). It can also be used to emphasize someone’s humanity (e.g., compassion, dignity). Plural: "seres humanos".
target_language_example: Todos os seres humanos merecem respeito.
native_language_example: All human beings deserve respect.

meaning: to be more (e.g., more + adjective); to be more than (in comparisons).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to express becoming/being to a greater degree: “ser mais + adjective” (ser mais paciente = to be more patient). It’s also common in comparisons with “do que” or “que”: “ser mais … do que/que …” (to be more … than …).
target_language_example: Eu quero ser mais paciente.
native_language_example: I want to be more patient.

meaning: a living being; a living creature (an organism).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any organism that is alive (humans, animals, plants, etc.). It’s common in science/biology contexts and in general statements like “every living being needs water.” Plural: “seres vivos.”
target_language_example: A água é essencial para todo ser vivo.
native_language_example: Water is essential for every living being.

meaning: "I wonder if…" / "could it be that…?" (used to introduce a doubt or possibility).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese to soften a question or express uncertainty. Often used before a clause ("Será que ele vem?") and can also introduce polite requests ("Será que você pode me ajudar?"). It’s not about the future of the verb "ser" here; it functions as a fixed question phrase.
target_language_example: Será que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain today?

additional_notes: A common cultural/religious reference in Christianity. Used in formal or informal contexts to talk about moral vices (often jokingly or metaphorically). Typically refers to: soberba (pride), avareza (greed), luxúria (lust), inveja (envy), gula (gluttony), ira (wrath), preguiça (sloth).
target_language_example: No filme, os personagens representam os sete pecados capitais.
native_language_example: In the movie, the characters represent the seven deadly sins.

additional_notes: Name of the day of the week. In Portuguese, weekdays are often written with a hyphen (segunda-feira, terça-feira, etc.). Commonly used with em (“on”): em sexta-feira, na sexta-feira (“on Friday”/“this Friday”).
target_language_example: A reunião é na sexta-feira.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Friday.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is straightforward, needs no further explanation, or is final. Common in spoken Portuguese and casual writing; you can use it after giving a reason or instruction to stress simplicity or certainty.
target_language_example: É só seguir as instruções—simples assim.
native_language_example: Just follow the instructions—just like that.

meaning: green light; permission to go ahead.
additional_notes: Used literally for a green traffic light, and figuratively to mean authorization/approval to proceed ("get the green light"). Often appears with verbs like "dar" (to give) or "ter" (to have): "dar sinal verde" = to give the go-ahead.
target_language_example: O chefe deu sinal verde para começarmos o projeto.
native_language_example: The boss gave the green light for us to start the project.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to apologize or express sympathy. Often used for bad news (“I’m sorry to hear that”) as well as for a mistake (“Sorry!”). You can add “por…” to specify the reason: “Sinto muito pelo atraso” (“I’m sorry about the delay”).
target_language_example: Sinto muito, eu cheguei atrasado.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to our Solar System (the Sun and the bodies that orbit it), especially in school/science contexts. Often appears with an article: "o Sistema Solar". Can also be used more generally to mean any star system, depending on context.
target_language_example: Na escola, estamos a estudar o Sistema Solar.
native_language_example: At school, we are studying the Solar System.

additional_notes: Used to talk about letting your mind wander or imagining things while you’re awake (often because you’re bored, distracted, or lost in thought). It can be used literally (daydreaming) or more generally to mean having unrealistic fantasies. You can also hear it as a verb phrase: “Estou sonhando acordado.”
target_language_example: Eu estava na aula e comecei a sonhar acordado.
native_language_example: I was in class and I started daydreaming.

additional_notes: Used as an honorific when referring to a king or queen. It’s very formal and typically appears in ceremonial language, history, news, invitations, or official contexts. Often capitalized: "Sua Majestade". You may also see the plural "Suas Majestades" (Their Majesties).
target_language_example: Sua Majestade, a Rainha, chegou ao palácio.
native_language_example: Her Majesty the Queen arrived at the palace.

additional_notes: Refers to a (usually fictional) hero with special powers. Feminine form: "super-heroína". Plural: "super-heróis" / "super-heroínas". Often used with verbs like "ser" (to be) and "virar" (to become), and in phrases like "filme de super-herói" (superhero movie).
target_language_example: Meu irmão quer ser um super-herói quando crescer.
native_language_example: My brother wants to be a superhero when he grows up.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived or ended up without harm (often after a trip, scare, or danger). It agrees with the person: masculine singular “são e salvo”, feminine singular “sã e salva”, masculine plural “sãos e salvos”, feminine plural “sãs e salvas”.
target_language_example: Ainda bem que vocês chegaram sãos e salvos.
native_language_example: Good thing you arrived safe and sound.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Portuguese to add an important contrast, often like “only/just that…” → “but…”. It can correct what was just said (“I wanted to go, só que I can’t”) or add an exception (“Everything is ready, só que the keys are missing”). Often interchangeable with “mas”, but “só que” tends to feel more like a twist or setback.
target_language_example: Eu queria ir, só que estou sem dinheiro.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but I don’t have any money.

meaning: "Yeah right" / "not!" (used to cancel what you just said, ironically).
additional_notes: Very common in informal speech and online. You say something, then add “só que não” to show you mean the opposite (sarcasm/irony). Often used after a pause: “Eu adorei… só que não.”
target_language_example: Eu adorei fazer a prova… só que não.
native_language_example: I loved taking the test… not.

additional_notes: Very common, informal spoken form of “está bem.” Used to agree, accept something, or say “that’s fine.” Can also be said with a different tone to mean reluctant acceptance (like “fine…”). In writing, you may also see “tá” without the accent, but “tá bem” reflects the pronunciation.
target_language_example: Tá bem, eu vou com você.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll go with you.

meaning: "We’re in this together" / "I’ve got your back."
additional_notes: Very common informal Brazilian Portuguese slang (a contracted form of "estamos juntos"). Used to show solidarity, support, or agreement—often as a friendly reply to thanks, good news, or a shared plan (similar to "we’re together" / "you can count on me").
target_language_example: Valeu pela ajuda! — Tamo junto!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help! — I’ve got your back!

additional_notes: Used to talk about degree or intensity. Very common in negative or softening statements: “não… tanto assim” = “not… that much / not really that…”. Can also be used to question or confirm intensity: “Tanto assim?” = “That much?” / “Is it really that much?”.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de café, mas não tanto assim.
native_language_example: I like coffee, but not that much.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no preference between options or that the choice/result isn’t important. Common in everyday speech; tone depends on context—can sound neutral (“either is fine”) or a bit dismissive/indifferent if said bluntly. Often used alone as an answer or followed by a choice: “Tanto faz A ou B.”
target_language_example: —Você quer pizza ou hambúrguer? —Tanto faz.
native_language_example: —Do you want pizza or a burger? —Either way / I don’t mind.

additional_notes: Common in school contexts. In Brazil, you may also hear "lição de casa" (especially for younger students). Plural: "tarefas de casa". Literally "house task," but it’s used like English "homework."
target_language_example: Tenho muita tarefa de casa para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of homework to do today.

additional_notes: Uses the object pronoun te (“you”) + amo (“I love”). Common in romantic contexts; with family/friends, many speakers prefer “eu te amo” for emphasis or “eu te adoro” / “gosto muito de você” as softer options (regional/personal preference). In European Portuguese, “amo-te” is more typical than “te amo.”
target_language_example: Eu te amo.
native_language_example: I love you.

additional_notes: Common in Brazil. You can also just say "celular" in everyday speech. In Portugal, "telemóvel" is more common. "Celular" in Brazilian Portuguese refers to a mobile phone (not a landline/"telefone fixo").
target_language_example: Você pode me ligar no meu telefone celular?
native_language_example: Can you call me on my cell phone?

additional_notes: Used to talk about time when you’re not working/studying and are free to do what you want. Common in phrases like "no meu tempo livre" (in my free time) and "ter tempo livre" (to have free time).
target_language_example: No meu tempo livre, eu gosto de ler e ouvir música.
native_language_example: In my free time, I like to read and listen to music.

additional_notes: A common proverb used to emphasize that time is valuable and wasting time has a cost. Often said in work or productivity contexts, sometimes as a reminder to be efficient or quick.
target_language_example: Vamos nos apressar — tempo é dinheiro.
native_language_example: Let’s hurry up—time is money.

additional_notes: Polite, very common way to signal you want to ask something (in class, at work, in a meeting, etc.). Literal structure: “I have” (tenho) + “a question” (uma pergunta). You can also use it to get someone’s attention before the question: “Tenho uma pergunta, por favor.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, tenho uma pergunta: onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: where is the bathroom?

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about relevance or connection between things. Very common in spoken Portuguese: “não tem nada a ver” = “it has nothing to do with it / it’s not related.” Note: there is also “ter a ver com (algo/alguém)” = “to have to do with (something/someone).”
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com o que eu disse.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what I said.

additional_notes: Often followed by a noun: “ter alguém/algo como + noun” = “to consider someone/something (as) …”. Example: “Tenho-o como amigo.” In everyday speech, it can also appear with an infinitive to mean “to have a way to / to be able to”: “Não tenho como pagar agora.” = “I can’t pay right now / I have no way to pay right now.”
target_language_example: Eu te tenho como um amigo.
native_language_example: I consider you a friend.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express obligation or necessity: "ter de + infinitivo". It conjugates like "ter": "tenho de", "tens de", "tem de", "temos de", "têm de". Very common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese, "ter que" is often more common, with a similar meaning. It’s not usually translated word-for-word as "have of" in English.
target_language_example: Tenho de ir agora.
native_language_example: I have to go now.

meaning: to keep in mind; to bear in mind.
additional_notes: Common in advice, reminders, and planning. Often followed by a clause with “que” (e.g., “Tenha em mente que…” = “Keep in mind that…”). Conjugates with “ter” (tenho/tem/temos/têm) and can also appear as an infinitive after another verb (“É bom ter em mente…”).
target_language_example: Tenha em mente que amanhã é feriado.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that tomorrow is a holiday.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity. Conjugate "ter" to match the subject + "que" + an infinitive: "eu tenho que fazer", "ele tem que ir", "nós temos que estudar". A common alternative is "ter de" (often slightly more formal).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu tenho que ir agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: to be right; to have a good reason.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say someone is correct: "Você tem razão" = "You’re right." It can also mean "to have a reason" (often with "para" or "de"): "Tenho razão para/de reclamar" = "I have a reason to complain." Opposite: "não ter razão" (to be wrong / to have no reason).
target_language_example: Você tem razão — precisamos sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: You’re right — we need to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place (city/region/country) where someone was born or originally comes from. Common in more formal or literary contexts; in everyday speech you may also hear "minha cidade natal" (my hometown) or "país de origem" (country of origin). Often used with possessives: "minha/sua/nossa terra natal".
target_language_example: Voltei à minha terra natal depois de muitos anos.
native_language_example: I returned to my homeland after many years.

additional_notes: Name of the weekday. Often used with the preposition "na" to mean "on Tuesday" (e.g., "na terça-feira"). In Portuguese, weekdays are commonly written in lowercase: "terça-feira". The word "feira" is part of several weekday names (segunda-feira, terça-feira, etc.).
target_language_example: Tenho uma reunião na terça-feira.
native_language_example: I have a meeting on Tuesday.

additional_notes: Used to refer to or address someone named Paula who is your aunt (“tia” can be your blood relative or, especially in Brazil, a close family friend treated like an aunt). In direct address, it’s common to use “Tia + first name” as a respectful, familiar way to speak to an older woman close to the family.
target_language_example: A tia Paula vai vir almoçar com a gente hoje.
native_language_example: Aunt Paula is going to come have lunch with us today.

additional_notes: Used in medical contexts to talk about a person’s blood classification (e.g., A, B, AB, O, plus Rh factor like positive/negative). Common on medical forms and when donating blood. You may also hear "grupo sanguíneo" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Qual é o seu tipo sanguíneo?
native_language_example: What is your blood type?

additional_notes: Onomatopoeia for the repetitive ticking sound of a clock. Often used with verbs like "ouvir" (to hear) or in expressions like "o tique-taque do relógio" (the tick-tock of the clock).
target_language_example: À noite, só se ouvia o tique-taque do relógio.
native_language_example: At night, you could only hear the tick-tock of the clock.

meaning: to take your hat off (to someone); to admire/respect someone.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone or show respect for what they did. Commonly followed by "para" (or "por") + person/thing: "Tiro o chapéu para você". Often appears in the emphatic form "Tiro o chapéu" / "Tem que tirar o chapéu" (You’ve got to give it to them).
target_language_example: Tiro o chapéu para a Maria: ela terminou o projeto antes do prazo.
native_language_example: I take my hat off to Maria: she finished the project before the deadline.

meaning: to make fun of; to tease (someone).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese and informal. Often used with "de" + person/thing: "tirar sarro de alguém" (make fun of someone). Can be playful teasing among friends or mean-spirited mocking depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Para de tirar sarro de mim!
native_language_example: Stop making fun of me!

additional_notes: A common household item: a cloth that covers a table (especially for meals). Often used with the verb "pôr/colocar" (to put on): "Põe a toalha de mesa". Sometimes shortened to just "toalha" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Você pode pôr a toalha de mesa antes do jantar?
native_language_example: Can you put the tablecloth on before dinner?

additional_notes: Common in instructions (especially on phones/screens) meaning you should tap a specific spot: "Toca aqui para continuar." In conversation it can also be said while raising your hand to invite a high five, similar to "High five!". Often used informally and in a friendly tone.
target_language_example: Toca aqui para abrir o menu.
native_language_example: Tap here to open the menu.

additional_notes: Often means “all my/your/his/her life” when used with a possessive: “toda a minha vida” (my whole life). It can also mean “always/forever” in casual speech, especially in Portugal: “Ele reclama toda vida” (He’s always complaining). Depending on context, it may refer to a long time (lifelong) or to a habitual action (always).
target_language_example: Moro aqui toda a minha vida.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here my whole life.

additional_notes: Very common, everyday way to refer to all people in general. It’s often used with singular verb agreement (like "everyone" in English): "Todo mundo sabe" (Everyone knows). You can also say "Todo mundo" to mean “all of us/you/them” depending on context.
target_language_example: Todo mundo está cansado hoje.
native_language_example: Everyone is tired today.

meaning: every single day; day in, day out.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens daily, often with a sense of annoyance or repetition (like complaining about a routine). It’s an idiomatic intensifier: literally it’s “every holy day,” but in practice it just means “every day” with extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Ele me liga todo santo dia.
native_language_example: He calls me every single day.

additional_notes: Used as a short exclamation after you do/say something that proves someone wrong, wins a point, or surprises them. Common in playful banter, but it can sound rude if said aggressively. Literally “take this/that,” with “toma” = “take” (informal command). Often said alone or followed by an explanation.
target_language_example: Eu falei que ia conseguir — toma essa!
native_language_example: I told you I’d do it — take that!

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to be in charge of.
additional_notes: Commonly used with "de" + noun/pronoun: "tomar conta de" (take care of / look after). It can mean caring for a person/animal (babysit/petsit), handling a responsibility, or managing something (e.g., a shop, a task). In everyday speech it can also mean "to deal with" or "to handle" a problem.
target_language_example: Você pode tomar conta das crianças hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Can you look after the kids tonight?

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to be responsible for.
additional_notes: Used when someone is caring for a person/animal/thing (babysitting, watching a pet, minding belongings) or managing something (being in charge of a task or place). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: “tomar conta das crianças”, “tomar conta dele/dela”, “tomar conta da casa”.
target_language_example: Você pode tomar conta do meu cachorro neste fim de semana?
native_language_example: Can you look after my dog this weekend?

meaning: to be careful; to take care (be cautious).
additional_notes: Common everyday warning/advice meaning “be careful.” Often used as an imperative: “Toma/Tome cuidado!” You can also use it with “com” + noun/pronoun to specify what to be careful with: “tomar cuidado com o carro / com isso.” Similar to “ter cuidado,” but “tomar cuidado” is very common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Toma cuidado com os carros ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Be careful with the cars when crossing the street.

meaning: a very vulgar insult: “go f*** yourself” / “go f*** off” (literally, “take it in the ass”).
additional_notes: Very offensive Brazilian Portuguese profanity. Used to express anger, contempt, or to tell someone to go away; not appropriate in polite conversation, with strangers, or at work. Can also be used as a crude exclamation of frustration (e.g., after something goes wrong), but it’s still highly vulgar.
target_language_example: Ah, tomar no cu! Nada dá certo hoje.
native_language_example: Ah, f*** this! Nothing goes right today.

meaning: to have a drink (often a beer).
additional_notes: Very common in Brazil in casual speech, often meaning “to grab a beer” or “go for a drink,” usually alcoholic. It can imply a relaxed social plan: "Vamos tomar uma?" Literally it’s “to take one,” but the meaning is “to drink/have one (drink).”
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vamos tomar uma no bar?
native_language_example: After work, shall we go have a drink at the bar?

additional_notes: Used to express a hope or wish about something, often for the future. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (present subjunctive for a future/uncertain result: “Tomara que dê certo.”; imperfect subjunctive for a more unlikely or more distant wish: “Tomara que desse certo.”). You can also use “Tomara!” alone to mean “I hope so!”
target_language_example: Tomara que você consiga o emprego.
native_language_example: I hope you get the job.

additional_notes: Means schoolwork done at home. In Brazil, it’s often shortened to “tarefa (de casa)” or just “tarefa”; in Portugal you may also hear “TPC” (trabalho para casa). Plural: “trabalhos de casa”.
target_language_example: Ainda não fiz o meu trabalho de casa.
native_language_example: I still haven’t done my homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shared transportation services available to everyone (e.g., buses, metro/subway, trains, trams). Often appears with verbs like “pegar” (to take/catch) or “usar” (to use): “pegar o transporte público”.
target_language_example: Eu vou para o trabalho de transporte público.
native_language_example: I go to work by public transportation.

additional_notes: Used for the number 36 in counting, giving ages, prices, dates, addresses, etc. In Portuguese, numbers from 21 to 99 are usually formed as “tens + e + ones” (e.g., trinta e seis = 30 and 6).
target_language_example: Eu tenho trinta e seis anos.
native_language_example: I am thirty-six years old.

additional_notes: Used for counting and for dates/ages (e.g., “dia trinta e um” = the 31st day of the month). In some contexts you may also see “no trinta e um” in the expression “estar todo no trinta e um,” meaning to be very dressed up/elegant (more idiomatic).
target_language_example: Tenho trinta e um anos.
native_language_example: I am thirty-one years old.

additional_notes: Literally “three points.” Used to refer to the punctuation mark (…) in writing, and also to the “more options” icon (⋮ or …) in apps/menus (e.g., “tap the three dots”).
target_language_example: Clica nos três pontos para ver mais opções.
native_language_example: Tap the three dots to see more options.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mother when addressing one person informally (tu). In everyday speech it can be affectionate or neutral (e.g., asking about someone’s mom), but it can also appear in insults/jokes depending on tone and context, so use with care. The more formal version is "sua mãe".
target_language_example: Como está a tua mãe?
native_language_example: How is your mother?

meaning: “It’s all good / OK”; also “How are you?”
additional_notes: Very common, semi-formal everyday phrase. Used as a question (“Tudo bem?” = “Are you OK?/How are you?”) and as an answer (“Tudo bem.” = “I’m fine/OK.”). Can also be used to agree/accept (“Tudo bem.” = “OK, sure.”). Often heard with “tudo bem com você?” (Brazil) or “tudo bem contigo?” / “tudo bem consigo?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Oi! Tudo bem? — Tudo bem, e você?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you? — I’m fine, and you?

additional_notes: Very common informal spelling/pronunciation of "está bem". Used to agree (“OK”), to accept something (“Fine.”), or to end a discussion (“Alright then”). Tone depends on context: it can sound friendly/neutral, or reluctant/annoyed (like English “Fine.”).
target_language_example: Tá bem, eu te ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Very common informal contraction of “está bom.” Used to agree, accept, or acknowledge (sometimes meaning “fine, OK” depending on tone). You’ll often hear it alone as a response.
target_language_example: Tá bom, eu te ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese conversation. It comes from "está ligado" (literally "(it) is connected"), but it’s usually used as a casual way to check understanding or agreement, similar to English "you know?" or "you get it?". Often appears at the end of a sentence, but can also be used alone as a response meaning "yeah, I know / I get it".
target_language_example: A gente se encontra às oito, tá ligado?
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight, you know?/got it?

meaning: as soon as; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen immediately after another action/event: "tão logo +" (often with a verb). It can sound slightly formal in some contexts, and is common in writing. Similar to "assim que". You may also see "tão logo quanto" meaning "as soon as" (emphasizing immediacy).
target_language_example: Tão logo eu chegar em casa, eu te ligo.
native_language_example: As soon as I get home, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: A sport played on a table with small paddles and a light ball. Also called "pingue-pongue" in Brazilian Portuguese (more informal/colloquial). Note that "tênis" by itself can mean the sport tennis or (in Brazil) tennis shoes; "tênis de mesa" is specifically the sport table tennis.
target_language_example: Eu jogo tênis de mesa aos sábados.
native_language_example: I play table tennis on Saturdays.

meaning: “I know / I’m aware” or “I get it.”
additional_notes: Very common informal Brazilian Portuguese. It’s a contraction of “estou ligado” (literally “I’m connected”), but in everyday speech it often means you understand something or you’re aware of a situation (similar to “I know,” “got it,” “I’m with you”). Often used as a quick response to show understanding.
target_language_example: —A festa foi cancelada. —Tô ligado.
native_language_example: —The party was canceled. —Yeah, I know / Got it.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hug.” Very common at the end of messages, emails, and letters as a warm, friendly closing (often written as "Um abraço," or "Um abraço!"), similar to “Hugs,” “Take care,” or “Best.” You can make it stronger with "um grande abraço" (“a big hug”) or use plural "abraços" (“hugs”).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela ajuda. Um abraço!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help. Hugs!/Best!

additional_notes: Reciprocal expression used when two or more people do the same action to each other. Often appears with reflexive/reciprocal verbs like "ajudar" (help), "ver" (see), "amar" (love), "respeitar" (respect). You may also see variations like "uma à outra" (all feminine), or plural forms such as "uns aos outros" / "umas às outras" depending on gender and number.
target_language_example: Eles se ajudam um ao outro quando precisam.
native_language_example: They help each other when they need to.

meaning: “a kiss.” Often used as a friendly sign-off: “kiss(es).”
additional_notes: Literally “a kiss.” In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s very common at the end of messages or phone calls as an affectionate but often non-romantic goodbye (similar to “kisses,” “x,” or “love” in English). You may also hear the plural “beijos” (“kisses”).
target_language_example: Tchau! Um beijo, até amanhã.
native_language_example: Bye! Kisses, see you tomorrow.

meaning: one day; one fine day (often: suddenly/at some point).
additional_notes: Used to set the scene in storytelling or to mean that something happened unexpectedly at some later time. Often appears as “Até que um belo dia...” (“Until one day...”) and doesn’t necessarily refer to a literally ‘beautiful’ day.
target_language_example: Até que um belo dia ele resolveu mudar de cidade.
native_language_example: Until one day he decided to move to another city.

additional_notes: Common in everyday Portuguese to mean “a little” (quantity or duration). Often used with de + noun (“um bocado de água” = “a bit of water”) or after a verb/adjective (“espera um bocado” = “wait a bit”, “está um bocado frio” = “it’s a bit cold”). Similar meaning to “um pouco”; “um bocado” can sound slightly more informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Espera um bocado, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait a bit, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a particular day (“on a day”) or an unspecified future/unknown time (“someday”). Often appears in phrases like “Um dia vou…” (“One day I will…”). Can also introduce a story: “Um dia, eu estava…” (“One day, I was…”).
target_language_example: Um dia vou visitar Portugal.
native_language_example: One day I’m going to visit Portugal.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Portuguese to mean “a lot/loads.” Often used as **um monte de + noun** (“a lot of …”): *um monte de gente* (lots of people). It can also be used more generally to mean “a lot” about quantity, time, or effort: *trabalhei um monte* (I worked a lot). Literally it’s “a heap/pile,” so the word-by-word translation doesn’t usually match the natural English phrase.
target_language_example: Tenho um monte de coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have loads of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say things/people will be handled individually, in sequence. Common with verbs like fazer, ver, analisar, chamar: fazer um por um (do one by one), chamar um por um (call one by one).
target_language_example: Vamos revisar os documentos um por um.
native_language_example: Let’s review the documents one by one.

additional_notes: Used to express a small amount or degree. Common after verbs (e.g., esperar, falar, comer) and in polite requests to soften what you’re asking: "Espere um pouco" (“Wait a moment”). Can also mean “for a little while” depending on context.
target_language_example: Pode falar um pouco mais devagar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Literally “one hour.” With durations it means “one hour” (often with “por”: “por uma hora” = “for an hour”). In everyday speech it can also mean “later/on some occasion,” similar to “one of these days” or “later” (“Uma hora eu te ligo.”).
target_language_example: Uma hora eu te ligo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you later.

meaning: “No way!” / “Yeah, right!” (an emphatic refusal or disbelief).
additional_notes: Very informal (Brazilian Portuguese). Often used alone as an interjection to reject an idea, deny a request, or show disbelief/irritation. Stronger equivalents in English can be “my ass!” or “in your dreams!”, so use with care. You’ll also hear it in longer phrases like “(isso é) uma ova!” or “(ele/ela) uma ova!”.
target_language_example: Você vai me emprestar seu carro? — Uma ova!
native_language_example: Are you going to lend me your car? — No way!

additional_notes: Literally means “a portion.” Very commonly used with “de” ("uma porção de + noun"). Depending on context, it can mean an actual portion/serving (food, a piece of something) or, more loosely, “a lot of / many” (especially in Brazilian Portuguese).
target_language_example: Tem uma porção de coisas pra fazer hoje.
native_language_example: There are a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Literally, “uma pá” is the tool (a shovel/spade). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s also a common informal way to say “a lot of” before a noun: “uma pá de + [noun]” (like “a ton of…”).
target_language_example: Tem uma pá de gente aqui.
native_language_example: There are tons of people here.

additional_notes: Literally “one time.” Common uses: (1) frequency/time: “once” (Uma vez por semana = once a week); (2) “once” meaning “at some point in the past” (Eu fui lá uma vez = I went there once); (3) in storytelling: “Era uma vez…” = “Once upon a time…”. Also appears in the structure “uma vez que …” meaning “since/given that …” (more formal).
target_language_example: Eu só fui ao Porto uma vez.
native_language_example: I only went to Porto once.

meaning: since / because / given that (because of the fact that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or explanation, especially in more formal or written Portuguese. It’s similar to “since” meaning “because,” not “since” meaning “from a time in the past.” Often followed by a verb clause: “Uma vez que + [sentence], ...”.
target_language_example: Uma vez que está chovendo, vamos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Since it’s raining, we’re going to stay at home.

meaning: "Go figure" / "who knows" (said when something doesn’t make sense).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese as a short, slightly ironic comment when you don’t understand someone’s behavior or a situation. Often used alone or after describing something confusing: "Ele disse que não vem, mas está aqui. Vai entender." It’s informal and expresses puzzlement or disbelief.
target_language_example: Ela reclamou que estava sem dinheiro, mas comprou um celular novo. Vai entender.
native_language_example: She complained that she had no money, but she bought a new phone. Go figure.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a possibility (often a precaution or unlikely scenario), similar to English “what if…” or “just in case…”. It can also mean “it might happen that…”. Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese and informal writing. Often followed by a verb in the present or past (e.g., “vai que ele chega cedo…”).
target_language_example: Leva um casaco, vai que esfria mais tarde.
native_language_example: Take a jacket, just in case it gets colder later.

additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to say you don’t know (and it may be impossible to know) the reason for something. Often follows a question or a statement of uncertainty, and can sound mildly resigned or ironic. Similar to "sei lá" in meaning, but "vai saber" can imply that the answer is unknowable or unpredictable.
target_language_example: Ele não veio hoje—vai saber por quê.
native_language_example: He didn’t come today—who knows why.

additional_notes: A very vulgar insult used to tell someone off aggressively. Common in arguments and can easily escalate a situation; avoid in polite conversation. Variations include “vai te foder” and, with extra emphasis, “vai se foder, cara!”
target_language_example: Se você não vai ajudar, vai se foder.
native_language_example: If you’re not going to help, fuck off.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese. Often appears as "vai ver que..." to mean "probably / it may be that..." (a speculation). It can also be used on its own to reassure or insist: "Vai ver" = "You'll see." Literally it’s "go see," but in these uses it functions more like "you’ll see" or "probably."
target_language_example: Vai ver que ele esqueceu.
native_language_example: He probably forgot.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Common patterns: “Vale a pena + infinitive” (Vale a pena tentar. = It’s worth trying.) and “Vale a pena” as a standalone response (Yes, it’s worth it.). In the negative: “Não vale a pena” (It’s not worth it / Don’t bother.).
target_language_example: Vale a pena visitar o museu.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting the museum.

additional_notes: Very common phrase using the imperative of “ir” (to go): “vamos” = “let’s (we) go,” and “lá” = “there.” Used to start doing something, encourage someone, move a conversation forward, or signal acceptance (“ok then”). Often said on its own, or followed by an action: “Vamos lá ver…” (“Let’s see…”).
target_language_example: Vamos lá, temos de sair agora.
native_language_example: Come on, we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Imperative of "vir" (to come) + "cá" (here). Used to call someone closer to you (often: “Come here for a second”). Very common in speech; depending on tone it can be friendly, insistent, or even a mild scolding. It can also be used to get someone’s attention before a question (like “hey, tell me…”).
target_language_example: Vem cá um momento, preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, I need to talk to you.

meaning: to see stars (to feel dizzy or dazed, often after a hit).
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning you feel dizzy, stunned, or momentarily disoriented—often from bumping your head or getting hit.
