It can also be used more loosely for strong dizziness (e.g., from low blood pressure), but the 'after a blow' meaning is very typical. Literal translation is possible, but the intended meaning is usually figurative.
target_language_example: Bati com a cabeça na porta e comecei a ver estrelas.
native_language_example: I hit my head on the door and started seeing stars.

meaning: “Look!” / “Just look.” (used to call attention or show surprise).
additional_notes: Common in informal speech as a discourse marker to get someone’s attention or introduce a comment, often expressing surprise, emphasis, or mild disbelief. It can also appear as “Vê só” (more common in Brazil) or “Veja só” (more polite).
target_language_example: Vê só, já são dez horas!
native_language_example: Look, it’s already ten o’clock!

meaning: to really commit to/support (a team, company, or cause).
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning to show strong loyalty and dedication—like someone who proudly wears the team shirt. Often used at work (about employees) and in sports/fan contexts. It can also be literal (“to put on a shirt”), but the idiomatic sense is very frequent.
target_language_example: No novo emprego, ela vestiu a camisa e ajudou o time desde o primeiro dia.
native_language_example: In the new job, she really committed and helped the team from day one.

additional_notes: Used to talk about traveling to the past or future (real or fictional). Often appears with the verb “viajar”: “viajar no tempo” (to time-travel).
target_language_example: Você acredita em viagem no tempo?
native_language_example: Do you believe in time travel?

meaning: viceroy (a ruler governing a territory on behalf of a king).
additional_notes: A formal/historical title. In Portuguese it often refers to officials who governed colonies or large regions in the name of the Portuguese king (e.g., in the colonial period). The plural is usually “vice-reis.”
target_language_example: O vice-rei governava a colônia em nome do rei.
native_language_example: The viceroy governed the colony in the king’s name.

additional_notes: Used when talking about religious or spiritual beliefs about what happens after someone dies. "Após" means "after" (more formal than "depois"), and "a morte" is "death."
target_language_example: Muitas religiões acreditam na vida após a morte.
native_language_example: Many religions believe in life after death.

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s social activities and interactions (friends, parties, going out, events). Common with verbs like "ter" (to have) and "sair" (to go out): "ter uma vida social". You can also say "minha/sua vida social" (my/your social life).
target_language_example: Eu quase não tenho vida social durante a semana.
native_language_example: I hardly have a social life during the week.

meaning: video game; sometimes also a game console.
additional_notes: In Portuguese, you’ll very often see this written as one word: “videogame”. It can mean the game itself (“um videogame legal”) or, depending on context, the console (“ganhei um videogame”).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de jogar video game no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I like to play video games on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about white wine. In Portuguese it’s literally “white wine” (vinho = wine, branco = white). You may also hear it with an article: “um vinho branco” (a white wine) or “o vinho branco” (the white wine).
target_language_example: Eu queria um copo de vinho branco, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of white wine, please.

additional_notes: Standard term for red wine (wine made from dark grapes). Often used on menus and when ordering drinks. In Portugal and Brazil, you might also see "vinho branco" (white wine) and "vinho rosé" (rosé).
target_language_example: Para mim, um copo de vinho tinto, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Cardinal number used for counting and giving quantities, ages, dates, times, prices, etc. In Portuguese, numbers between 21 and 99 are typically formed with the pattern “tens + e + ones” (e.g., vinte e dois).
target_language_example: Tenho vinte e dois anos.
native_language_example: I am twenty-two years old.

additional_notes: Used for the number 24 in counting, prices, dates, addresses, and time. Often used in time expressions like “vinte e quatro horas” (24 hours).
target_language_example: A loja fica aberta vinte e quatro horas.
native_language_example: The store is open 24 hours.

additional_notes: The number 26. In Portuguese, numbers from 21 to 99 are typically formed as “tens + e + ones” (e.g., vinte e seis = 20 and 6). Used for ages, dates, quantities, prices, etc.
target_language_example: Eu tenho vinte e seis anos.
native_language_example: I am twenty-six years old.

additional_notes: Used to count or give numbers (age, quantity, dates, etc.). In Portuguese, numbers from 21 to 99 are usually formed with “e” (and): e.g., vinte e dois (22), trinta e cinco (35).
target_language_example: Tenho vinte e um anos.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

additional_notes: Used in health/nutrition contexts (food, supplements, immunity). In Portuguese it’s typically written as “vitamina C” (lowercase “vitamina” + the letter).
target_language_example: Eu tomo vitamina C todos os dias.
native_language_example: I take vitamin C every day.

meaning: “See?” / “Did you see that?” (used to call attention or emphasize a point).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese as a conversational tag, often at the end of a sentence to highlight something surprising, to confirm what you just said, or to mean “See, I told you.” It’s informal and usually said as “Viu só?” with a rising intonation.
target_language_example: Eu disse que ia chover, viu só?
native_language_example: I told you it was going to rain—see?

additional_notes: Common fixed expression said after you discover something new or make a mistake—often with a tone of acceptance or mild surprise. It can be used alone as a comment, or after a situation: “Ah, vivendo e aprendendo.”
target_language_example: Achei que a loja abria às oito, mas abre às nove — vivendo e aprendendo.
native_language_example: I thought the store opened at eight, but it opens at nine—live and learn.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun “você” (common in Brazil) with “falar” (to speak) + the language. In conversation it’s often a question: “Você fala português?” (rising intonation or a question mark). As a statement, it means the person speaks Portuguese. In Portugal, people often use “tu falas português?” instead.
target_language_example: Você fala português?
native_language_example: Do you speak Portuguese?

meaning: “Do you love me?” / “You love me.” (depending on intonation).
additional_notes: Literally “you (formal-ish) love me.” In writing it’s usually a statement (“You love me.”). In speech, rising intonation makes it a yes/no question (“Do you love me?”). Common in romantic contexts. Uses "você" (common in Brazil); more intimate/informal alternatives include "tu me amas" (some regions) and "você me ama?" with a question mark to be explicit.
target_language_example: Você me ama?
native_language_example: Do you love me?

additional_notes: Used when you leave the decision to the other person (often neutral, sometimes slightly indifferent depending on tone). Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Can also imply “whatever you think is best.”
target_language_example: A gente vai de ônibus ou de carro? Você que sabe.
native_language_example: Are we going by bus or by car? You decide.

additional_notes: A common conversation starter, especially when flirting (like English “Do you come here often?”). Uses the present tense to ask about someone’s usual habit. “Você” is common in Brazil; in Portugal you might hear “Vens sempre aqui?” (informal) or “O senhor/a senhora vem sempre aqui?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Você vem sempre aqui ou é a primeira vez?
native_language_example: Do you come here often, or is it your first time?

additional_notes: A friendly expression used by shop staff, hosts, or service workers when someone is leaving, inviting them to return. Literally “return always,” but it’s used like “come back soon/anytime.” Often said as “Volte sempre!” or “Volte sempre, viu?”
target_language_example: Obrigado pela visita — volte sempre!
native_language_example: Thanks for coming — come back anytime!

additional_notes: A very formal way to address a royal person (a prince/princess, or sometimes other high-ranking royalty). It’s usually written with capital letters (Vossa Alteza) and used in direct address (often with “Vossa Alteza, …”). In modern everyday Portuguese it’s rare except in ceremonial, historical, or fictional contexts. Related forms: “Sua Alteza” (“His/Her Highness”) when talking about them, not to them.
target_language_example: Vossa Alteza, posso fazer uma pergunta?
native_language_example: Your Highness, may I ask a question?

additional_notes: A very formal way to address a king or queen. Used in direct address (often with a capital M: “Majestade”) and sometimes preceded by a title like “Sua/Vossa Majestade”. In modern everyday Portuguese it’s rare and mostly appears in historical contexts, ceremonies, or fiction.
target_language_example: Vossa Majestade deseja que eu comece a cerimônia?
native_language_example: Does Your Majesty want me to begin the ceremony?

additional_notes: Common way to say you will consider something and decide later. Often implies “not sure yet” or a polite delay. You can add what you’ll think about with “em/nisso”: “Vou pensar nisso.”
target_language_example: Não sei ainda, vou pensar e te aviso.
native_language_example: I don’t know yet; I’ll think about it and let you know.

meaning: A very vulgar way to say “go f*** yourself” / “go to hell.”
additional_notes: Extremely offensive Brazilian Portuguese insult. Used to tell someone off in anger or contempt; not appropriate in polite conversation or with strangers, coworkers, or elders. Literally refers to a sexual act (roughly “go take it up the ass”), which is why it’s so crude.
target_language_example: Ele me xingou, e eu respondi: “Vá tomar no cu!”
native_language_example: He insulted me, and I replied: “Go f*** yourself!”

meaning: video game; videogame (game console/video gaming in general).
additional_notes: Common spelling in Brazil is “videogame” (one word) or “vídeo game” (two words). It can refer to a video game itself (“um videogame”) or to a game console (“um videogame/um vídeo game”). You may also see “jogo de videogame” for a specific game.
target_language_example: Meu irmão ganhou um vídeo game novo no aniversário.
native_language_example: My brother got a new video game console for his birthday.

additional_notes: Used in chess when the king is in check and has no legal moves to escape, meaning the game is over. It can also be used figuratively to mean someone has been defeated or has no way out ("cornered").
target_language_example: Com essa jogada, foi xeque-mate.
native_language_example: With that move, it was checkmate.

meaning: at the edge of; by (the side of).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something located next to a place (often water), or very close to a border/limit. Common in fixed phrases like “à beira-mar” (by the sea) and “à beira da estrada” (by the roadside). Can also be used figuratively as “à beira de” + noun/infinitive to mean “on the verge of” (e.g., “à beira de chorar” = about to cry).
target_language_example: O hotel fica à beira-mar.
native_language_example: The hotel is by the sea.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens without being physically present or close. Very common with work/study/services: "trabalho à distância" (remote work), "aulas à distância" (distance learning). It can also mean physically far away: "vi de longe / à distância" (I saw it from afar).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho à distância três dias por semana.
native_language_example: I work remotely three days a week.

meaning: by force; forcibly; by sheer effort (in the end).
additional_notes: Commonly means doing something against someone’s will or using force (physical or figurative): "tirar à força" (to pull/remove by force), "obrigar à força" (to force). It can also mean achieving something only through persistence/effort, often implying difficulty: "Consegui à força" (I managed, but only with a lot of effort).
target_language_example: Ele entrou à força, mesmo com a porta trancada.
native_language_example: He forced his way in, even though the door was locked.

additional_notes: Commonly indicates position or direction. Use it for location (“à frente de” = “in front of”) or for something coming next (“mais à frente” = “later on / further ahead”). It can also be used in giving directions (“Siga em frente” = “Go straight ahead”).
target_language_example: O banco fica à frente da farmácia.
native_language_example: The bank is in front of the pharmacy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or context that affects a decision or opinion. Common in more formal writing and speech. Often followed by a noun or situation: “à luz de novas informações” (“in light of new information”).
target_language_example: À luz de novas informações, vamos mudar o plano.
native_language_example: In light of new information, we’re going to change the plan.

additional_notes: Used to show that one thing happens gradually in proportion to another: “as/while X happens, Y happens/changes.” Very common with verbs in the present tense for general statements (À medida que o tempo passa...) and with the imperfect in the past (À medida que eu crescia...). Similar to “conforme,” but emphasizes a progressive change over time.
target_language_example: À medida que o dia avança, fica mais quente.
native_language_example: As the day goes on, it gets hotter.

additional_notes: Commonly means something is done manually, without a machine ("fazer à mão"). It can also mean something is readily available/within reach ("ter ... à mão"). Usually appears after the noun/verb it modifies.
target_language_example: Prefiro fazer o molho à mão e manter uma caneta à mão.
native_language_example: I prefer to make the sauce by hand and keep a pen on hand.

meaning: at night; in the evening (after it gets dark).
additional_notes: Common time expression used to say when something happens. Often contrasts with de manhã (in the morning), à tarde (in the afternoon), and de dia (during the day). You can use it with verbs like trabalhar, sair, estudar, dormir, etc.
target_language_example: Eu estudo à noite.
native_language_example: I study at night.

additional_notes: Common uses: (1) "deixar/colocar à parte" = to set aside; (2) "à parte" meaning separately/individually (not together): "pagamos à parte" = we pay separately; (3) "à parte (isso)" = apart from that / besides that. Also used like an aside: "À parte isso, tudo bem."
target_language_example: À parte isso, o resto está tudo bem.
native_language_example: Apart from that, everything else is fine.

meaning: at first; in principle; from the outset.
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese. Used to give an initial assumption or starting point (often meaning “as things stand” or “in theory”), which can be contrasted with what happens later (e.g., “à partida... mas depois...” = “at first/in principle... but then...” ).
target_language_example: À partida, parece uma boa ideia, mas temos de ver o custo.
native_language_example: At first/in principle, it seems like a good idea, but we have to see the cost.

meaning: at first sight; at first glance.
additional_notes: Used to describe a first impression or initial judgment, before thinking more carefully or learning more information. Often appears with verbs like "parecer" (to seem) or "achar" (to think).
target_language_example: À primeira vista, parece fácil, mas é mais complicado do que eu pensava.
native_language_example: At first glance, it seems easy, but it’s more complicated than I thought.

meaning: aimlessly; for no reason; idle/doing nothing.
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Use it to describe someone who is wandering without a plan ("andar à toa") or not doing anything productive ("ficar à toa"). It can also mean "for nothing/in vain" in some contexts ("falar à toa" = to talk nonsense / to talk for no reason).
target_language_example: No domingo, eu fiquei à toa em casa e depois andei à toa pelo bairro.
native_language_example: On Sunday, I lazed around at home and then wandered around the neighborhood with no plan.

meaning: for sale; on sale (available to buy).
additional_notes: Used to say something is being offered for purchase. Common on signs, in ads, and online listings (e.g., "Casa à venda"). It can also be used for tickets/products ("Ingressos à venda"). Often translates as "for sale" rather than "on sale" (discount).
target_language_example: Este carro está à venda.
native_language_example: This car is for sale.

additional_notes: Common in two main uses: (1) Payment terms: "pagamento à vista" means you pay the full amount right away (often in cash or immediate transfer), as opposed to paying in installments ("a prazo", "parcelado"). (2) Seeing/recognition: in expressions like "reconhecer à vista" (“recognize on sight”).
target_language_example: Posso pagar à vista ou parcelado no cartão?
native_language_example: Can I pay in full right away or in installments on the card?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they’re welcome to relax or to do something without hesitation (like taking a seat, asking questions, serving themselves, etc.). Also used to say you yourself feel comfortable in a place: "Estou à vontade." Often appears in the expression "Fique à vontade" (singular) / "Fiquem à vontade" (plural).
target_language_example: Fique à vontade para se sentar e fazer perguntas.
native_language_example: Feel free to sit down and ask questions.

additional_notes: Common adverb meaning something happens occasionally (not always). Often used at the beginning or middle of a sentence. It’s close in meaning to “de vez em quando” (“from time to time”).
target_language_example: Às vezes eu trabalho até tarde.
native_language_example: Sometimes I work late.

additional_notes: Used for water at a low temperature (e.g., from the tap or in a drink). Often contrasted with “água quente” (hot water) and “água morna” (lukewarm water). In Brazil you may also see it as “Água Fria” in place names (e.g., a neighborhood or city).
target_language_example: Prefiro tomar banho com água fria no verão.
native_language_example: I prefer to shower with cold water in the summer.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for water that comes from a faucet. Often used when asking if it’s safe to drink or when ordering water (in some places you might hear “água do cano” too).
target_language_example: Aqui é seguro beber água da torneira?
native_language_example: Is it safe to drink tap water here?

meaning: mineral water (bottled water, usually still or sparkling).
additional_notes: Common in restaurants and shops when ordering bottled water. You may hear "água mineral sem gás" (still) or "água mineral com gás" (sparkling). Often contrasted with "água da torneira" (tap water).
target_language_example: Queria uma água mineral sem gás, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a still mineral water, please.

additional_notes: A common noun for the sea animal. It’s usually feminine: a água-viva / as águas-vivas. Often used at the beach when warning about stings (queimar/picar).
target_language_example: Cuidado: tem água-viva na água!
native_language_example: Careful: there are jellyfish in the water!

additional_notes: Used for the decorated tree (real or artificial) people put up at Christmas. Often appears with verbs like "montar" (to put up/set up) and "decorar" (to decorate): "montar a árvore de Natal", "decorar a árvore de Natal".
target_language_example: Vamos montar a árvore de Natal neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: Let’s put up the Christmas tree this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to express resignation/acceptance when something unpleasant or disappointing happens (similar to “oh well”). Often said after a small setback or to show that things can’t be changed. Literally “it is the life,” but in English you’d normally say “that’s life.”
target_language_example: Perdi o autocarro… é a vida.
native_language_example: I missed the bus… that’s life.

additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) to say something is positive or desirable: "É bom que você esteja aqui" = "It’s good that you’re here." (2) very commonly, to warn or insist on something, similar to "you’d better" (can sound firm or slightly threatening depending on tone): "É bom que você chegue na hora" = "You’d better arrive on time." Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "venha", "chegue", "faça").
target_language_example: É bom que você chegue cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: You’d better arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common, informal-sounding conversational phrase used to agree, confirm, or wrap something up. Often said after someone explains something (“Exactly”), or to conclude a decision (“That’s it then”). Also used as encouragement/approval (“You got it”). In speech it’s frequently shortened to “isso aí!” or “é isso!”
target_language_example: —Então a gente se encontra às 7, na entrada. —É isso aí!
native_language_example: —So we’ll meet at 7, at the entrance. —That’s right!

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used to say something is very easy, or sarcastically to mean the opposite (that something is hard/annoying): “É mole?” can mean “You’ve got to be kidding!” It’s informal. Literally it means “it’s soft,” but that’s not the intended meaning in most everyday uses.
target_language_example: Ele acha que vai passar na prova sem estudar? É mole!
native_language_example: He thinks he’s going to pass the test without studying? Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Used to express acceptance or resignation about a situation that can’t be changed. Often said after something disappointing or inconvenient, meaning “that’s just how things are.”
target_language_example: O voo foi cancelado, é o que é.
native_language_example: The flight was canceled; it is what it is.

additional_notes: Common on signs in public places (restaurants, airports, buildings). Literally “it is prohibited to smoke.” Often appears as just “Proibido fumar.”
target_language_example: Aqui é proibido fumar.
native_language_example: Smoking is prohibited here.

meaning: a particle used to add emphasis in questions, or to introduce an explanation (“it’s that…/it’s because…”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Portuguese. In questions it often appears after a question word without changing the basic meaning: “Onde é que…?” / “O que é que…?” (roughly “Where is it that…?” → simply “Where…?”). It can also start an explanation or excuse: “É que eu…” = “It’s that… / The thing is… / It’s because…”.
target_language_example: Onde é que fica a estação?
native_language_example: Where is the station?

additional_notes: Used for protective glasses worn to block sunlight. Singular: "óculos de sol" (usually treated as plural in Portuguese, like in English). You can also say "uns óculos de sol" (some sunglasses) or "meus óculos de sol" (my sunglasses).
target_language_example: Esqueci meus óculos de sol em casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my sunglasses at home.

additional_notes: Literally “dark glasses.” Used for sunglasses in general. You’ll often see it without an article (e.g., in shopping lists) or with an article: “os óculos escuros.”
target_language_example: Não esquece os óculos escuros; vai fazer muito sol.
native_language_example: Don’t forget the sunglasses; it’s going to be very sunny.
